Vision–Language–Action Systems

A senior engineer's field manual: the mathematics, the architectures, the sensor stack, and the deployment reality — with a very deep treatment of multimodal input encoding.

Revision 1 · drafted 11 September 2026 · centred on bimanual dexterous manipulation
Every quantitative claim is attributed to a named source. Claims that are arguments rather than published results are explicitly labelled as such.

§0How to read this

This manual is organised for two different reading modes, and both are worth using.

Linear, once. Parts I–II build the mathematics of action generation from behavioural cloning up to flow-matching action experts. Part III — the longest by a wide margin — is the multimodal core: how you actually turn a point cloud, a six-axis wrench, a fingertip deformation map, a contact microphone, or an event stream into tokens a policy can use, and how those tokens coexist with 256 visual tokens per camera without being crushed. Part IV takes four complete systems — T-Rex, π0\pi_0π0​ and π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​, RDT-1B, and OpenVLA — and reads each one backwards from its deployment constraint to its architecture, with the tensor shapes stated explicitly. Part V is deployment. Part VI covers world models, reinforcement learning, and uncertainty. Part VII is reference: worked system designs, a question bank to test yourself against, and the paper map.

Concepts first, papers second. Each idea is introduced on its own terms — what problem it solves, what it costs — before any paper is named. The papers then appear as evidence: this group tried it, at this scale, and this is what happened. Where two papers made opposite choices, both are given, because in most of this field the literature has not converged and a confident synthesis would be a fabrication.

Non-linear, repeatedly. Every chapter opens with a Core ideas box that states the chapter's content in a few sentences, and closes with Key takeaways that compress it again. Tables and figures are designed to be re-read cold. If you have one hour to refresh the whole field, read only those boxes plus Chapter 20.

Tensor shapes are given in (batch, ...) order throughout and match the executed code in the companion code/ directory. Every PyTorch listing in this document was run on real tensors before being printed here; the shapes and numbers in the prose are the shapes and numbers the code actually produced.

A warning about flow-matching sign conventions

The two most important papers in this manual use opposite conventions for which end of the flow trajectory is noise. π0\pi_0π0​ takes x0∼N(0,I)x_0\sim\mathcal N(0,I)x0​∼N(0,I) as noise and integrates t:0→1t:0\to1t:0→1 toward the action. T-Rex takes x0=Ademox_0=\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{demo}}x0​=Ademo as the clean action, x1=ϵx_1=\boldsymbol\epsilonx1​=ϵ as noise, and integrates τ:1→0\tau:1\to0τ:1→0. Both are correct; they differ only in the direction you traverse the same straight line. Getting this backwards — in an explanation or in code — inverts your velocity target and the model learns nothing. Chapter 3 states both explicitly and Chapter 9 uses the T-Rex convention because that is what the paper uses.

0.2On verification

Robotics moves fast enough that a guide written from memory is a liability. Every architectural detail, hyperparameter, and success rate in this manual was taken from the primary source, and the source is linked at the point of claim. Three categories are marked explicitly:

  • Published result — a number or mechanism stated in a paper, with a link.
  • Argument — a derivation or back-of-envelope model that follows from stated premises but is not itself an empirical finding. The attention-mass model of modality drowning in Chapter 8 is the most important example.
  • Company communication — blog-post-level claims from industrial labs (Generalist AI's GEN-0/GEN-1, Physical Intelligence blog posts) that are directionally informative but not peer-reviewed or reproducible. Flagged wherever used.
Part I

Foundations of Action Generation

Why imitation dominates manipulation, what breaks when you use it naively, and the generative machinery that fixes the breakage.

1Imitation learning and its two structural failures

Core ideas

Behavioural cloning is supervised learning on expert demonstrations. It fails in two structurally different ways that people constantly conflate. Covariate shift is a distribution problem: small errors take the robot somewhere the expert never went, and errors compound quadratically in the horizon. Multimodality is a target problem: several actions are equally correct, and a unimodal regression head averages them into an action that is wrong. Covariate shift is attacked by changing where your data comes from (DAgger) or by making fewer decisions per episode (action chunking). Multimodality is attacked by changing the head (generative models). Neither fix addresses the other problem.

1.1Why imitation, and not reinforcement learning

The honest answer is not that imitation learning produces better policies. Asymptotically it does not: a policy trained on demonstrations is bounded by the demonstrator, while reinforcement learning is bounded only by the reward. Imitation dominates contact-rich manipulation for three practical reasons.

Reward design for contact is brutal. Write down a dense reward for "insert the key and turn it" that does not admit a degenerate solution involving jamming the key sideways with maximum force. You cannot easily. The tasks where RL shines — locomotion, games — have rewards that are either given by the environment or expressible as a simple functional of state. Manipulation rewards are a research problem in themselves.

Real-robot exploration is expensive and unsafe. A dexterous hand exploring randomly against a rigid environment destroys itself and the objects. Simulation helps but the sim-to-real gap for contact and deformation is precisely where it is widest — the friction, compliance, and deformation models that matter most for manipulation are the ones simulators approximate worst.

Demonstrations are comparatively cheap. A teleoperator with a decent interface produces tens of demonstrations per hour. T-Rex's dataset is 7,755 episodes and 100 hours collected by teleoperators over ten weeks[T-Rex, App. G]. That is a large but entirely tractable industrial effort; the equivalent in real-robot RL is not.

So the field's structure is: imitate to get a competent policy, then use reinforcement learning as a post-training stage to exceed the demonstrator (Chapter 17). The interesting engineering is almost entirely in making the imitation stage work.

1.2Behavioural cloning and compounding error

Behavioural cloning fits πθ(a∣o)\pi_\theta(\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{o})πθ​(a∣o) by maximum likelihood on pairs drawn from the expert's state distribution dπ⋆d_{\pi^\star}dπ⋆​. The moment you run the learned policy, the state distribution becomes dπθd_{\pi_\theta}dπθ​​, and the training guarantee — which was about dπ⋆d_{\pi^\star}dπ⋆​ — no longer applies.

The classic result makes the damage precise. If the policy's expected per-step classification error under the expert's distribution is ϵ\epsilonϵ, then over a horizon TTT:

J(πθ)−J(π⋆)  ≤  O ⁣(ϵT2)J(\pi_\theta) - J(\pi^\star) \;\le\; \mathcal{O}\!\left(\epsilon T^2\right)J(πθ​)−J(π⋆)≤O(ϵT2)
(1.1)

The intuition behind the square is the part worth carrying: the quadratic comes from the part most often quoted and least often justified. One factor of TTT is the obvious one: you pay an error at each of TTT steps. The second factor of TTT is that once you make a mistake at step ttt, you are off-distribution for all remaining T−tT-tT−t steps, and the guarantee ϵ\epsilonϵ says nothing about your error rate there — the worst case is that you are wrong at every subsequent step. Summing T−tT-tT−t over ttt gives T2/2T^2/2T2/2.

DAgger[Ross et al. 2011] removes the second factor by making training distribution equal deployment distribution: roll out the current learner, ask the expert to label the states the learner actually visits, aggregate into the dataset, retrain, repeat. The bound becomes

J(πθ)−J(π⋆)  ≤  O ⁣(ϵT)J(\pi_\theta) - J(\pi^\star) \;\le\; \mathcal{O}\!\left(\epsilon T\right)J(πθ​)−J(π⋆)≤O(ϵT)
(1.2)

The essential point, and the one most often missed: DAgger's win is distributional, not architectural. It does not make the network better at any fixed state. It makes the set of states you trained on match the set of states you encounter. Anything else that achieves that alignment — on-policy corrections, expert interventions during autonomous rollouts — buys the same thing. Physical Intelligence's RECAP recipe for π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ makes exactly this move, combining demonstrations, real-time expert corrections when the robot errs, and autonomous experience[π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​].

DAgger's cost is that it needs an expert available online, which for a dexterous teleoperation rig means a human in a glove-and-tracker setup for the whole training loop. That is why the practical literature moved toward robot-gated variants that only interrupt the human when the policy's own uncertainty is high (Chapter 18).

1.3Multimodality: the failure that more data cannot fix

Suppose an obstacle sits directly ahead and the demonstrations go around it — half to the left, half to the right. Both are correct. A network trained with mean-squared error on this data does not learn "left or right". It learns the conditional mean.

arg⁡min⁡a^ E ⁣[∥a^−a∥22∣o]=E[a∣o],arg⁡min⁡a^ E ⁣[∥a^−a∥1∣o]=median(a∣o)\arg\min_{\hat{a}}\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat a - a\|_2^2 \mid \mathbf{o}\right] = \mathbb{E}[a\mid\mathbf{o}], \qquad \arg\min_{\hat{a}}\ \mathbb{E}\!\left[\|\hat a - a\|_1 \mid \mathbf{o}\right] = \mathrm{median}(a\mid\mathbf{o})arga^min​ E[∥a^−a∥22​∣o]=E[a∣o],arga^min​ E[∥a^−a∥1​∣o]=median(a∣o)
(1.3)

For a symmetric two-mode distribution the mean sits exactly between the modes — straight into the obstacle. The L1L_1L1​ median is better behaved (it picks a mode for asymmetric distributions rather than interpolating) which is part of why L1L_1L1​ regression heads work surprisingly well in practice, but it still collapses on symmetric bimodality.

This is aleatoric uncertainty: it is a property of the data-generating process, not of your model's ignorance. Collecting ten times more demonstrations does not reduce it; it estimates the same bimodal distribution more precisely, and the mean of a more precisely estimated bimodal distribution is still in the middle. This is the single cleanest argument for why generative action heads replaced Gaussian regression heads, and it compresses to one sentence: more data shrinks epistemic error, but multimodality is aleatoric, so no amount of data removes the incentive for a unimodal head to average.

1.4Action chunking

Instead of predicting at\mathbf{a}_tat​, predict the whole sequence At:t+H\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H}At:t+H​ and execute some or all of it open-loop. This one change buys three distinct things.

It divides the compounding-error horizon. The policy now makes T/HT/HT/H decisions per episode instead of TTT. Substituting into (1.1), the quadratic term becomes O(ϵ(T/H)2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon (T/H)^2)O(ϵ(T/H)2) in the number of policy decisions. This is a real reduction, not a reparameterisation, because the errors that compound are the ones introduced at decision boundaries.

It removes temporal multimodality. The "go left or right" ambiguity is largely a question about the trajectory, not about the instantaneous velocity. A per-step policy can sample "left" at step ttt and "right" at step t+1t+1t+1, producing incoherent dithering. A chunk commits to one coherent sub-trajectory.

It models non-Markovian demonstrations. Human teleoperators pause, hesitate, and produce oscillatory corrections. These are not functions of the current state, so a Markovian per-step policy cannot represent them; a chunk can.

The trap

Chunking does not remove chunk-level multimodality. If two entire sub-trajectories are both valid, an L2L_2L2​ head will still average them. You need chunking and a generative head; they solve different halves of the problem. The second trap is that longer is not better: an over-long chunk executes blind for too long and cannot react. This is the central tension that Chapter 14 (deployment) and Chapter 9 (T-Rex's asynchronous refinement) exist to resolve.

A third, subtler failure: near-zero actions are a low-loss attractor. Demonstrations contain pauses; a chunk of zeros has low error on those segments and is never catastrophically wrong elsewhere. Policies that are under-trained or trained on pause-heavy data will freeze. Shorter chunks and rebalancing the demonstration mix help.

1.5Absorbing the residual mode: chunking with a latent variable

Chunking removes the timestep-to-timestep ambiguity of §1.4 but not all of it. Two demonstrators can take genuinely different routes through the whole chunk, and averaging those is as invalid as averaging two single actions. That leaves a choice. Either the head is generative, which is Chapter 3, or the ambiguity is pushed into an explicit latent variable that the decoder is conditioned on: at training time the latent is inferred from the demonstration, so the decoder's job becomes deterministic given it, and at test time the latent is fixed and the decoder emits one coherent style rather than a blend. That is a conditional variational autoencoder, and it is the cheaper of the two answers.

ACT (Action Chunking with Transformers)[Zhao et al. 2023] is the architecture that made chunking standard, and it remains the backbone of tactile-dexterous baselines — ViTacFormer is explicitly ACT-style[ViTacFormer]. It is a transformer encoder–decoder that emits HHH actions in one forward pass, wrapped in a conditional variational autoencoder.

The CVAE is the part worth understanding. During training, an encoder sees the ground-truth action sequence plus proprioception and compresses it into a latent "style" variable zzz. The decoder then reconstructs the actions from observations and zzz. Because zzz carries the information about which of several valid executions this demonstration was, the decoder no longer has to average — the ambiguity has been explained away by a variable it is given. At inference zzz is set to zero (the prior mean), which selects a canonical, "average-style" execution.

LACT=∥At:t+H−A^t:t+H∥1⏟reconstruction  +  β DKL ⁣(qϕ(z∣A,q) ∥ N(0,I))⏟style regulariser\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ACT}} = \underbrace{\big\|\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H} - \hat{\mathbf{A}}_{t:t+H}\big\|_1}_{\text{reconstruction}} \;+\; \beta\, \underbrace{D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(q_\phi(z\mid \mathbf{A},\mathbf{q}) \,\|\, \mathcal{N}(0,I)\big)}_{\text{style regulariser}}LACT​=reconstruction​At:t+H​−A^t:t+H​​1​​​+βstyle regulariserDKL​(qϕ​(z∣A,q)∥N(0,I))​​
(1.4)

ACT also introduced temporal ensembling: run the policy every step, so that at time ttt you hold several overlapping chunk predictions made at t,t−1,t−2,…t, t-1, t-2,\dotst,t−1,t−2,…, and average them with exponentially decaying weights. This smooths the executed trajectory and is a genuinely useful trick — but note it is an averaging operation, so it reintroduces exactly the mode collapse that chunking was meant to avoid, whenever overlapping chunks disagree about which mode to take. Real-Time Chunking (§14.4) is the modern replacement that keeps the smoothness without the averaging.

Key takeaways
  1. Imitation dominates manipulation for practical reasons (reward design, safety, data cost), not because it has a higher ceiling. It does not.
  2. Covariate shift gives O(ϵT2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T^2)O(ϵT2); DAgger's on-policy relabelling gives O(ϵT)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T)O(ϵT). The win is distributional, not architectural.
  3. Multimodality is aleatoric. L2L_2L2​ gives the conditional mean, L1L_1L1​ the median; both fail on symmetric bimodality. No quantity of data fixes this — only a different head does.
  4. Action chunking cuts the number of compounding decisions from TTT to T/HT/HT/H and kills temporal multimodality, but not chunk-level multimodality. You need both chunking and a generative head.
  5. ACT's CVAE explains away demonstration style with a latent zzz; temporal ensembling smooths output but re-averages modes, which is why RTC superseded it.

2Action representation for dexterous bimanual systems

Core ideas

The action space is the first design decision and the one you cannot cheaply change later. Three axes matter: joint versus end-effector (feasibility versus transferability), delta versus absolute (invariance versus drift), and how you parameterise rotation. For dexterous hands a fourth appears: arms and fingers want different conventions, and modern systems use both simultaneously. Rotation deserves genuine care — SO(3)SO(3)SO(3) has no continuous embedding in fewer than five dimensions, so Euler angles and quaternions are both actively harmful as regression targets, and the 6D Gram–Schmidt parameterisation is the standard fix.

2.1Joint space versus end-effector space

The trade is exact and worth stating crisply.

Table 2.1 — Action space trade-offs. Real systems mix them.
PropertyJoint anglesEnd-effector SE(3)SE(3)SE(3)
Feasibility at executionAlways achievable — the command is the joint targetNeeds inverse kinematics; can fail at singularities or outside the reachable set
Cross-embodiment transferPoor — joint indices and limits are robot-specificGood — the pose of a hand in space is embodiment-agnostic
Null-space / redundancyExplicitly controlledLeft to the IK solver, which may pick different elbow configurations frame to frame
Learning from human videoRequires retargetingNatural — human wrist poses are already SE(3)SE(3)SE(3)

The cross-embodiment argument is the reason large pretrained VLAs favour end-effector actions. EgoScale pretrains on 20,854 hours of egocentric human video by retargeting human wrist motion and hand poses into a unified action space, and reports that the resulting motor prior transfers to robots with lower-DoF hands than the one it was tuned for[EgoScale]. That only works because the representation is not tied to a specific kinematic chain.

The dexterous resolution is to use both. T-Rex uses relative end-effector delta control for the bimanual arms and absolute joint control for the fingers[T-Rex, §5.1]. This is not a compromise; it is the right answer for a specific reason. The arm's job is to place the hand somewhere in the world, which is a spatial, transferable, scene-relative quantity — deltas in SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) are the natural encoding. The fingers' job is to attain a configuration, and finger IK is both ill-conditioned (many contacts, tight workspace) and pointless to abstract, since finger joint targets are what the low-level controller wants anyway. Executing this requires differential inverse kinematics on the arm side only; T-Rex uses Pink/Pinocchio, filters the resulting joint commands through a low-pass filter, and hands them to a 300 Hz cascaded PID (proportional–integral–derivative) loop.

The resulting action vector for a bimanual 22-DoF-per-hand system is 62-dimensional. It is worth unpacking where that comes from, because an unaccounted dimension is the commonest silent bug in a bimanual action spec:

Table 2.2 — Reconstructing T-Rex's 62-dimensional action vector. The arm term uses a 6D rotation plus 3D translation per wrist; finger joints are absolute.
ComponentPer sideBoth sides
Wrist translation delta36
Wrist rotation delta (6D)612
Hand joint targets (Sharpa Wave, 22 DoF)2244
Total3162

Note how strongly the hand dominates: 44 of 62 dimensions, roughly 71%, are fingers. This single ratio explains a great deal about dexterous VLAs. It is why π0\pi_0π0​'s fixed 32-dimensional padded action space is inadequate for this class of robot, why retargeting quality dominates data quality, and why per-finger tactile sensing is worth its complexity — you have 44 dimensions of actuation whose consequences are almost entirely invisible to a head camera.

2.2Delta versus absolute

Predict deltas for the arm. An absolute SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) target is expressed in some fixed base frame, so a policy that learns "move the hand to (0.4,0.1,0.3)(0.4, 0.1, 0.3)(0.4,0.1,0.3)" has memorised a workspace layout and breaks the moment the table moves. A delta — "move 2 cm along the current approach direction" — is invariant to where the scene sits, so the same skill generalises across layouts.

The cost of deltas is integration drift. Errors accumulate in the integrated pose because nothing pins the absolute position. Two standard mitigations: include the current absolute pose in the observation (so the policy can correct, even though it outputs deltas), and keep the control loop closed at a rate fast enough that visual feedback re-anchors the estimate. For the fingers the same logic inverts — absolute joint targets have no drift and the "layout" a finger configuration refers to is the hand itself, which never moves relative to the fingers.

2.3Rotation: the classic trap

This is the single most reliable technical trap in manipulation, so it is worth understanding the topology rather than memorising the answer.

SO(3)SO(3)SO(3), the group of 3D rotations, is topologically the real projective space RP3\mathbb{RP}^3RP3. A continuous, injective map from SO(3)SO(3)SO(3) into Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd that is also invertible by a continuous function — which is what a regression head needs, since the network outputs a point in Rd\mathbb{R}^dRd and something must turn it back into a rotation — does not exist for d<5d < 5d<5[Zhou et al. 2019]. The practical consequence is that any 3- or 4-parameter representation has discontinuities, and at those discontinuities the regression target jumps while the underlying rotation moves smoothly. The network is asked to fit a discontinuous function and produces artefacts near the seam.

Table 2.3 — Rotation parameterisations. The right-hand column is what actually goes wrong during training, which is the part that matters in practice.
RepresentationDimFailure mode as a regression target
Euler angles3Gimbal lock (loses a DoF at ±90°\pm90°±90°); wraps discontinuously at ±π\pm\pi±π, so a tiny physical rotation can demand a 2π2\pi2π jump in the target
Axis–angle3Discontinuous at π\piπ; the zero rotation is a singular point where the axis is undefined
Quaternion4Double cover: qqq and −q-q−q are the same rotation, so the training target is ambiguous. Two identical demonstrations can carry opposite-sign labels and the network regresses toward zero
6D (Gram–Schmidt)6None. Continuous, differentiable, always maps to a valid rotation
Rotation matrix9Valid but over-parameterised; the network must learn orthonormality it is never structurally guaranteed
Discretised bins—Fine for classification heads (used by token-based VLAs); resolution is capped by bin count

The 6D representation works by having the network emit two arbitrary 3-vectors and then constructing a valid rotation from them by Gram–Schmidt: normalise the first to get column one, orthogonalise and normalise the second against it to get column two, and take the cross product for column three. Every point in R6\mathbb{R}^6R6 (except the measure-zero set where the two vectors are parallel) maps continuously to a valid rotation, and the map is differentiable, so gradients flow.

"Why 6D and not 5D, if 5 is the theoretical minimum?"

Because the theorem is an existence result about continuous embeddings, not a construction. It guarantees some continuous 5-dimensional embedding of RP3\mathbb{RP}^3RP3 exists; it does not hand you a smooth, surjective, cheaply-computable map from a raw 5-tuple back to SO(3)SO(3)SO(3). Gram–Schmidt on two 3-vectors is exactly that, in six dimensions, in four lines of code. The extra dimension buys an enormous simplification and costs nothing.

def rot6d_to_matrix(d6):
    """(..., 6) -> (..., 3, 3). Gram-Schmidt on the first two columns (Zhou et al. 2019)."""
    a1, a2 = d6[..., :3], d6[..., 3:]
    b1 = F.normalize(a1, dim=-1)
    b2 = F.normalize(a2 - (b1 * a2).sum(-1, keepdim=True) * b1, dim=-1)
    b3 = torch.cross(b1, b2, dim=-1)
    return torch.stack((b1, b2, b3), dim=-2)

def matrix_to_rot6d(R):
    return R[..., :2, :].flatten(start_dim=-2)      # the third column is redundant

Executed on random inputs this gives orthonormality error 1.9×10−71.9\times10^{-7}1.9×10−7, determinant exactly +1.0000+1.0000+1.0000, and round-trip error 1.8×10−71.8\times10^{-7}1.8×10−7 — i.e. it is exact to float32. Note that matrix_to_rot6d simply drops the third row: it is recoverable by cross product, which is why the representation is 6 and not 9 numbers.

See also — Appendix D

Everything above is about the absolute orientation a network emits. The companion question — how a stream of measured poses becomes the delta targets of §2.2 in the first place, and how you average, interpolate or add noise to poses without leaving the group — is the exponential and logarithm pair between SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) and its Lie algebra se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3). That is standard material rather than a finding of any paper here, so it sits out of the main line in Appendix D: Rodrigues' formula and the SO(3)SO(3)SO(3) logarithm, twists and screws, the body-frame versus base-frame trap, geodesic averaging for temporal ensembling, and an interactive figure that computes all of it live. The one-line summary to carry forward is that absolute orientations get 6D + Gram–Schmidt; relative orientations get se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) twists, and the appendix explains why those two answers are consistent.

2.4Normalisation

First, what is being normalised. The subject is the action vector the head regresses — the 62 numbers of Table 2.2 — and, separately and with its own statistics, the proprioceptive observation vector fed to the state encoder. Images are not included: they have their own preprocessing. Neither are language tokens, nor the tactile and force streams, which need per-sensor treatment for reasons specific to them (§13.3). And the normalisation is per dimension: the index iii in equation (2.1) runs over the 62 action channels one at a time, and the two quantiles q1(i)q_1^{(i)}q1(i)​ and q99(i)q_{99}^{(i)}q99(i)​ are computed once, over every timestep of every episode in the training set, then frozen and shipped with the checkpoint.

Given that, the choice of statistic. Action dimensions arrive in wildly different units — metres, radians, newtons — and teleoperation data contains spikes. Min–max normalisation is the wrong default because a single tracker glitch at 500 units compresses the entire useful signal range into a sliver near zero. Quantile normalisation maps the 1st and 99th percentile to [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] and clips.

a~(i)=clip ⁣(2 a(i)−q1(i)q99(i)−q1(i)−1,  −1,  1)\tilde a^{(i)} = \mathrm{clip}\!\left(2\,\frac{a^{(i)} - q_{1}^{(i)}}{q_{99}^{(i)} - q_{1}^{(i)}} - 1,\; -1,\; 1\right)a~(i)=clip(2q99(i)​−q1(i)​a(i)−q1(i)​​−1,−1,1)
(2.1)

But not every channel should go through it, and the 62-dimensional vector is a good illustration because it contains three kinds of quantity with three different answers.

Table 2.4 — What to do with each block of the 62-dimensional action vector. The question to ask of a channel is not "what are its units" but "is its scale set by the data or by a construction".
BlockDimsTreatmentWhy
Wrist translation delta6Quantile-normalise, per axisMetres, heavy-tailed, and the three axes genuinely differ in typical travel. Exactly what equation (2.1) is for
Wrist rotation delta (6D)12Leave aloneAlready bounded in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] and O(1)\mathcal{O}(1)O(1) by construction, not by accident of the data. Rescaling per entry costs accuracy for nothing — see below
Hand joint targets44Quantile-normalise, per jointRadians, but joint ranges differ by more than an order of magnitude between a thumb abduction and a distal flexion. One shared scale would let the widest joint set the resolution for all 44
(if present) gripper open/close1Leave aloneA two-valued channel has no meaningful 1st and 99th percentile. Map it to {−1,+1}\{-1,+1\}{−1,+1} by hand

Three rules that are easy to get wrong:

  • Compute statistics per dimension, never pooled across dimensions. A single global scalar pair for all 62 channels lets the 44 finger dimensions set the scale for the 6 translation dimensions, and the arm stops moving.
  • Compute statistics globally over the dataset, not per timestep within a chunk. Rescaling each timestep independently injects artificial jitter and destroys the temporal smoothness that makes a chunk compressible (and that FAST tokenisation, §3.4, depends on).
  • Compute statistics on your data when fine-tuning. Inheriting the base model's normalisation statistics is a silent, common bug: your actions land in a narrow band of the model's expected range and the policy outputs tiny motions. The mirror-image bug is forgetting to invert equation (2.1) on the way out — the policy predicts in normalised units and the controller expects metres and radians.

The rotation row deserves the argument spelled out, because the usual one-line justification is wrong. Quantile-normalising the 6D channel does not produce invalid rotations: Gram–Schmidt always returns a valid rotation matrix, which is the whole point of the representation (§2.3) — over the 20,000-sample simulation in code/f_norm6d.py the determinant stays at 111 to 7×10−167\times10^{-16}7×10−16. The damage is subtler and therefore worse. In that simulation — small wrist deltas of about 0.040.040.04 rad with 2%2\%2% teleoperation jerks at 0.350.350.35 rad — the per-entry 1st/99th percentiles span only 0.0460.0460.046 for the two near-diagonal entries and 0.0800.0800.080 for the four off-diagonal ones, so the six channels get affine rescalings differing by nearly a factor of two, and an L1L_1L1​ loss over them no longer weighs the six numbers the way the rotation geometry does. Worse, 4.2%4.2\%4.2% of samples are clipped in at least one entry, and those land a mean 8.2°8.2°8.2° and up to 17.7°17.7°17.7° away from the rotation they were supposed to encode — a large error, in a perfectly valid rotation matrix, with nothing anywhere to flag it. The general principle is the one in the table caption: normalise what the data scaled, leave alone what a construction scaled.

2.5Retargeting: the step that quietly determines data quality

For dexterous systems there is a stage between "human moved" and "robot action" that does not exist for parallel grippers, and it is where a large fraction of real-world data quality is won or lost. T-Rex's teleoperation stack reads wrist SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) poses from VIVE trackers and fingertip positions relative to the hand base from Manus gloves, then retargets fingertips to the Sharpa Wave hand using differential IK built on Pinocchio and CasADi[T-Rex, App. D]. ViTacFormer instead uses a mechanically-coupled exoskeleton glove, which sidesteps retargeting entirely by making the human's finger joints drive the robot's directly[ViTacFormer].

The trade is instructive. Optical and IMU (inertial measurement unit) gloves are comfortable and fast to collect with, but retargeting is a lossy, human-hand-to-robot-hand mapping that introduces systematic error — and crucially, it introduces error in the fingertip contact geometry, which is precisely the quantity a tactile policy needs to be accurate. An exoskeleton is uncomfortable and embodiment- specific but has no retargeting gap. T-Rex's own failure analysis names this: several failures are attributed to "the data distribution of the teleoperated data" and to insufficient fine-grained finger dexterity.

Key takeaways
  1. Joint space is always feasible but embodiment-specific; end-effector space transfers but needs IK. Dexterous systems use both: relative SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) deltas for arms, absolute joint targets for fingers.
  2. Fingers are ~71% of a bimanual dexterous action vector (44 of 62). That ratio is why retargeting quality and per-finger sensing matter so much.
  3. SO(3)=RP3SO(3)=\mathbb{RP}^3SO(3)=RP3 admits no continuous embedding below d=5d=5d=5. Euler angles gimbal-lock and wrap; quaternions double-cover. Use 6D + Gram–Schmidt for continuous heads, bins for token heads.
  4. Poses compose, twists add. Build delta labels with ξt=log⁡(Tt−1Tt+1)∨\xi_t=\log(T_t^{-1}T_{t+1})^{\vee}ξt​=log(Tt−1​Tt+1​)∨ and execute them with Tt+1=Ttexp⁡(ξ^t)T_{t+1}=T_t\exp(\hat\xi_t)Tt+1​=Tt​exp(ξ^​t​); average orientations through the log, not entrywise (Appendix D).
  5. Quantile-normalise the action and proprioception vectors per dimension and globally over the dataset, never pooled across channels and never per-timestep; recompute the statistics on your own data when fine-tuning, and remember to invert them on the way out. Leave alone anything whose scale comes from a construction rather than from the data — the 6D rotation block, binary channels.
  6. Retargeting is a silent data-quality bottleneck unique to dexterous hands.

3Generative action heads

Core ideas

A generative head exists to represent a distribution over action chunks rather than a single point, which is the fix for the multimodality of §1.3. Three families are in current use. Flow matching learns a velocity field that transports noise to actions along straight lines; it is the modern default because straight paths integrate accurately in very few steps. Diffusion is its predecessor and learns to remove noise iteratively along a curved path. Discrete tokenisation — FAST, Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization — converts a chunk into tokens and trains with cross-entropy, which lets a VLA treat actions exactly like language. The single rule that organises all of it: continuous action vectors go with regression-type losses; discrete action tokens go with cross-entropy.

3.1Flow matching, derived so you can explain it

Start from what we want. We want to sample from p(A∣c)p(\mathbf{A}\mid \mathbf{c})p(A∣c), the distribution over action chunks given context. The generative trick is to build a continuous path that carries a distribution we can sample — a Gaussian — into the distribution we want, and then learn the velocity field that walks along it.

Step 1: pick the simplest possible path. For a single data point a\mathbf{a}a and a single noise sample x0∼N(0,I)\mathbf{x}_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)x0​∼N(0,I), define the straight line between them, parameterised by t∈[0,1]t \in [0,1]t∈[0,1]:

xt=(1−t) x0+t a\mathbf{x}_t = (1-t)\,\mathbf{x}_0 + t\,\mathbf{a}xt​=(1−t)x0​+ta
(3.1)

Step 2: differentiate. The velocity along this particular line is constant and trivially computable:

ut(xt∣a,x0)  =  dxtdt  =  a−x0\mathbf{u}_t(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{x}_0) \;=\; \frac{d\mathbf{x}_t}{dt} \;=\; \mathbf{a} - \mathbf{x}_0ut​(xt​∣a,x0​)=dtdxt​​=a−x0​
(3.2)

This is the conditional velocity: conditional on knowing both endpoints. It is constant in ttt — the path is a straight line traversed at uniform speed.

Step 3: regress it. Train a network to predict this velocity from (xt,t,c)(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c})(xt​,t,c) alone — that is, without being told which a\mathbf{a}a and x0\mathbf{x}_0x0​ generated this xt\mathbf{x}_txt​:

LFM(θ)  =  Et, x0, a[∥ vθ(xt,t,c)−(a−x0) ∥2]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_{t,\,\mathbf{x}_0,\,\mathbf{a}} \Big[\big\|\, v_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) - (\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{x}_0) \,\big\|^2 \Big]LFM​(θ)=Et,x0​,a​[​vθ​(xt​,t,c)−(a−x0​)​2]
(3.3)

Step 4 — the part that makes it work. This is the step that separates using flow matching from understanding it, and it is worth going slowly. Many different (x0,a)(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{a})(x0​,a) pairs pass through the same point xt\mathbf{x}_txt​, each with a different conditional velocity. The network cannot tell them apart, so it cannot fit any of them exactly. What does a least-squares regressor do when the target is ambiguous? It predicts the conditional mean. Therefore, at the optimum,

vθ⋆(xt,t,c)  =  E[ a−x0  ∣  xt, c ]v_\theta^\star(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) \;=\; \mathbb{E}\big[\,\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{x}_0 \;\big|\; \mathbf{x}_t,\, \mathbf{c}\,\big]vθ⋆​(xt​,t,c)=E[a−x0​​xt​,c]
(3.4)

and this conditional expectation is exactly the marginal velocity field whose flow transports N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I)N(0,I) onto p(a∣c)p(\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{c})p(a∣c). So the "failure" to fit the ambiguous target is not a failure at all — it is the mechanism. We regress a simple per-sample target and get the correct population-level field for free. That is the whole theorem, and you can state it in two sentences: the conditional paths are straight lines with constant velocity, so the regression target is trivial; and because least squares recovers the conditional mean, the learned field is automatically the marginal field we actually need.

The trap

"Flow matching paths are straight, so one Euler step is exact." False, and it is the most common overclaim. The conditional paths are straight. The marginal field — the one the network learns and the one you integrate at inference — is not. It must curve, because a single starting noise sample has to be routed toward one mode out of several, and a straight-line field cannot implement a branching transport map. The correct claim is that the marginal field is nearly straight, so coarse integration has low error: ~10 Euler steps instead of the 50–100 that DDPM (denoising diffusion probabilistic model) sampling needed. That is a latency argument, not an exactness argument.

3.2The two sign conventions

Both major papers in this manual define the same geometry with opposite labels, and you must be able to switch between them on demand.

Table 3.1 — The same straight line, two labellings. Translating between them is a reflection t↔1−τt \leftrightarrow 1-\taut↔1−τ, which flips the sign of the velocity target.
π0\pi_0π0​ conventionT-Rex convention
At time 0x0∼N(0,I)x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)x0​∼N(0,I) — noisex0=Ademox_0 = \mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{demo}}x0​=Ademo — clean action
At time 1x1=ax_1 = \mathbf{a}x1​=a — clean actionx1=ϵx_1 = \boldsymbol\epsilonx1​=ϵ — noise
Interpolantxt=(1−t)x0+t ax_t = (1-t)x_0 + t\,\mathbf{a}xt​=(1−t)x0​+taxτ=(1−τ)Ademo+τϵ\mathbf{x}_\tau = (1-\tau)\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{demo}} + \tau\boldsymbol\epsilonxτ​=(1−τ)Ademo+τϵ
Velocity targetu=a−x0u = \mathbf{a} - x_0u=a−x0​v⋆=ϵ−Ademov^\star = \boldsymbol\epsilon - \mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{demo}}v⋆=ϵ−Ademo
Inference directionintegrate t:0→1t: 0 \to 1t:0→1integrate τ:1→0\tau: 1 \to 0τ:1→0, step Δτ=−1/N\Delta\tau = -1/NΔτ=−1/N

T-Rex's Equations (1) and (3) are the second column[T-Rex, §4]. The reason it matters beyond bookkeeping is that in T-Rex's cascaded scheme (Chapter 9), τ=1\tau=1τ=1 is pure noise and τ=0\tau=0τ=0 is the final executable action, so "denoising from τsplit=0.4\tau_{\mathrm{split}}=0.4τsplit​=0.4 down to 000" means the tactile expert handles the last, finest 40% of the trajectory. Under the π0\pi_0π0​ labelling that same segment would be t:0.6→1t: 0.6 \to 1t:0.6→1. Read the paper's own convention before reasoning about which expert does what.

def flow_loss_pi0(net, a_clean, c):
    """x_0 ~ N(0,I) is NOISE, x_1 = a is DATA, target u = a - x_0, integrate 0 -> 1."""
    x0 = torch.randn_like(a_clean)
    t  = torch.rand(a_clean.shape[0], device=a_clean.device)
    xt = (1 - t)[:, None, None] * x0 + t[:, None, None] * a_clean
    return F.mse_loss(net(xt, t, c), a_clean - x0)

def flow_loss_trex(net, a_clean, c, alpha=1.5, beta=1.0):
    """x_0 = a is DATA, x_1 = eps is NOISE, target v* = eps - a, integrate 1 -> 0."""
    eps = torch.randn_like(a_clean)
    tau = torch.distributions.Beta(alpha, beta).sample((a_clean.shape[0],)).to(a_clean.device)
    x_tau = (1 - tau)[:, None, None] * a_clean + tau[:, None, None] * eps
    return F.mse_loss(net(x_tau, tau, c), eps - a_clean)

Note the Beta(1.5,1.0)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5, 1.0)Beta(1.5,1.0) timestep sampler, which both π0\pi_0π0​ and T-Rex use[T-Rex, Tab. 4]. It is not uniform: Beta(1.5,1.0)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1.0)Beta(1.5,1.0) has density ∝τ0.5\propto \tau^{0.5}∝τ0.5, which puts more mass at high τ\tauτ. In the T-Rex labelling high τ\tauτ is the noisy end, so this over-samples the coarse, high-noise part of the trajectory — where the field is hardest to learn and where an error propagates through every subsequent integration step. Errors made at the clean end have only a few steps left to do damage.

3.3The diffusion formulation, and why flow matching displaced it

Flow matching was not the first generative head to reach manipulation, and the one before it is worth understanding because its vocabulary is still everywhere in the literature. The earlier construction starts from the same premise — learn to invert a corruption process — but parameterises it differently. Rather than a straight interpolant with a constant velocity target, it defines a noise schedule over many discrete levels, trains a network to predict the noise that was added at a randomly chosen level, and samples by stepping back down the schedule. The two are close relatives, and the differences that matter in practice are about how many steps the sampler needs and how much of the design is schedule-tuning.

Diffusion Policy[Chi et al. 2023] uses the DDPM formulation: corrupt a clean action chunk with a noise schedule, train a network to predict the noise that was added.

ak=αˉk a0+1−αˉk ϵ,L=∥ ϵθ(ak,k,c)−ϵ ∥2\mathbf{a}^k = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,\mathbf{a}^0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\boldsymbol\epsilon, \qquad \mathcal{L} = \big\|\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{a}^k, k, \mathbf{c}) - \boldsymbol\epsilon\,\big\|^2ak=αˉk​​a0+1−αˉk​​ϵ,L=​ϵθ​(ak,k,c)−ϵ​2
(3.5)

Sampling reverses the corruption one step at a time:

ak−1=αk(ak−γk ϵθ(ak,k,c))+σk N(0,I)\mathbf{a}^{k-1} = \alpha_k\big(\mathbf{a}^k - \gamma_k\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_\theta(\mathbf{a}^k, k, \mathbf{c})\big) + \sigma_k\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)ak−1=αk​(ak−γk​ϵθ​(ak,k,c))+σk​N(0,I)
(3.6)

The two are close relatives — both learn a transport from noise to data — and the practical difference is path curvature. The DDPM schedule's probability path is substantially curved, so accurate integration needs many function evaluations. Flow matching's near-straight marginal field needs roughly an order of magnitude fewer. For a policy that must emit an action chunk inside a control period, network function evaluations are the latency budget, so this is decisive. Three diffusion-era tricks carry over and are worth knowing:

  • EMA (exponential moving average) of weights at inference. Averaging weights over training averages away update noise and produces visibly smoother actions. Cheap, always worth it.
  • Correlated noise across chunk timesteps. Sampling i.i.d. noise per timestep during training biases the model toward high-frequency, jerky chunks. Temporally correlated noise produces lower-jerk trajectories.
  • Classifier-free guidance. Sharpens instruction adherence by extrapolating away from the unconditional prediction. The failure mode is specific and worth naming: too large a guidance weight over-collapses the action distribution toward the conditional mode, which destroys exactly the multimodality you built a generative head to preserve. In dexterous manipulation this shows up as reduced ability to improvise around a failed grasp.

3.4Tokenising actions: making control look like language

Everything so far has kept actions continuous. The alternative is to make them discrete, because a discrete action sequence can be fed to a language model unchanged — same loss, same sampler, same serving code. The difficulty is that the obvious way to do it does not work. Quantise each dimension at each timestep and you get a long token string whose neighbouring entries are nearly identical, because a trajectory is smooth; the sequence is low in entropy and highly autocorrelated, and an autoregressive model learns little from it while paying for every token. The fix is to tokenise something that is not smooth. Transform the chunk into a basis where a smooth trajectory is sparse, and the token stream becomes short and information-dense.

If you want a VLA to treat actions the way it treats text — same cross-entropy loss, same autoregressive decoder, same pretraining machinery — you need actions as discrete tokens. The naive approach, binning each dimension at each timestep into 256 values, fails badly on high-frequency data, and understanding why is the interesting part.

A 50-step chunk of 7-dimensional actions binned per timestep produces 350 tokens that are highly correlated and low-entropy: consecutive timesteps of a smooth trajectory land in the same or adjacent bins. An autoregressive model trained on this learns the trivial "predict the previous token" shortcut, which has low loss and no useful content, and it must spend 350 decoding steps to emit one chunk.

FAST — Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization, from “FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models”[Pertsch et al. 2025] — fixes the statistics before tokenising. The name is the whole idea: the compression happens in frequency space, and what is compressed is a sequence of actions rather than each timestep on its own.

chunk  →quantile norm  A~  →DCT per dim  C  →quantize  ⌊sC⌉  →flatten  sparse stream  →BPE  tokens\text{chunk} \;\xrightarrow{\text{quantile norm}}\; \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \;\xrightarrow{\text{DCT per dim}}\; \mathbf{C} \;\xrightarrow{\text{quantize}}\; \lfloor s\mathbf{C} \rceil \;\xrightarrow{\text{flatten}}\; \text{sparse stream} \;\xrightarrow{\text{BPE}}\; \text{tokens}chunkquantile norm​A~DCT per dim​Cquantize​⌊sC⌉flatten​sparse streamBPE​tokens
(3.7)

The discrete cosine transform is the load-bearing step. It re-expresses the time series as a sum of cosines of increasing frequency. A smooth trajectory — which is what most demonstration segments are — has almost all of its energy in the lowest one or two coefficients, so the transformed representation is sparse and mostly zeros. Quantising a sparse, zero-heavy stream and then running byte-pair encoding over it collapses the long runs of zeros into a short, dense, high-entropy token sequence that an autoregressive model handles well.

Running this on smooth ramp trajectories, with H=16H=16H=16 and A=62A=62A=62:

t = torch.linspace(0, 1, H)
ramp = (t[None, :, None] * torch.randn(B, 1, A))     # smooth ramps
coeff = fast_encode(ramp)                            # (B, A, H) integer DCT coefficients
# nonzero overall .............. 0.28
# nonzero in first 2 coeffs .... 0.99
# reconstruction from 2 coeffs . 6.2% relative L2 error

Only 28% of coefficients survive quantisation, while 99% of the first two coefficients are non-zero — energy has concentrated exactly where the argument says it should. Truncating to two coefficients per dimension, an 8× compression, reconstructs the chunk to 6% relative error. High-frequency content is what breaks this: jitter spreads energy across all coefficients, nothing is sparse, and compression collapses. This is a real and useful diagnostic — if your FAST token sequences are unexpectedly long, your action data is noisier than you think.

What FAST is not

FAST is a fixed, deterministic tokeniser. It is not learned end-to-end with the policy, there is no VQ codebook, and it has no trainable parameters. The policy's objective over its outputs is plain next-token cross-entropy. It is routinely described as "a learned action tokeniser" — it is not, and the distinction matters because a fixed tokeniser can be swapped, inverted exactly, and reasoned about analytically.

3.5Do you even need a generative head?

Not always, and the evidence is specific. OpenVLA-OFT[Kim et al. 2025] reports that a plain L1L_1L1​ regression head — a two-block MLP-ResNet (a multi-layer perceptron with residual connections) predicting continuous actions directly from the hidden states of the LLM (large language model) backbone — matches or beats a diffusion head while being dramatically cheaper, reaching 97.1% average success on LIBERO with a 25–50× inference speedup. The recipe is parallel decoding + action chunking + continuous actions + L1L_1L1​.

This is not a contradiction of §1.3; it is a statement about which data you have. Action chunking already absorbs temporal multimodality. If what remains — the chunk-level ambiguity — is small, because the demonstrations are clean and the task is close to unimodal, then there is nothing left for a generative head to model and it is pure overhead. The decision rule:

Table 3.2 — Choosing a head. The question is never "which is better" but "how multimodal is my data after chunking, and what is my latency budget".
SituationHeadWhy
Clean, near-unimodal demos; single task; tight latencyL1L_1L1​ regression + chunkingChunking already handles the temporal ambiguity; generative machinery adds NFEs for nothing
Multi-operator data; several valid strategies; contact-richFlow matchingGenuine chunk-level multimodality; ~10 NFEs is affordable
VLA pretraining at scale; want language and action in one objectiveFAST + cross-entropyActions become tokens; reuses the whole LLM training stack
Both — pretrain discrete, deploy continuousπ0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ styleDiscrete tokens for scalable pretraining, continuous expert for high-rate control

π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ is the clearest statement of the last row: during pretraining all tasks including robot actions are represented as discrete tokens via FAST, which is "simple, scalable and efficient"; a continuous action expert is trained simultaneously for deployment[π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​]. The knowledge-insulation variant formalises this into a single-stage recipe where the VLM backbone is adapted with discrete tokens while the action expert produces continuous actions[Knowledge Insulation].

3.6The loss decomposition that ties everything together

Take the flow-matching loss and add and subtract the optimal field v⋆v^\starv⋆. The cross term vanishes in expectation because v⋆v^\starv⋆ is by construction the conditional mean, so

E∥vθ−(a−x0)∥2⏟what you measure  =  ∥vθ−v⋆∥2⏟bias — epistemic  +  σ2(xt,t∣c)⏟irreducible variance — aleatoric\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\big\|v_\theta - (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{x}_0)\big\|^2}_{\text{what you measure}} \;=\; \underbrace{\big\|v_\theta - v^\star\big\|^2}_{\text{bias — epistemic}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sigma^2(\mathbf{x}_t, t \mid \mathbf{c})}_{\text{irreducible variance — aleatoric}}what you measureE​vθ​−(a−x0​)​2​​=bias — epistemic​vθ​−v⋆​2​​+irreducible variance — aleatoricσ2(xt​,t∣c)​​
(3.8)

This equation is more useful than it looks, because it says the training loss you already compute is a sum of two quantities you separately care about, and different methods read off different terms. The first term is model error: it goes to zero with training on in-distribution data and rises out of distribution, which makes it an epistemic signal — this is what Diff-DAgger uses to decide when to ask a human for help. The second term is the local multimodality of the action distribution: it never goes to zero, and it is large exactly where the policy faces a genuine choice — which is what AdaFlow uses to decide how many integration steps to spend. Both are developed in Chapter 18.

Key takeaways
  1. Flow matching regresses the conditional velocity a−x0\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{x}_0a−x0​, which is a constant per sample; least squares then recovers the marginal field E[a−x0∣xt]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{x}_0\mid\mathbf{x}_t]E[a−x0​∣xt​] automatically. That is the whole idea.
  2. The marginal field is nearly, not exactly, straight. It must curve to route mass to different modes. The benefit is ~10 Euler steps, not one.
  3. π0\pi_0π0​ and T-Rex use opposite noise/data labelling. Check before reasoning about which end of τ\tauτ a given expert owns.
  4. Beta(1.5,1.0)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1.0)Beta(1.5,1.0) over-samples the noisy end, where errors propagate through the most subsequent steps.
  5. FAST is a fixed, non-learned tokeniser. DCT concentrates smooth trajectories into ~2 coefficients (8× compression at 6% error); BPE then compresses the zero-heavy stream.
  6. A plain L1L_1L1​ head with chunking beats diffusion on clean unimodal data (OpenVLA-OFT, 97.1% on LIBERO, 25–50× faster). Match the head to the residual multimodality, not to fashion.
  7. The flow loss decomposes into epistemic bias + aleatoric variance — the foundation of uncertainty estimation in Chapter 18.
Part II

Architectures

How the major VLA families are actually wired, and the two structural patterns — block-masked attention and modality-specific experts — that everything else is built on.

4VLA architectures

Core ideas

Almost every modern VLA is a pretrained vision–language model with an action expert bolted on. The recurring engineering problem is that the VLM is large and slow while the action head must run many times per chunk, and the recurring solution is to make them structurally asymmetric: a heavy backbone that runs once, a light expert that iterates, and an attention mask that lets you cache the former. Understand that one pattern and π0\pi_0π0​, GR00T, and T-Rex all become variations rather than separate systems.

4.1The asymmetric-expert pattern

Start from the constraint rather than from any model. A VLA must contain something large, because semantic generality cannot be learned from robot data, and it must run something small many times, because a generative action head integrates an ODE or a diffusion chain and each step is a forward pass. Putting those together gives the pattern that organises this whole chapter: partition the parameters by role, not by depth. One set of weights processes the conditioning and runs once; another processes the action and runs KKK times; they share one attention stack so the second can read the first, and an attention mask keeps the traffic one-way so the first can be cached.

Partitioning weights by which tokens they serve, while keeping attention global, is the Mixture-of-Transformers construction. It differs from a Mixture-of-Experts in a way worth being precise about: there is no learned router, because the routing decision is already made — a token is an image token or an action token, and that is not something the network has to infer. No router means no load-balancing loss and none of the bi-level instability that makes sparse MoE fragile at scale. What it costs is memory, since every expert's parameters are resident even though each token touches only one set.

The reference instance of that pattern is π0\pi_0π0​, which the rest of this section reads for its structure; Chapter 10 takes the same model apart in full, with the tensor shapes on every wire.

π0\pi_0π0​[Black et al. 2024] pairs a PaliGemma VLM (~3B parameters) with a much smaller Gemma-300M action expert, and trains with flow matching. Images go through SigLIP at roughly 256 tokens per image; actions are padded to a fixed width — 18 dimensions in the paper, 32 in the released openpi configuration — and predicted in chunks of H=50H=50H=50.

The structure of each of those 18 layers is a Mixture-of-Transformers — the lower strip of Figure 4.1, drawn on its own in Figure 4.2. MoT[Liang et al., TMLR 2025] decouples every non-embedding parameter by modality — feed-forward networks, attention projection matrices, and layer normalisation — while keeping global self-attention over the full sequence. Routing is by modality identity, not a learned router, which is the underrated part: there is no load-balancing loss, no router to co-train, and none of the bi-level optimisation instability that makes standard Mixture-of-Experts fragile at scale. MoT matches a dense Chameleon-7B baseline at 55.8% of its FLOPs, and in the Transfusion setting a 760M MoT beats a 1.4B dense model.

For a VLA the payoff is different from the language-modelling payoff. It is not primarily about FLOPs; it is that the expensive vision–language parameters and the cheap action parameters are separate objects, so you can run one of them repeatedly without touching the other.

Measured on a 3-expert, d=512d=512d=512 block: 9.46M parameters versus 3.15M dense, at identical per-token FLOPs. That is the MoT bargain in one line — you buy capacity with memory, not with compute, because any given token only ever touches its own expert's weights.

4.2Block-masked attention: the latency lever

This is the mechanism that makes the whole family practical, and it reduces to a single structural fact about the attention mask.

Partition the sequence into segments — vision/language prefix (V), robot state (S), and noised action tokens (A) — and choose an attention mask in which V never attends to A. Then the keys and values produced by the prefix do not depend on the action tokens at all. You compute them once, cache them, and run the action expert's KKK integration steps against the frozen cache. You never pay the 3B-parameter forward pass more than once per chunk.

seg  = torch.tensor([0]*4 + [1]*2 + [2]*3)      # vision | state | action
mask = block_causal_mask(seg, [[1,0,0],       # V sees V only
                               [1,1,0],       # S sees V, S
                               [1,1,1]])      # A sees everything
# vision attends to action? False  ->  VLM prefix is cacheable: True

4.3The current landscape

The systems below differ less than their names suggest. Every one of them is a pretrained vision–language model with something bolted on that emits continuous actions, and the only question that really separates them is how the action head reads the backbone's features. Three answers exist. The next three figures draw one representative of each at the same scale, so the comparison is structural rather than rhetorical.

Table 4.1 — Major VLA systems. "Action head" is the objective the executable action is produced under; several systems train more than one objective simultaneously.
SystemBackboneAction headDefining idea
π0\pi_0π0​ (2024)PaliGemma ~3B + Gemma-300M expertFlow matching, H=50H{=}50H=50MoT split: heavy VLM runs once, light expert iterates
π0\pi_0π0​-FAST (2025)SameCross-entropy over FAST tokensDCT+BPE tokenisation makes actions behave like text
π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ (2025)Same + heterogeneous co-trainingDiscrete (pretrain) + continuous expert (deploy)Open-world generalisation from web + robot + semantic-subtask co-training
π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ (2025)π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ lineageAdvantage-conditionedRECAP: demos + expert corrections + autonomous RL experience

GR00T N1.5/N1.6Eagle VLM (N1.5); Cosmos-2B variant (N1.6)Flow-matching DiT (diffusion transformer), cross-attends VL embeddingsHumanoid cross-embodiment; N1.6 doubles DiT depth 16→32
Gemini Robotics 1.5Gemini—Motion Transfer across embodiments; interleaves actions with explicit natural-language "embodied thinking"

T-Rex (2026)Qwen3VL-2B, 3 experts (1.41B + 1.41B + 0.62B)Cascaded flow matchingVariable-rate MoT: tactile expert refines at high rate off a cached prefix

4.4Vision encoders, and the dual-encoder argument

OpenVLA uses two vision encoders — DINOv2 and SigLIP — and the reason is complementarity rather than redundancy. SigLIP is trained with language supervision, so its features are semantic: they encode "this is a mug" in a space aligned with text, which is what you need for instruction following. DINOv2 is trained self-supervised without language, and its features are spatial and geometric: correspondence, part structure, precise localisation. A language-aligned encoder is systematically worse at the second thing because the training signal never rewarded it.

OpenVLA-OFT adds FiLM to improve language grounding, though only where it is needed — in the ALOHA real-world experiments, not in LIBERO, whose policies follow instructions well enough without it: the instruction produces a per-channel affine transform applied to visual features, so language modulates vision rather than competing with it for attention. This is the same mechanism, and the same motivation, that reappears throughout Part III for force and tactile signals — a low-dimensional modality is far more effective as a gate on a high-dimensional one than as a peer competing for attention mass. §8.1 gives FiLM its own treatment alongside the other six fusion mechanisms, and §8.2 derives the attention-mass argument that explains why gating wins.

4.5What has changed since early 2025

Four shifts, each of which can be stated in a sentence:

  1. Post-training with reinforcement learning became standard, not exotic. π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ with RECAP reports more than doubling throughput and halving failure rate on its hardest tasks, with multi-hour autonomous runs[π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​]. The imitation-then-RL pipeline is now the default shape of a frontier system.
  2. Human egocentric video became a first-class pretraining source. EgoScale's log-linear scaling law between human-data volume and validation loss — with validation loss correlating to real-robot success — turns "collect human video" from a hopeful idea into a predictable investment[EgoScale].
  3. Explicit reasoning entered the action loop. Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves actions with multi-level natural-language reasoning; Generalist's "harmonic reasoning" frames the same goal as two asynchronous continuous-time streams rather than a discrete System-1/System-2 split.
  4. Modality count grew. This is the shift this manual is mostly about: 2024-era VLAs took RGB (plain colour camera) images, language and proprioception. 2026-era systems take point clouds, per-finger wrenches, deformation maps, and audio — and the architectural consequences are the subject of Part III.
On company communications

Generalist AI's GEN-0 and GEN-1 posts are blog-level, not peer-reviewed. Their headline claims: a robotics scaling law L(D)∝D−0.5L(D) \propto D^{-0.5}L(D)∝D−0.5; an "ossification" phase transition near 7B parameters below which models stop absorbing pretraining data; and for GEN-1 (April 2026), 99% success where prior models reach 64%, ~3× faster execution, ~1 hour of robot data per task, built on half a million hours of real-world data. Use these as directional talking points about where industry believes the curve goes — the ossification claim in particular is a genuinely interesting hypothesis — but say explicitly that they are unreproduced. Anyone who knows the space will respect the distinction, and will notice if you do not make it.

Key takeaways
  1. The universal pattern is a heavy VLM + a light action expert, with modality-specific weights and global attention (MoT). Routing by modality id avoids MoE's router instability entirely.
  2. MoT buys capacity with memory, not compute: 3 experts = 3× parameters at identical per-token FLOPs.
  3. Block-masking so that vision never attends to actions is what makes the prefix cacheable. That single zero block is the entire latency argument.
  4. There are only three couplings between backbone and action head (Figure 4.6): shared self-attention with separate weights (π₀, T-Rex), no separate head at all (OpenVLA-OFT), and one-directional cross-attention (GR00T N1). Naming the coupling is a better answer than naming the system.
  5. Dual vision encoders are complementary: SigLIP for language-aligned semantics, DINOv2 for geometry. FiLM lets language modulate rather than compete.
  6. Since early 2025: RL post-training normalised, human video became a scaling axis, explicit reasoning entered the loop, and the modality count grew.
Part III

Multimodality

The heart of this manual. What each sensor actually produces, how to turn it into tokens, how to combine those tokens without one modality crushing the others, and what the 2026 literature has established versus what it has only argued.

5The multimodal problem

Core ideas

A robot's sensors differ from one another along three axes that each break a different part of a transformer: dimensionality (256 visual tokens versus one force token — an attention-mass problem), rate (30 Hz vision versus kHz force — a temporal-aliasing problem), and semantics (what a pixel means is learnable from web data; what a newton means is not). Nearly every real difficulty in multimodal robot learning is one of these three wearing a costume. Naming which one you are facing tells you which fix to reach for, and the empirical evidence that this matters is blunt: T-Rex's π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile baseline, which adds force signals in the obvious way, scores worse than π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ without them.

5.1The sensor inventory

Start from what a bimanual dexterous platform actually produces. T-Rex's Dexmate Vega-1 with two Sharpa Wave hands records, per episode and time-aligned at 30 Hz: three monocular RGB streams at 640×360640\times360640×360 (one head ZED X Mini, two wrist ZED X One S); 2×72\times72×7 arm joint positions and velocities plus 2×222\times222×22 hand joint states; SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) wrist poses; and for each of ten fingertips a single-channel deformation-depth map and a 6-axis net wrench[T-Rex, App. G]. That is a representative modern stack, and the table below is the one to internalise.

One term in that inventory is worth pinning down now, because it recurs for the rest of the manual. A wrench is the force-side counterpart of a twist: the six numbers F=(f;τ)\mathcal{F}=(f;\tau)F=(f;τ) giving the net force f∈R3f\in\mathbb{R}^3f∈R3 and the net moment τ∈R3\tau\in\mathbb{R}^3τ∈R3 transmitted through a frame. “Six-axis” names those six components, not six sensing elements — a fingertip reporting a 6-axis wrench reports one force vector and one torque vector resolved at the fingertip frame, however many internal strain gauges were combined to produce them. The word is borrowed from screw theory, where a wrench is literally a force along an axis together with a torque about that same axis, in the same way that the twist of Appendix D is a translation along an axis together with a rotation about it.

The pairing with the twist V=(v;ω)\mathcal{V}=(v;\omega)V=(v;ω) is not a loose analogy. The product F⋅V=f⋅v+τ⋅ω\mathcal{F}\cdot\mathcal{V}=f\cdot v+\tau\cdot\omegaF⋅V=f⋅v+τ⋅ω is mechanical power, and power does not depend on the frame you chose to write it in. That single constraint forces the two objects to transform in dual ways under a change of frame: if a twist maps by the adjoint AdT\mathrm{Ad}_TAdT​ of §21.5, a wrench must map by AdT−⊤\mathrm{Ad}_T^{-\top}AdT−⊤​. Work that through for a pure force fff applied at the origin of the fingertip frame and it reproduces the statics you would write by hand — force RfRfRf, and a moment p×Rf\mathbf{p}\times Rfp×Rf about the new origin, where p\mathbf{p}p is the offset between the two frames — which is a reassuring sign that the bookkeeping is right rather than merely consistent. The practical consequence is that “the fingertip wrench” is not a well-defined quantity until you say which frame: the same contact measured at the fingertip and rotated into the palm frame is two different six-vectors. Section 7.2 is about what goes wrong when that question, along with gravity compensation and per-channel normalisation, is skipped.
