5.2The three structural difficulties

Difficulty 1 — dimensional imbalance

With one camera at 256 tokens, a dozen language tokens, one proprioception token and one force token, the context is 270 tokens long and the force token is 1 in 270 of it. Add two more cameras and it is 1 in 782. Under approximately uniform attention at initialisation, the gradient reaching the force encoder scales with the attention mass its token receives, so the force encoder trains hundreds of times more slowly than the vision encoder. Chapter 8 develops this carefully, including the important caveat that it is an argument about initialisation, not a theorem about trained networks.

Difficulty 2 — rate mismatch

Vision arrives at 30 Hz. Contact transients — the micro-slip that tells you the key is about to fall, the force spike that tells you the peg found the hole — live at hundreds of hertz. If you fuse force into the same token sequence as vision at the vision rate, you have resampled force to 30 Hz, and the transients are gone before any architecture gets to see them. You have kept the modality and thrown away the reason you added it.

This is why the strongest contact-rich systems are all two-rate systems. RDP runs a slow latent diffusion policy at 1–2 Hz and a fast tactile-conditioned decoder at 20–30 Hz, with the fast network taking under 1 ms so it could in principle run above 300 Hz[RDP]. T-Rex runs a slow action expert once per 16-step chunk and a fast tactile expert four times within it, at intra-chunk offsets {0,4,8,12}\{0,4,8,12\}{0,4,8,12}[T-Rex, §4.2]. Different mechanisms, identical diagnosis.

Difficulty 3 — no pretraining substrate

A vision encoder arrives knowing what objects are, because the internet is full of labelled images. There is no internet of fingertip wrenches. Every non-visual modality must be learned from robot data alone, which is three to five orders of magnitude scarcer. Three strategies have emerged, and they are best held in mind as a set, because each concedes something the other two keep:

  • Self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled sensor data. Sparsh pretrains on 460k+ tactile images with masking and self-distillation, and reports a 95.1% average improvement over task- and sensor-specific end-to-end training across the six TacBench tasks when all models get only 33–50% of the labels[Sparsh]. Sparsh-X extends this to four touch modalities at once (image, audio, IMU, pressure) over ~1M contact-rich interactions, lifting policy success by 63% over an image-only encoder[Sparsh-X].
  • A dedicated mid-training stage. T-Rex's central claim: you do not need tactile data during the expensive large-scale pretraining phase at all. Pretrain visuomotor priors on human video, then spend 100 hours of tactile-synchronised robot data on a mid-training stage that grounds those priors in contact dynamics, then post-train on ~100 task demonstrations. Their ablation isolates the value: pretraining alone gives 34% average, mid-training alone 45%, both 65%[T-Rex, Tab. 3].
  • Physical grounding as an auxiliary objective. Rather than hoping the tactile encoder learns something useful from the action loss alone, supervise it against a physical quantity. TaF-VLA grounds high-dimensional tactile observations in interaction forces[TaF-VLA]; ViTacFormer predicts future tactile signals; T-Rex adds a future-visual-latent prediction loss with weight λfuture=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{future}}=0.5λfuture​=0.5 explicitly "to align this tactile modality with the broader visual context during mid-training".

5.3The three "easy" modalities

Before the hard ones, three that are largely solved — with one landmine each.

RGB

A ViT (vision transformer) or SigLIP encoder at ~256 tokens per image. The landmine is implicit 3D. Mainstream VLAs consume only 2D RGB with no depth, no point cloud, and no camera extrinsics, so all geometry is inferred from monocular cues, multi-view consistency, and action–image correlations seen during training. This mostly works, and it is both the trick and the weakness: the policy is brittle to viewpoint change, novel camera heights, and precise depth-dependent tasks, and collecting more data from the same viewpoint does not fix it because it does not add the missing information. Chapter 6 is about supplying that information explicitly.

Language

Tokenised by the VLM's own tokenizer. The landmine is that language is routinely ignored: with a dozen language tokens against hundreds of visual ones, and a training set where the visual scene usually determines the task anyway, the policy learns to read the scene and skip the instruction. The diagnostic is trivial and you should always run it — swap the instruction while holding the scene fixed and see whether behaviour changes. The fix is FiLM conditioning (OpenVLA-OFT+) or classifier-free guidance. Note this is structurally the same problem as force drowning, and it is instructive that the accepted fix for language is multiplicative modulation rather than more tokens.

Proprioception

An MLP into one or two tokens. The landmine is causal confusion, specifically the copycat problem. Joint state at time ttt is extremely predictive of the action at time ttt — because the action at t−1t-1t−1 produced that state, and actions are temporally smooth. A policy can drive training loss down by learning at≈g(qt)\mathbf{a}_t \approx g(\mathbf{q}_t)at​≈g(qt​), essentially integrating its own momentum, while never learning to look at the scene. Loss looks excellent; the robot confidently continues whatever it was doing and ignores the object.

Causal confusion is not covariate shift

These get conflated constantly and have different fixes. Covariate shift is a test-time distribution problem — you end up in states the expert never visited. Fix: DAgger, chunking, on-policy corrections. Causal confusion is a training-time predictor problem — you learned a spurious variable that correlates with the action but does not cause it. Fix: proprioception dropout, historical-frame dropout, and forcing visual reliance. They co-occur in practice (a copycat policy drifts off-distribution fast) but attacking one does not address the other. GR00T's fine-tuning recipe applies state dropout with probability 0.2 for exactly this reason[T-Rex, App. E].

5.4The cautionary result

The single most useful empirical fact in this part of the manual is T-Rex's Table 1. Compare two rows:

Table 5.2 — Adding tactile naively makes things worse. Average success rate (%) over 12 contact-rich tasks, 16 trials each. Source: T-Rex, Tab. 1.
MethodAvg. successWhat changed
π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​17Vision + language + state
π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile6Same, plus 6D force/torque from all 10 fingers concatenated into the state input
EgoScale35Large-scale egocentric pretraining, no tactile
T-Rex65Tactile via VQ-VAE + deformation encoder + asynchronous tactile expert

Adding the tactile modality in the obvious way — concatenate the wrenches onto the state vector — cost eleven points of absolute success rate, a 65% relative degradation. The same information, encoded and fused properly, is worth thirty points over the strongest visual baseline. The paper's own phrasing is that this "highlights the importance of effective tactile integration".

Why would adding information hurt? Three mechanisms, all developed later in this Part, and being able to enumerate them is the difference between knowing the result and understanding it:

  1. It perturbs a pretrained representation. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​'s state encoder was pretrained; widening its input with 60 new, unnormalised, high-variance dimensions shifts the distribution the downstream layers expect. You have damaged a good representation to add a signal the model cannot yet use.
  2. A single-timestep wrench is nearly useless. What matters in contact is df/dtd\mathbf{f}/dtdf/dt — the onset, the slip, the release. One sample carries almost none of that, and carries the sensor's bias drift at full strength. §7.3 shows why temporal encoding is not optional.
  3. It is a shortcut risk. Force correlates with phase of task extremely strongly (free space → contact → release). A policy can learn to read phase off the force magnitude and stop attending to vision — causal confusion again, with a new variable.
Key takeaways
  1. Sensors differ along three axes — dimensionality, rate, and pretrainability — and each breaks a different part of the architecture. Diagnose which one you face before choosing a fix.
  2. A force token is 1 in 270 of a one-camera context and 1 in 782 with three cameras. Cameras make drowning worse, linearly.
  3. Contact transients live above 100 Hz. Fusing force at the vision rate destroys them. Every strong contact-rich system is a two-rate system.
  4. There is no internet of wrenches. Three substitutes: SSL on unlabelled sensor data (Sparsh, +95.1% on TacBench), a dedicated mid-training stage (T-Rex: 34% → 45% → 65%), and physical grounding as an auxiliary loss.
  5. RGB's landmine is implicit 3D; language's is being ignored; proprioception's is causal confusion. The language fix — multiplicative modulation rather than more tokens — is the template for force.
  6. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile scores 6% versus π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​'s 17%. Naive addition of a modality is not neutral, it is harmful. It is the single most useful number in this chapter.

6Encoding geometry: depth, point clouds, and 3D scene representations

Core ideas

A point cloud is a set, so its encoder must be permutation-invariant, and the cheapest way to achieve that is a shared per-point MLP followed by a symmetric pooling operation. That is PointNet, and its descendants differ only in how much local structure they preserve on the way to the pooled vector. The surprising empirical result is that for manipulation policies, the simplest possible encoder wins: 3D Diffusion Policy's three-layer MLP producing a 64-dimensional feature beats PointNet, PointNet++, PointNeXt and Point Transformer, including pretrained variants. Understanding why — the policy needs coarse spatial layout, not fine semantic geometry, and small encoders overfit less on 10–40 demonstrations — is worth more than memorising any architecture.

6.1Why a point cloud is not an image

Almost every point cloud in a manipulation stack begins as a depth image. The camera reports a distance per pixel; scaling each pixel’s viewing ray by that distance, through the camera intrinsics, places the measurement in space, and the extrinsics then carry it into the robot’s frame. Nothing is created along the way. The map is invertible given the intrinsics, and what comes out is a single viewpoint’s worth of front surfaces — the visible shell of the scene, with nothing behind it. A cloud from a passive stereo head, or from an active-stereo camera that projects its own pattern to survive untextured surfaces, is in that sense the depth image in different clothes.

What changes is the coordinate system, and the change is not cosmetic. In the image, a displacement of fixed physical size covers a pixel count that depends on how far away it happens to be, so a network reasoning about distance must first learn to undo the projection. After back-projection a centimetre is a centimetre anywhere in the frame. More consequentially, the extrinsics express the observation in the same frame the policy’s actions are written in: move the camera and every number in the depth image changes, while the cloud, given updated extrinsics, does not. Those two properties are the reason the cloud is worth forming at all — and they are also what make it awkward to feed to anything that expects a grid.

Three properties force the architecture, and each one rules out a family of encoders:

  1. Unordered. {p1,p2,p3}\{p_1, p_2, p_3\}{p1​,p2​,p3​} and {p3,p1,p2}\{p_3, p_1, p_2\}{p3​,p1​,p2​} are the same cloud. Any function of the cloud must be invariant to permutation, which rules out anything that indexes points by position in a tensor — including convolution and standard positional encoding.
  2. Irregular. Density varies with distance and surface angle. There is no grid, so "the neighbouring point" requires an explicit search.
  3. Metric. The coordinates are the signal. A 2 cm displacement means 2 cm, not "two pixels at unknown depth", which is exactly the information an RGB policy has to infer.

The permutation requirement has a clean solution. Any permutation-invariant function of a set can be approximated in the form

f({p1,…,pN})  ≈  ρ(□i=1..N ϕ(pi))f(\{p_1,\dots,p_N\}) \;\approx\; \rho\Big(\underset{i=1..N}{\square}\ \phi(p_i)\Big)f({p1​,…,pN​})≈ρ(i=1..N□​ ϕ(pi​))
(6.1)

where ϕ\phiϕ is a shared per-point network, □\square□ is a symmetric pooling operator (max or sum), and ρ\rhoρ is a post-pooling network. Invariance is structural, not learned: □\square□ does not care about ordering, so neither does fff. This is the Deep Sets / PointNet result and it is the single equation behind every encoder in this chapter.

6.2The preprocessing pipeline, which matters more than the encoder

DP3's recipe[Ze et al. 2024, §III-B], stated exactly, because each step is a decision:

  1. Single camera, depth at 84×8484\times8484×84. Chosen deliberately for practical deployability rather than surrounding the robot with cameras.
  2. Back-project to a point cloud using intrinsics and extrinsics.
  3. Discard colour. "We do not use color channels for better appearance generalization." Colour is the channel through which lighting and texture brittleness enters; geometry alone is more robust.
  4. Crop to a workspace bounding box. Removes table and floor, which are the majority of the points and carry no task information.
  5. Farthest point sampling to 512 or 1024 points. FPS, not uniform sampling — it "helps cover the 3D space sufficiently and reduces the randomness of point cloud sampling".

Step 5 deserves attention because it is the one people skip. Uniform random sampling over-represents dense regions (near surfaces, close to the camera) and can miss a thin structure entirely; worse, it produces a different subsample every frame, injecting observation noise that the policy sees as the world flickering. FPS greedily picks the point farthest from everything chosen so far, yielding an approximately uniform spatial cover and a far more stable subsample.

def farthest_point_sample(xyz, n_sample):
    """(B,N,3) -> (B,n_sample) indices. Greedy max-min-distance cover."""
    B, N, _ = xyz.shape
    idx  = torch.zeros(B, n_sample, dtype=torch.long, device=xyz.device)
    dist = torch.full((B, N), 1e10, device=xyz.device)
    far  = torch.randint(0, N, (B,), device=xyz.device)
    batch = torch.arange(B, device=xyz.device)
    for i in range(n_sample):
        idx[:, i] = far
        centroid  = xyz[batch, far].unsqueeze(1)                 # (B,1,3)
        dist      = torch.minimum(dist, ((xyz - centroid) ** 2).sum(-1))
        far       = dist.argmax(-1)                              # farthest from ALL chosen so far
    return idx

FPS is O(N⋅nsample)\mathcal{O}(N \cdot n_{\text{sample}})O(N⋅nsample​) and sequential in nsamplen_{\text{sample}}nsample​, so it is the preprocessing bottleneck: 4096 → 1024 is four million distance evaluations across 1024 sequential steps. In a real stack you do this on GPU, or use a voxel-grid downsample first to get NNN into the low thousands. The cost is a systems question before it is a modelling one, and it is usually the first thing to profile when a 3D policy misses its control deadline.

The permutation-invariance argument of §6.1 says an encoder must be a shared per-point map, a symmetric pool, and a post-net. It says nothing about how deep any of those should be, and the natural instinct is that more is better: hierarchical grouping, local neighbourhoods, attention between points. That instinct is borrowed from a setting where it was right — large-scale scene segmentation, with tens of thousands of points and a need for fine spatial detail — and manipulation is not that setting. A workspace-cropped cloud of a thousand points, consumed by a policy that needs to know roughly where the object is, is a much easier problem, and a large encoder on a small robot dataset mostly finds new ways to overfit. The section below is the empirical version of that claim.

6.3The DP3 encoder, and why simple wins

FPS 4096 -> (4, 1024, 3)
DP3Encoder -> (4, 64) | params 59.1k
permutation invariance: max |f(P) - f(perm P)| = 0.00e+00

Fifty-nine thousand parameters, a 64-dimensional output, and permutation invariance exact to the last bit — because max-pooling over a permuted axis returns identical values, not merely similar ones. Compare this to a SigLIP encoder's ~400M parameters producing 256 tokens of width 1152.

DP3's ablations are the interesting part. Against alternative representations, point clouds score 78.3 average versus substantially lower for RGB-D, depth images and voxels; the paper notes RGB-D and depth are "very close and not comparable to point clouds, indicating that the proper usage of depth information is essential". Against alternative encoders, DP3's MLP beats PointNet, PointNet++, PointNeXt and Point Transformer — including pretrained checkpoints — with PointNet scoring far below it.

"Why does the crude encoder beat the sophisticated one?"

This is a favourite question and the answer has three parts.

Task mismatch. PointNet++ and PTv3 were designed for semantic and part segmentation, which needs fine local geometry at every point. A manipulation policy conditioned on a 64-D summary needs something much coarser: roughly where the object is, roughly its extent, roughly where free space is. The fine detail the big encoders preserve is not what the diffusion head consumes.

Data regime. DP3 trains on 10 demonstrations in simulation and 40 in the real world. A 10M-parameter hierarchical encoder on 40 demonstrations overfits; a 59k-parameter one cannot.

Pretraining mismatch. Pretrained point encoders were trained on ShapeNet-style object scans or autonomous-driving LiDAR. Neither distribution resembles a cropped, 1024-point, single-view tabletop workspace cloud.

The right generalisation is not "big point encoders are bad". It is that encoder capacity should match the information the downstream head actually consumes and the data you actually have. On a 100-hour dataset with a 3B backbone the calculus changes, which is why the VLA-scale systems in §6.5 make different choices.

6.4When you do need local structure

A single global max-pool discards where each feature came from. For tasks that need relational geometry — inserting a peg into one of several holes, grasping a specific handle — a hierarchical encoder is justified.

PointNet++ set abstraction

Apply (6.1) recursively on local neighbourhoods: choose centroids by FPS, group each centroid's neighbours by ball query, encode each group with a small PointNet, and pool within the group. The output is a smaller cloud with richer per-point features, and you stack the operation.

The load-bearing line is rel = grouped - new_xyz. Subtracting the centroid makes each local patch translation-invariant, so the same geometric feature — an edge, a corner, a cylindrical surface — produces the same activation wherever it appears in the workspace. Without it the network must relearn every feature at every location, which is precisely the inductive bias convolution gives you on images and that this construction recovers for sets.

Point Transformer v3 and serialisation

PTv3[Wu et al., CVPR 2024] makes a different trade: abandon precise neighbour search entirely and order the points instead. Sort by a space-filling curve (Z-order/Morton or Hilbert), then apply ordinary patched self-attention along the resulting 1-D sequence. Because space-filling curves preserve locality, a contiguous window in the sorted sequence is approximately a spatial neighbourhood — and you have replaced an irregular kkk-NN search with a sort.

The bit-interleaving is the whole idea: taking one bit from each axis in turn means two codes that agree in their high bits must agree in the high bits of all three coordinates, i.e. they lie in the same coarse octree cell. Measured on a 1024-point cloud, the mean distance between consecutive points after Z-order sorting is 0.759 versus 2.957 for the original arbitrary ordering — a 3.9× improvement in locality, from a sort. PTv3 uses four such orderings (Z-order and Hilbert, each with and without axis transposition), shuffled between layers so the neighbourhoods vary, with patch size 1024. The reported result is a receptive field expanded from 16 to 1024 points with 3× the speed and 10× the memory efficiency of PTv2.

6.5Injecting 3D into a pretrained VLA

DP3 trains from scratch. A VLA already has a large pretrained 2D backbone you do not want to destroy, and the literature has converged on four distinct strategies. Being able to compare them is a strong answer to "how would you add depth to π0\pi_0π0​?"

Table 6.1 — Four ways to give a 2D VLA 3D. The axis that separates them is how much of the pretrained model they are willing to disturb.
StrategyExampleMechanismTrade-off
Additive side-injectionPointVLAFreeze the action expert; a separate point encoder's features are added into a few selected blocksPreserves 2D competence completely, no retraining; 3D influence is limited by where you inject
Positional encodingSpatialVLAEgo3D positional encoding injects 3D information into the existing 2D visual tokens; adaptive action gridsNo new tokens at all, so no drowning; geometry is implicit rather than explicit
Input–output realignmentBridgeVLAProject the point cloud into multi-view images; pretrain the VLM to emit 2D heatmaps; predict heatmaps then lift to actionsReuses the 2D backbone natively and is very data-efficient; constrained to what renders into views
Native 3D tokensDP3 / iDP3 lineagePoint encoder produces tokens or a conditioning vector directlyMost direct use of geometry; needs training from scratch or heavy adaptation

A practical note on frames. DP3 works in the world frame, which requires accurate extrinsic calibration and careful point-cloud segmentation. iDP3[Ze et al. 2024] identified this as the blocker for general-purpose robots and switched to egocentric 3D representations in the camera frame, scaled to 4096 points (from 1024), and replaced the MLP encoder with a pyramid convolutional encoder because "convolutional layers produce smoother behaviors than fully-connected layers when learning from human data". The result runs on a full-sized humanoid without camera calibration or point-cloud segmentation. If your robot has a moving head or base, use camera-frame representations; world-frame ones inherit every calibration error your kinematic chain accumulates.

6.6Other 3D representations

Table 6.2 — Beyond raw point clouds. DP3's ablation found voxels and depth images both underperform point clouds for policy conditioning, but each of these has a regime where it wins.
RepresentationWhat it isUse whenCost
Depth imageH×WH{\times}WH×W of ranges; a 2.5D gridYou want to reuse a CNN/ViT stack unchangedEntangles geometry with viewpoint; discontinuous at occlusion boundaries
Occupancy voxelsDiscretised 3D grid, sparse-conv processedExplicit free-space reasoning; collision checks; whole-workspace policies (PerAct)Memory grows as r3r^3r3; resolution/extent trade is brutal
Multi-view re-renderingRender the cloud into kkk virtual viewsYou want to keep a 2D pretrained backbone (RVT, BridgeVLA)Rendering cost; occlusion artefacts from virtual viewpoints
Feature fields (NeRF / 3DGS)Continuous field with distilled semantic featuresPersistent scene memory across viewpoints; language-queryable geometryPer-scene optimisation; not yet real-time for closed-loop control
Camera-extrinsics conditioningFeed Tcambase\mathbf{T}_{\text{cam}}^{\text{base}}Tcambase​ as tokens alongside RGBCheapest possible viewpoint robustness fixTells the policy where the camera is, not what the geometry is

6.7Does a VLA encode 3D implicitly?

Mostly yes, and the qualification is where all the engineering lives. π0\pi_0π0​, OpenVLA and OFT consume only 2D RGB. They nonetheless perform tasks requiring depth, so they must be recovering geometry from monocular cues (perspective, occlusion, shading, known object scale), from having multiple views (a third-person camera plus wrist cameras give stereo-like disparity implicitly), and from action–image correlations learned across training — the model has seen what a 2 cm motion looks like from this camera many thousands of times.

But there is no 3D inductive bias. Nothing in the architecture enforces that a rotation of the camera should induce the corresponding transformation of the scene representation. The consequences are exactly what you would predict: brittleness to viewpoint changes, to novel camera heights, and to tasks whose success depends on millimetre depth. And crucially — this is the part that matters for a data-collection plan — collecting more data from the same viewpoint does not fix it, because the missing quantity is information, not samples. Fixing it requires either explicit geometry (this chapter) or viewpoint augmentation that actually varies the extrinsics.

Key takeaways
  1. Permutation invariance is structural: shared per-point MLP → symmetric pool → post-net. With max-pooling it is exact, not approximate.
  2. Preprocessing dominates: drop colour for appearance generalisation, crop to the workspace, and use farthest point sampling, not uniform — uniform sampling makes the world flicker frame to frame.
  3. DP3's 59k-parameter, 64-D encoder beats PointNet++/PointNeXt/Point Transformer including pretrained ones. Match encoder capacity to what the head consumes and the data you have, not to benchmark prestige.
  4. PointNet++ recovers locality by subtracting the centroid (translation invariance). PTv3 recovers it by sorting along space-filling curves — measured 3.9× better consecutive-point locality from a sort alone.
  5. Four ways to add 3D to a pretrained VLA: additive side-injection (PointVLA), positional encoding (SpatialVLA), input–output realignment via heatmaps (BridgeVLA), native 3D tokens (DP3/iDP3).
  6. Use camera-frame (egocentric) clouds if the head or base moves; world-frame clouds inherit all your calibration error (iDP3).
  7. VLAs do encode 3D implicitly, with no 3D inductive bias. More same-viewpoint data cannot fix viewpoint brittleness — only information can.

7Encoding contact: force, torque, and touch

Core ideas

Contact sensing splits into two physically different signals that need different encoders. A wrench (3-axis force + 3-axis torque) is low-dimensional, fast, and its information is almost entirely temporal — the onset, the slip, the release. A deformation map is an image of the contact patch and its information is spatial — edges, shear direction, contact area. Encode the first with a temporal model over a window of frames and the second with a small convolutional network, then concatenate. This is precisely T-Rex's design, and its ablations show each half is worth roughly 6–11 points of success rate independently. The single most important practical point in this chapter: a single-timestep wrench is nearly useless, and that is most of why naive tactile conditioning fails.

7.1The sensor taxonomy

There is no best contact sensor, only a set of incompatible trade-offs, and choosing one is therefore a matter of deciding which of them you can afford to lose.

Table 7.1 — Contact sensor families. Cost figures are from RDP §III, which is unusually explicit about them.
FamilyExamplesOutputStrengthsWeaknesses
Force/torque sensorATI Mini45 (≈3,000 USD)6-axis wrench, directCalibrated physical units; robust; no post-processingExpensive; noisy during rapid motion; one measurement for the whole end-effector
Joint torque estimateFlexiv Rizon RDKEstimated TCP wrenchFree — already in the arm"Relatively larger noise… due to inaccurate dynamics model"; no per-finger resolution
Optical / vision-basedGelSight Mini (≈549 USD, 7×9 markers, 8 MP @ 25 FPS), GelSlim, DIGIT, MCTac (≈50 USD), 9DTactHigh-resolution image of gel deformationRich spatial contact geometry; cheap to fabricate; low signal noiseForce values only via "complex calibration"; bulky; gel wears out and must be replaced
Electrical (magnetic / capacitive / resistive)AnySkin, ReSkin, XELA uSkin, BioTacSparse taxel array or 3D force fieldCompact, thin, conformable to a fingertipLower spatial resolution; complex to manufacture; usually needs F/T calibration for real units
Hybrid fingertipSharpa Wave (T-Rex / ViTacFormer); Digit 360 (Sparsh-X)Deformation depth map and 6-axis wrench per fingertipBoth signal types at every fingertip — the modern dexterous standardTen sensors means ten calibrations and ten drift sources

The trend worth naming: dexterous platforms have converged on hybrid per-fingertip sensing. T-Rex records, for each of ten fingertips, "the estimated deformation depth and the 6-axis net wrench". That is not redundancy. The wrench tells you how hard and the deformation map tells you where and in what pattern, and their ablation confirms neither substitutes for the other: deformation-only scores 54, force-only scores 59, both score 65.

7.2Wrenches: frames, drift, and normalisation

Three preprocessing issues that will silently destroy a policy if ignored. None are deep; all are routinely skipped.

Frame

A wrench is expressed in some frame. A sensor-frame reading means "this much force along the sensor's xxx", which changes meaning completely as the hand rotates — the same physical push against a table reads as +z+z+z or −y-y−y depending on wrist orientation. If the policy also receives the wrist pose it can in principle learn the transformation, but you are spending capacity on trigonometry. Transforming into a task-relevant frame (world, or the object's frame if you have it) generally helps. The exception is when what matters is intrinsically sensor-relative — normal force into the fingertip pad is meaningful in the sensor frame and meaningless in the world frame.

Gravity and bias

A wrist F/T sensor measures the weight of everything distal to it, so its reading changes with orientation even in free space. You must subtract the modelled gravitational wrench of the hand plus any grasped object. Separately, all these sensors drift: the zero point wanders with temperature and over hours of operation. Standard practice is to tare — record the reading during a known no-contact period and subtract it — and to re-tare periodically. T-Rex names this as a live limitation: "sensor distortion, calibration drift across devices, and the absence of dense palm sensing".

Why drift is an architectural argument, not just a calibration chore

Drift is the stated reason T-Rex discretises force. From App. C: "To robustly process high-frequency tactile observations and mitigate inherent sensor drift, continuous multi-finger force sequences are discretized into a compact token space using a VQ-VAE." A continuous embedding moves whenever the sensor's zero moves. A discrete token does not move at all until the drift is large enough to cross a decision boundary in the codebook — the quantiser acts as a deadband. This is a genuinely elegant argument and a good thing to be able to make: quantisation is not merely compression here, it is robustness to a specific physical failure mode.

Normalisation — force and torque are not the same quantity

Forces are tens of newtons; torques are fractions of a newton-metre. Sharing a normalisation constant across all six channels means torque arrives at the network as numerical noise.

class WrenchNormalizer(nn.Module):
    """Force and torque have different units and ~100x different magnitudes: never share a scale.
    Signed log compresses impact spikes without destroying the small-force regime."""
    def __init__(self, f_scale=20.0, t_scale=1.0):
        super().__init__()
        self.register_buffer("s", torch.tensor([f_scale]*3 + [t_scale]*3))
        self.register_buffer("bias", torch.zeros(6))
    def tare(self, w_rest):
        self.bias = w_rest.reshape(-1, 6).mean(0)          # zero the no-contact offset
    def forward(self, w):                                  # w: (..., 6), wrench axis LAST
        z = (w - self.bias) / self.s
        return torch.sign(z) * torch.log1p(z.abs())
force:torque magnitude ratio    raw 39.55  ->  normalized 1.22

On realistic synthetic data (forces σ=20\sigma=20σ=20 N, torques σ=0.5\sigma=0.5σ=0.5 N·m) the raw force:torque magnitude ratio is 39.6; after per-channel-group scaling it is 1.22. Without this step a gradient-descent optimiser sees six channels of which three are ~40× larger, and the three small ones are effectively ignored. The signed-log compression matters for a second reason: impact transients produce force spikes an order of magnitude above steady contact, and a linear scale either clips them or squashes the delicate small-force regime where "gentle" lives.

7.3Temporal encoding: the central insight

Ask what you would learn from a single instantaneous wrench reading of 4.2 N. Almost nothing. Is that a firm stable grasp, the beginning of an impact, or the object slipping? All three produce 4.2 N at some instant. The information in contact is in the derivative structure.

Table 7.2 — The same contact event, read instantaneously versus over a window. Every row in the right column is invisible in the left.
Physical eventInstantaneous readingTemporal signature
Making contactSome forceSharp rising edge in ∥f∥\|\mathbf{f}\|∥f∥
Stable graspSome forceFlat, low-variance plateau
Incipient slipSome forceHigh-frequency oscillation in the shear components
Gross slipSome forceSudden drop in shear with normal force sustained
Peg finding a holeSome forceDiscontinuity in the force gradient as a constraint is released

This is precisely the deficiency that sank π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile, which "extends the original state input by concatenating single-step tactile observations" [T-Rex, App. E]. Contrast with the systems that work:

  • T-Rex: a per-finger VQ-VAE over ft−15:t\mathbf{f}_{t-15:t}ft−15:t​ — a 16-frame window.
  • ViTacFormer: 18 frames from 20 tactile channels → [18,60][18, 60][18,60], concatenated with frame-wise deltas [18,60][18,60][18,60] → a [18,120][18,120][18,120] input. Explicitly doubling the representation to hand the network the temporal difference rather than hoping it computes one[ViTacFormer, App.].
  • Sparsh: two tactile images at a temporal stride of 5, channel-concatenated, an ~80 ms window at 60 FPS — chosen because that is "the reaction time that humans need to adjust the grip force when detecting partial slip". For its V-JEPA variant, 4 frames at [t,t−2,t−4,t−6][t,t{-}2,t{-}4,t{-}6][t,t−2,t−4,t−6], ~100 ms[Sparsh §3].
  • Tactile-VLA: an MLP over "the concatenated history of HHH tactile measurements" producing "a single fused token representing the interaction's temporal dynamics"[Tactile-VLA §2.1].

Four independent groups, four architectures, one shared conclusion: encode a window, never a sample. And note the window lengths converge on 80–500 ms, which is roughly the human tactile reaction timescale — not a coincidence, since it is the timescale at which contact events are decidable.

T-Rex's VQ-VAE force encoder, in full

From App. C, stated precisely: per fingertip, raw 6-dimensional force vectors over T=16T=16T=16 frames; a 1-D temporal convolutional encoder that hierarchically downsamples via two strided blocks; temporal mean-pooling to a 256-dimensional continuous embedding; vector quantisation to the nearest neighbour in a learned codebook of size K=64\mathbf{K=64}K=64; EMA codebook updates with periodic re-seeding of underused entries from current batch activations; a symmetric decoder reconstructing the sequence; a magnitude-weighted MSE (mean squared error) loss; and convolutional weights shared across all five fingers with distinct learned finger-identity embeddings injected before encoding. The result is "one discrete token per finger per hand".

ztτ=[ Embvq(Ef(ft−15:t))⏟temporal, discrete ; Projf(ft)⏟instantaneous ; Projd(Ed(dt))⏟spatial ]\mathbf{z}^\tau_t = \Big[\ \underbrace{\mathrm{Emb}_{\mathrm{vq}}\big(E_f(\mathbf{f}_{t-15:t})\big)}_{\text{temporal, discrete}}\ ;\ \underbrace{\mathrm{Proj}_f(\mathbf{f}_t)}_{\text{instantaneous}}\ ;\ \underbrace{\mathrm{Proj}_d\big(E_d(\mathbf{d}_t)\big)}_{\text{spatial}}\ \Big]ztτ​=[ temporal, discreteEmbvq​(Ef​(ft−15:t​))​​ ; instantaneousProjf​(ft​)​​ ; spatialProjd​(Ed​(dt​))​​ ]
(7.1)

Equation (7.1) is T-Rex's Eq. (2) and it is worth reading as a design statement rather than a formula. Three terms, three different kinds of information, deliberately kept separate. The VQ term is the dynamics — drift-robust and discrete. The projection of ft\mathbf{f}_tft​ is the instantaneous value, kept continuous because quantising it would throw away the precise magnitude needed for force regulation. The deformation term is the spatial contact pattern. Removing the VQ term and keeping only the MLP costs 7 points of success rate; using deformation alone costs 11.

Three mechanisms in that listing deserve comment because each defends against a specific failure:

The straight-through estimator. argmin has zero gradient everywhere, so the encoder would receive none. Writing z+sg(zq−z)z + \mathrm{sg}(z_q - z)z+sg(zq​−z) gives the decoder the quantised value in the forward pass while routing the gradient straight back to zzz in the backward pass. It is a biased estimator and it works.

Magnitude weighting. The paper states this explicitly: "to prevent the codebook from collapsing onto dominant non-contact states, the network is optimized via a magnitude-weighted MSE loss, which assigns higher optimization penalties to frames experiencing high-force contacts." Most frames in any manipulation dataset are free-space. A uniform loss makes the optimal codebook one that reconstructs silence perfectly, which is exactly the wrong allocation of 64 codes.

Shared weights, distinct identity embeddings. Five fingers share the convolution — so the force-dynamics prior is learned once from 5× the data — while a per-finger learned embedding added before encoding lets a thumb behave differently from a little finger. The paper motivates this as "parameter efficiency and cross-digit scalability". This is a pattern worth stealing generally: share the mechanism, parameterise the identity.

Codebook collapse is real — a demonstration

Training the module above from scratch on synthetic contact data (40% of fingers making contact at a random onset within the window):

step   0 | active codes  1 / 64 | loss  5.809
step 100 | active codes  2 / 64 | loss  4.943
step 200 | active codes  5 / 64 | loss  6.576
step 300 | active codes 13 / 64 | loss  5.216

At initialisation, every input maps to a single code — textbook collapse. The EMA update plus dead-code re-seeding pulls utilisation up to 13 of 64 over 300 steps. It is not converged (real training runs far longer on real data), but the trajectory is the point: without re-seeding, codes that receive no assignments receive no gradient and stay dead forever, and the codebook degenerates to a handful of entries. If you implement a VQ tokeniser, log active-code count every epoch; it is the single most informative diagnostic and it fails silently.

7.4Spatial tactile: deformation maps and marker fields

The second half of a hybrid fingertip is an image of the contact patch. T-Rex describes it precisely: "a dense, single-channel spatial deformation map dt\mathbf{d}_tdt​ representing the local skin displacement field. These maps capture rich, high-frequency contact geometry, such as edges, slip, and shear patterns that are inherently lost in low-dimensional force vectors."

That last clause is the justification for carrying both. A 6-vector is the integral of the pressure distribution over the contact patch — total force and total moment. Two completely different contact configurations can integrate to the same wrench: a card gripped along its edge and a card gripped at one corner can produce identical net force. The deformation map distinguishes them, and for tasks like T-Rex's Sort Mahjong (tiles identified by surface texture) or Extract Card it is the only signal that can.

The encoder

T-Rex uses "a lightweight convolutional network adapted from a ResNet-18 backbone. The standard input stem is modified to ingest a single-channel input, and only the first three residual stages are retained. Each stage is appended with a 3×33\times33×3 convolutional layer that re-projects the intermediate feature maps to a fixed width of 128 channels." Critically: this encoder "is pre-trained within a self-supervised convolutional autoencoder framework and subsequently frozen during policy learning".

Three design decisions, each defensible:

  • Only three of four residual stages. Stage 4 exists in ResNet-18 to build high-level semantic abstractions for ImageNet classification. A deformation map has no semantics; it has geometry. Stage 4 would add parameters and destroy spatial resolution for nothing.
  • Single-channel stem. Trivial but load-bearing: reusing a 3-channel stem by replicating the map wastes two-thirds of the first layer's compute.
  • Frozen, autoencoder-pretrained. This buys a stable representation "without expanding the trainable parameter footprint of the policy network". It also sidesteps the drowning problem entirely for this branch — a frozen encoder cannot be starved of gradient, because it does not want any. This is an underrated trick and worth reaching for in a design.

Optical sensors: the marker-field alternative

For GelSight-style sensors you have a further choice. The raw tactile image is a photograph of an illuminated gel, so it carries the sensor's lighting, its marker pattern, and its manufacturing idiosyncrasies — none of which transfer. RDP's answer is to extract the marker displacement field by optical flow against a no-contact reference frame, then reduce it by PCA (principal component analysis):

def marker_field_pca(flow, n_comp=6):
    """RDP's optical-tactile representation: PCA over the (7x9 x 2) marker displacement field."""
    X  = flow.flatten(1)                          # (N, 2 * n_marker)
    Xc = X - X.mean(0, keepdim=True)
    U, S, V = torch.pca_lowrank(Xc, q=n_comp)
    return Xc @ V, V
# marker field (200, 63, 2) -> PCA (200, 6) | basis (126, 6)

RDP's stated rationale: "The use of PCA feature makes the model more robust to tracking errors and noise of marker deformation field. In addition, PCA features are more robust to texture and lighting changes due to damage or gel replacements." That last point is a deployment reality nobody mentions in papers about architectures — gels wear out, you replace them, and a policy trained on raw tactile pixels of the old gel now sees a distribution shift. A six-dimensional PCA projection of a displacement field is far more stable across that event.

RDP also uses the 3D deformation field Vt=[dx,dy,oz]V_t = [\mathbf{d}_x, \mathbf{d}_y, \mathbf{o}_z]Vt​=[dx​,dy​,oz​] as a unified representation across sensor types — the same structure describes a GelSight marker field, a cheap MCTac, and (with [fx,fy,fz][\mathbf{f}_x,\mathbf{f}_y,\mathbf{f}_z][fx​,fy​,fz​]) a plain force sensor. That abstraction is what let them demonstrate the same policy across three physically different sensors. If you are asked how to build a tactile stack that is not locked to one vendor, this is the answer: define a sensor-agnostic intermediate representation and calibrate each sensor into it.

7.5Learned tactile representations

Since there is no internet of touch, self-supervision on unlabelled tactile data is the closest available substitute, and Sparsh is the reference point.

Table 7.3 — Sparsh design choices and what each defends against. Source: Sparsh.
ChoiceDetailRationale
Background subtractionSubtract a no-contact reference frame (DIGIT, GelSight Mini markerless)Removes markers, lighting placement, and manufacturing variation; "provides the model with a reference to no-contact"
Temporal stackingIt⊕It−5I_t \oplus I_{t-5}It​⊕It−5​ channel-concatenated → Rh×w×6\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times 6}Rh×w×6~80 ms window at 60 FPS — the human reaction time for detecting partial slip
Video variant4 frames at [t,t−2,t−4,t−6][t, t{-}2, t{-}4, t{-}6][t,t−2,t−4,t−6] → ~100 msFiner temporal detail; V-JEPA variant gets the best slip-detection F1
Pretraining data460k+ tactile images across DIGIT, GelSight 2017, GelSight MiniCross-sensor generality
ObjectivesMAE, DINO, I-JEPA, V-JEPALatent-space objectives (DINO, I-JEPA) beat pixel-space (MAE), "indicating the merits of learning in latent space for tactile images"

The headline numbers: +95.1% average improvement over task- and sensor-specific end-to-end training across TacBench's six tasks when all models get 33–50% of the labels; force estimation error below 0.1 N with Sparsh (DINO) using as little as 1–10% of the labels; inference up to 112 FPS on an RTX 3080, so "Sparsh is limited by data streaming rates, and not by inference time".

Two findings worth carrying away. First, latent-space SSL beats pixel-space SSL for touch, and the reason generalises: a tactile image's pixels encode gel texture, marker positions and illumination, all of which are nuisance variables. An objective that forces pixel reconstruction spends capacity modelling them; a latent objective can discard them. This is the same argument JEPA makes for video (Chapter 15), arriving independently in a different modality. Second, the best objective depends on the task: DINO wins on force regression, V-JEPA on slip detection (it sees a 4-frame clip and slip is intrinsically temporal), MAE — masked autoencoding — on texture classification (it "heavily relies on pixel-level features", and texture is a pixel-level property). There is no single best tactile encoder.

Sparsh-X[Sparsh-X] extends this to the Digit 360's four simultaneous touch modalities — tactile image, audio, IMU, and pressure — fusing them with a transformer backbone using self-distillation (DINO loss) and bottleneck fusion over ~1M contact-rich interactions. It reports +63% policy success over an end-to-end tactile-image model and +90% robustness in recovering object state from touch. Note what "bottleneck fusion" is doing: a small number of shared tokens that all modalities must route information through, which forces cross-modal agreement instead of letting each modality maintain a private channel. That is an architectural answer to modality imbalance and it recurs in Chapter 8.

7.6Force as an output, not just an input

Everything so far treats contact as something you perceive. The more powerful move is to make force part of the action space, so the policy commands a target force and a low-level controller realises it.

Tactile-VLA does exactly this: the action expert "outputs an augmented action vector ata_tat​ that explicitly specifies the target position PtargetP_{\text{target}}Ptarget​ and the target contact force FtargetF_{\text{target}}Ftarget​"[Tactile-VLA §2.1]. A hybrid position-force controller then converts the force target into a position correction:

ΔF=Ftarget−Fmeasured,Phybrid=Ptarget+K ΔF⋅1[∥ΔF∥>τ]\Delta F = F_{\text{target}} - F_{\text{measured}}, \qquad P_{\text{hybrid}} = P_{\text{target}} + K\,\Delta F \cdot \mathbb{1}\big[\|\Delta F\| > \tau\big]ΔF=Ftarget​−Fmeasured​,Phybrid​=Ptarget​+KΔF⋅1[∥ΔF∥>τ]
(7.2)

Three things make this work. It is position-dominant — the command ultimately sent is a position, "acknowledging that most manipulation tasks are dominated by precise kinematic motion, with force control required merely during contact phases". There is a deadband τ\tauτ — corrections apply only when the force error exceeds a threshold, "to enhance operational smoothness", which prevents the controller from chattering on sensor noise in free space. And the two force channels are decoupled: Cartesian position regulates the net external force on the object while gripper width regulates the internal grasping force, "thus dictating how firmly the object is held". Those are independent physical quantities and conflating them is a classic bug.

Impedance is not force control

Classic impedance control[Hogan 1985] makes the manipulator behave like a spring-damper: it achieves passive compliance, a relationship between deviation and force, and it is what keeps a robot safe on contact. Tactile-VLA is explicit that its objective is different — "unlike classic impedance control which aims for passive compliance, our objective is the active tracking of a target force." If you are asked how to make a policy press with 5 N, "use impedance control" is an incomplete answer: impedance gives you a stiffness, and you still need an outer loop that servos the measured force to 5 N.

The payoff is semantic, and it is the most striking result in Tactile-VLA. Because force is in the action space and language is in the input, the model learns the mapping from adverbs to newtons. Trained to associate "softly" and "hard" with force profiles on a USB-insertion task, it transfers that understanding zero-shot to charger insertion, a task for which it learned only the motion and never saw a force-related instruction. It also applies commonsense without being told — firm grasps for heavy objects, gentle ones for fragile ones, on unseen objects. The paper's framing is that "the VLM's prior knowledge already contains semantic understanding of physical interaction; by connecting it to the robot's tactile sensors with only a few demonstrations, we can activate this prior knowledge."

That is a genuinely important idea for a senior discussion: the web-scale VLM already knows that eggs need gentler handling than hammers. The bottleneck was never that knowledge, it was the absence of an interface between it and a force controller. Putting force in the action space is that interface.

7.7The long tail: audio, events, IMU, thermal

Contact audio

A piezoelectric contact microphone is the cheapest high-bandwidth contact sensor that exists, and ManiWAV[Liu et al. 2024] built an "ear-in-hand" gripper around one for in-the-wild data collection. Audio "provides rich information for robot interaction and object properties through contact, and can ease the learning of contact-rich robot manipulation skills, especially when visual information alone is ambiguous or incomplete". RDP's cost comparison applies here too: acoustic sensors "provide a wide range of alternative tactile feedback at a much lower cost".

The encoding question is the interesting one. Audio arrives at 16–44 kHz as a scalar stream — about a thousand samples per vision frame. You do not feed samples to a transformer. You compute a log-mel spectrogram and treat it as an image:

One second of 16 kHz audio — sixteen thousand numbers — becomes a single token. The mel scale matters because it is logarithmic in frequency, matching both human perception and the physics: the resonant modes that identify a material are multiplicatively, not additively, spaced. The log compression handles the enormous dynamic range between a whisper of scraping and an impact.

What audio is uniquely good at: detecting the instant of contact (a sharp broadband transient, far crisper than a force sensor's mechanical response); identifying material from impact sound; and detecting slip through the characteristic broadband friction noise. What it is bad at: anything spatial. It has no idea where the contact is. It is a natural partner for force, which knows magnitude and direction but responds too slowly to catch the transient.

Event cameras

An event camera emits an asynchronous stream of (t,x,y,p)(t, x, y, p)(t,x,y,p) tuples — a pixel fired at time ttt with polarity ppp — with microsecond latency, very high dynamic range, and no motion blur. For high-speed manipulation this is compelling; the difficulty is that the representation choice dominates everything, because a transformer wants dense tensors and events are a sparse spatiotemporal point cloud.

The standard encoding is a voxel grid with bilinear interpolation in time, which is what preserves the sub-frame timing that justified using an event camera in the first place:

An honest assessment: event cameras in manipulation are promising but not established. The 2025 literature (SEBVS and the CVPR event-vision workshop line) reports event-based policies outperforming RGB baselines with faster reaction and better robustness to motion blur and lighting, but there is no event-camera equivalent of π0\pi_0π0​ or T-Rex. If asked, say you would use one where its advantages are decisive — high-speed dynamic tasks, catching, harsh or variable lighting — and that you would treat the representation (voxel grid versus time surface versus learned event-to-frame) as the primary design decision rather than the backbone.

IMU and thermal

An IMU on the wrist or fingertip measures accelerations and angular rates at high rate, and is excellent at detecting impacts and vibration signatures — Sparsh-X includes it as one of its four touch modalities for exactly that reason. Encode it like force: a window, normalised per channel group (accelerometer and gyroscope have different units), through a small temporal convolution. Its weakness is drift, which makes integrated position from an IMU useless over any horizon that matters. Thermal is genuinely niche but has one killer application: detecting recent contact. A surface a human or robot just touched is warmer, which gives you a short-term memory of interaction that no other modality provides. Encode as a single-channel image. Cite it as an example of thinking about what information a task actually needs rather than reaching for standard sensors.

Key takeaways
  1. Wrench and deformation map are physically different signals needing different encoders: temporal for the first, spatial for the second. T-Rex's ablation: force-only 59, deformation-only 54, both 65.
  2. Normalise force and torque separately — a 39.6:1 raw magnitude ratio becomes 1.2:1. Tare for bias, compensate gravity, and choose your frame deliberately.
  3. A single-timestep wrench is nearly useless. Every working system encodes an 80–500 ms window. This is the main reason π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile failed.
  4. T-Rex quantises force with a K=64K{=}64K=64 VQ-VAE specifically to be robust to drift: a discrete code does not move until the drift crosses a decision boundary.
  5. Magnitude-weighted reconstruction loss stops the codebook spending its capacity on free space. Log active-code count — collapse is real and silent (1 of 64 codes live at init).
  6. Freeze an autoencoder-pretrained deformation encoder: stable features, no extra policy parameters, and immune to gradient starvation.
  7. Use a sensor-agnostic intermediate representation (RDP's 3D deformation field, or PCA over marker flow) so gel replacement and vendor changes do not break the policy.
  8. Latent-space SSL beats pixel-space for touch (Sparsh); the best objective is task-dependent — DINO for force, V-JEPA for slip, MAE for texture.
  9. Putting target force in the action space with a hybrid position-force controller lets language modulate physical interaction — Tactile-VLA transfers "softly" zero-shot across tasks. Impedance control ≠ force tracking.
  10. Audio catches the contact instant and material identity but has no spatial information; encode as log-mel, one token per second of audio.

8Fusion architectures and modality imbalance

Core ideas

Once every modality is a set of tokens, you must decide how they interact. The options form a spectrum from concatenate everything and let attention sort it out to keep the streams separate and let one gate the other. The choice is driven by two quantities: the token-count ratio between modalities, and the rate ratio. When the counts are lopsided you get drowning; when the rates are lopsided you get aliasing. This chapter derives the drowning argument honestly — stating clearly where it is a theorem, where it is an approximation, and where it is a hypothesis — and then surveys the fixes that are actually published against the ones that merely sound good.

8.1The fusion spectrum

Table 8.1 — Fusion mechanisms. The last column is the question to ask yourself before choosing.
MechanismHowCostUsed byChoose when
Token concatenationAll modalities in one sequence; full self-attentionO(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^2)O(L2)Tactile-VLA, π0\pi_0π0​Token counts are comparable and you want maximum flexibility
Cross-attentionOne stream queries another; streams stay separateO(NaNb)\mathcal{O}(N_a N_b)O(Na​Nb​)ViTacFormer, GR00T DiTTwo streams of very different length; you want explicit control over who reads whom
FiLMConditioning signal emits per-channel scale and shiftO(d)\mathcal{O}(d)O(d)OpenVLA-OFT+Low-dimensional modality should gate a high-dimensional one
Perceiver / bottleneckFixed learned latents cross-attend the raw tokensO(Nnlat)\mathcal{O}(N n_{\text{lat}})O(Nnlat​)Sparsh-X bottleneck fusionOne modality has enormous token count; you need a fixed budget
Mixture-of-TransformersPer-modality weights, global attentionSame FLOPs, more paramsπ0\pi_0π0​, T-RexModalities have conflicting training dynamics but must interact richly
Mixture-of-Experts routingLearned router over modality-aware expertsSparseForceVLA (FVLMoE)You want context-dependent routing, not fixed-by-modality
Late fusion / separate ratesIndependent branches combined near the outputLowRDP, T-Rex tactile expertRates differ by an order of magnitude or more

Cross-attention

ViTacFormer's version is bidirectional and the paper is explicit: "The keys and values from visual observations are calculated with the queries from tactile signals and vice versa. Finally, the cross-attention-based features are concatenated into hidden states."

The structural advantage over concatenation is that the tactile stream has its own queries. With 10 tactile tokens and 256 visual ones, the tactile→vision attention matrix is 10×25610\times25610×256: every tactile token gets a full, normalised distribution over the visual tokens, and that distribution sums to one regardless of how many visual tokens there are. Adding a camera does not dilute it. Compare with concatenated self-attention, where the tactile token is one key among 270 and its share falls as you add cameras. This is a real and under-appreciated argument for cross-attention in exactly the asymmetric regime robotics lives in.

ViTacFormer's ablation supports it: "Removing the cross-attention module and replacing it with naive concatenation leads to a significant performance drop, particularly in the Peg Insertion and Cap Twist tasks… the model fails to dynamically weigh the importance of tactile features when visual features are ambiguous (e.g., during occlusion)."

FiLM

FiLM conditions by emitting a per-channel affine transform rather than a token:

FiLM(x∣c)=(1+γ(c))⊙x+β(c),[γ;β]=Wc\mathrm{FiLM}(\mathbf{x} \mid \mathbf{c}) = \big(1 + \gamma(\mathbf{c})\big)\odot \mathbf{x} + \beta(\mathbf{c}), \qquad [\gamma;\beta] = W\mathbf{c}FiLM(x∣c)=(1+γ(c))⊙x+β(c),[γ;β]=Wc
(8.1)

Two properties make FiLM the right default for low-dimensional modalities. It is multiplicative, so the conditioning signal does not compete for attention mass at all — it reaches into every visual channel simultaneously and reweights it, which is a far larger lever than one token among 270. And with zero-initialised weights it is exactly the identity at initialisation, so bolting it onto a pretrained backbone cannot degrade the pretrained behaviour on step zero. That property matters enormously given the π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile result: the failure there was partly that new inputs perturbed a good representation, and a zero-initialised FiLM structurally cannot.

Perceiver bottleneck

class PerceiverResampler(nn.Module):
    """Fixed learned latents cross-attend the raw token soup. Decouples downstream cost
    from input length: 4096 point-cloud tokens collapse to n_latent regardless of N."""
    def forward(self, x):                                   # (B,N,d) -> (B,n_latent,d)
        q = self.latents.unsqueeze(0).expand(x.shape[0], -1, -1)
        z = q + self.attn(q, x, x, need_weights=False)[0]
        return z + self.ff(z)
# Perceiver: (4, 4096, 512) -> (4, 64, 512)

This is the right tool when one modality's raw token count is unbounded — point clouds, long audio, multi-camera video. It also gives you an explicit token budget per modality, which turns drowning from an emergent property into a design parameter you set.

8.2Modality drowning, derived carefully

Epistemic status

What follows is an argument, not a published theorem, and it is labelled that way wherever it is used. The attention-mass calculation is exact under its stated assumption; that assumption (approximately uniform attention) holds at initialisation and degrades as training proceeds. The published literature on modality imbalance addresses it mainly through gradient modulation (OGM-GE, AGM), loss balancing, and reweighting — not through attention-logit bias. I flag below precisely which fixes are empirically validated in robotics and which are reasoned proposals.

Take a softmax attention layer. For a query iii, the weight on key jjj is

αij=exp⁡(qi⊤kj/d)∑j′=1Lexp⁡(qi⊤kj′/d)\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(q_i^\top k_j/\sqrt{d})}{\sum_{j'=1}^{L}\exp(q_i^\top k_{j'}/\sqrt{d})}αij​=∑j′=1L​exp(qi⊤​kj′​/d​)exp(qi⊤​kj​/d​)​
(8.2)

At initialisation, qqq and kkk are near-isotropic random projections of near-isotropic features, so the logits are small and roughly exchangeable, giving αij≈1/L\alpha_{ij}\approx 1/Lαij​≈1/L. The total attention mass flowing to a modality mmm occupying nmn_mnm​ tokens is therefore

Am  =  ∑j∈mαij  ≈  nmL\mathcal{A}_m \;=\; \sum_{j \in m}\alpha_{ij} \;\approx\; \frac{n_m}{L}Am​=j∈m∑​αij​≈Lnm​​
(8.3)

Now the consequence. The value vector of a force token enters the output only through ∑jαijvj\sum_j \alpha_{ij} v_j∑j​αij​vj​, so the gradient that reaches the force encoder's parameters is scaled by αi,force\alpha_{i,\text{force}}αi,force​. Two encoders receiving gradients whose magnitudes differ by a factor of nvis/nforcen_{\text{vis}}/n_{\text{force}}nvis​/nforce​ do not learn at the same rate. Under a fixed learning rate, the force encoder is effectively training with a learning rate hundreds of times smaller.

def attention_mass(n_vis, n_lang, n_prop, n_force, n_cam=1):
    L = n_vis * n_cam + n_lang + n_prop + n_force
    return {"context_len": L, "force_share": n_force / L, "vision_share": n_vis * n_cam / L}
1 cam(s): L= 270 | force share 0.00370 (1 in  270) | vision share 0.948
2 cam(s): L= 526 | force share 0.00190 (1 in  526) | vision share 0.973
3 cam(s): L= 782 | force share 0.00128 (1 in  782) | vision share 0.982
adding 2 cameras shrinks the force token's share by 2.90x

The scaling is the part worth stating explicitly because it is counterintuitive and actionable: every camera you add makes your force signal harder to learn. Vision already commands 94.8% of the context with one camera and 98.2% with three. Nothing about the force sensor changed; you drowned it by improving your vision stack.

Where the argument is weak, and how to sharpen it

The obvious objection is: "attention is not uniform after training — a trained network learns to attend to force when force matters." The objection is correct, and the repair is not to retreat from the claim but to narrow it.

The argument is about optimisation dynamics, not expressive capacity. Nothing prevents a trained transformer from placing 90% of its attention on a force token at the moment of contact. The question is whether gradient descent will find that solution, starting from a state where the force branch receives 1/270 of the gradient signal and its encoder therefore produces near-random features — which in turn gives the attention mechanism no reason to attend to it. It is a chicken-and-egg problem, and the empirical shape of the π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile result (adding force made things worse) is consistent with the network never escaping it.

The honest summary: the uniform-attention calculation is an initialisation-time argument that explains why the optimisation is badly conditioned; it is not a claim that the architecture cannot represent the solution. Say that and you have given a better answer than the calculation alone.

8.3The fixes, sorted by evidence

Table 8.2 — Remedies for modality imbalance. The evidence column is the part that matters.
FixMechanismEvidence
Vision-corruption curriculum (FACTR)Corrupt the visual input with decreasing intensity during training, so the policy must initially rely on forcePublished, robotics. +43% generalisation to unseen objects vs. no curriculum [FACTR]
Dedicated expert with its own parameters (T-Rex)A separate tactile expert owns the last segment of the flow trajectory; it cannot be bypassed because the action is not finished without itPublished, robotics. 65% vs 6% for naive concatenation; async vs sync worth +5
Force-aware MoE after the VLM (ForceVLA)6-axis force is projected to dedicated tokens and fused via an MoE module during action decoding, preserving pretrained VL representationsPublished, robotics. +23.2% success; 80% plug insertion [ForceVLA]
Architectural asymmetry (RDP)Tactile enters only the decoder, so the latent action chunk structurally cannot encode reactive detail — the decoder must use touchPublished, robotics. >35% improvement over visual IL baselines
Auxiliary prediction objectivePredict future tactile (ViTacFormer) or future visual latents (T-Rex, λfuture=0.5\lambda_{\text{future}}{=}0.5λfuture​=0.5) so the tactile encoder gets gradient from a dense taskPublished, robotics. Removing it "significantly degrades performance"
Gradient modulation (OGM-GE, AGM)Directly rescale per-modality gradients during backprop to suppress the dominant modalityPublished, general multimodal ML; not, to my knowledge, demonstrated on a VLA
Cross-attention instead of concatenationTactile gets its own queries, so its attention distribution is normalised independently of nvisn_{\text{vis}}nvis​Published, robotics (ViTacFormer ablation), though framed as fusion quality rather than imbalance
FiLM gatingLow-dim modality modulates rather than competesPublished for language (OpenVLA-OFT+); the extension to force is a reasonable proposal
Additive attention-logit biasA learned per-modality pre-softmax bias guarantees an attention floorArgument only. Mechanically sound and easy to implement, but I am not aware of a published robotics result validating it. Present as a hypothesis

The logit-bias proposal, stated properly

Since this is the fix most often reached for, it is worth writing down precisely — both so you can implement it and so you can be honest about its status.

αij=softmaxj ⁣(qi⊤kjd+bm(j))    ⟹    αij∝ebm(j)⋅exp⁡ ⁣(qi⊤kjd)\alpha_{ij} = \mathrm{softmax}_j\!\left(\frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d}} + b_{m(j)}\right) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; \alpha_{ij} \propto e^{b_{m(j)}}\cdot \exp\!\left(\frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d}}\right)αij​=softmaxj​(d​qi⊤​kj​​+bm(j)​)⟹αij​∝ebm(j)​⋅exp(d​qi⊤​kj​​)
(8.4)

The mechanism is visible in the right-hand form: a pre-softmax additive bias becomes a post-softmax multiplicative factor ebme^{b_m}ebm​ on every key of modality mmm, independent of key content. That independence is exactly why it survives where the obvious alternatives do not:

  • Why not scale the force embedding? Because LayerNorm renormalises it away. Any constant rescaling of a feature vector is undone by the very next normalisation layer.
  • Why not upweight a force-related loss term? Because that shapes the readout, not the mixing. You can make the network predict forces accurately from an auxiliary head while the action head still ignores the force tokens.
  • Why pre-softmax and not post-softmax? A post-softmax reweighting breaks normalisation; you would have to renormalise, which reintroduces the competition.
class BiasedAttention(nn.Module):
    """Additive PRE-softmax logit bias per modality. gate_dim>0 makes it state-conditioned,
    computed from a signal that is NOT itself drowned (e.g. raw force magnitude).
    NOTE: principled, but not validated in a published robotics result. A hypothesis."""
    def forward(self, x, modality_id, gate_input=None):
        q, k, v = [t.view(B, L, self.h, self.dh).transpose(1,2) for t in self.qkv(x).chunk(3,-1)]
        logits = q @ k.transpose(-1,-2) / math.sqrt(self.dh)
        b = self.bias.unsqueeze(0).expand(B, -1, -1)              # (B, heads, n_modality)
        if self.gate is not None:
            b = b + self.gate(gate_input).view(B, self.h, self.n_modality)   # state-conditioned
        key_bias = torch.gather(b, 2, modality_id.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, self.h, -1))
        logits = logits + key_bias.unsqueeze(2)                   # broadcast over the QUERY axis
        a = logits.softmax(-1)
        return self.o((a @ v).transpose(1,2).reshape(B, L, d)), a
force-key attention mass: before 0.00349 -> after bias=+4: 0.15794 (45.2x)

A bias of +4+4+4 raises the force token's attention mass 45-fold, from 0.35% to 15.8% — close to e4≈54.6e^4 \approx 54.6e4≈54.6, the discrepancy being the renormalisation. The mechanism works exactly as derived.

The follow-up question: why a static bias is wrong

Having proposed a fixed bias, the natural next question is when it hurts. Force matters during contact. In free space, the fingertip wrench is near zero plus noise, and forcing the policy to spend 16% of its attention on noise is actively harmful — you have traded one misallocation for another. So the bias should be state-conditioned: bm=bm(state)b_m = b_m(\text{state})bm​=bm​(state).

And then the trap inside the trap: what do you condition the gate on? If you compute the gate from the full attended representation, you have re-introduced drowning inside the gate — the gate's input is dominated by vision, so it will not learn to fire on contact. The gate must be computed from a signal that is not itself drowned: raw force magnitude ∥ft∥\|\mathbf{f}_t\|∥ft​∥ through a tiny dedicated branch, or the flow-matching timestep τ\tauτ, or a lightweight proprioception feature. Being able to identify that recursion is the difference between a good answer and an excellent one.

8.4Rate mismatch and the two-rate solution

The second structural problem is temporal. A kHz force stream fused into a 30 Hz token sequence has been decimated by a factor of 33. By Nyquist, everything above 15 Hz is aliased, and contact transients live well above 15 Hz. The information is destroyed before any architecture sees it — no attention mechanism can recover it.

Hence the two-rate architecture, which by 2026 is the consensus answer. Both leading systems reach it by different routes:

Table 8.3 — Two-rate contact architectures.
RDPT-Rex
Slow streamLatent Diffusion Policy over latent action chunks, 1–2 HzAction expert, flow matching τ:1→0.4\tau: 1 \to 0.4τ:1→0.4, once per 16-step chunk
Fast streamAsymmetric Tokenizer decoder, 20–30 Hz (<1 ms inference, could run >300 Hz)Tactile expert, τ:0.4→0\tau: 0.4 \to 0τ:0.4→0, 4× per chunk at offsets {0,4,8,12}\{0,4,8,12\}{0,4,8,12}
How tactile entersDecoder only — the encoder never sees itTactile tokens + cached KV; the tactile expert never sees raw vision
Why that forces its useThe latent chunk structurally cannot encode reactive detail, so the decoder must supply it from touchThe action is not executable until the tactile expert finishes the trajectory
Slow-stream outputA latent action chunk Z∈Rt×d\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{t\times d}Z∈Rt×dA partially-denoised action x^τsplit\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\tau_{\text{split}}}x^τsplit​​ + a KV cache

RDP's asymmetry deserves a sentence of its own because it is the cleverest idea in that paper: "we utilize tactile representation solely as input in the decoder. This deliberate asymmetry in structure is designed to ensure that the latent action chunk retains only high-level feedback strategies, while the precise locations are predicted by the decoder with the tactile information." An information-theoretic argument for why the policy must use touch — it is not encouraged to, it is unable to do otherwise, because the reactive detail is not present in the latent it was given. Architectural constraint beats loss weighting every time.

Key takeaways
  1. Fusion spans concatenation → cross-attention → FiLM → bottleneck → MoT → MoE → late fusion. Choose on the token-count ratio and the rate ratio.
  2. Cross-attention beats concatenation in the asymmetric regime because the small modality gets its own queries, so its attention distribution does not dilute as you add cameras.
  3. FiLM is multiplicative and identity-at-init — it cannot damage a pretrained backbone, which matters given how π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile failed.
  4. Drowning: under uniform attention a force token gets nm/Ln_m/Lnm​/L — 1/270 at one camera, 1/782 at three. Adding cameras drowns force.
  5. State the argument's limits: it is about optimisation conditioning at initialisation, not expressive capacity. That caveat is the mark of understanding it.
  6. Published fixes: FACTR's vision-corruption curriculum (+43%), T-Rex's dedicated expert, ForceVLA's force MoE (+23.2%), RDP's decoder-only asymmetry (>35%), auxiliary prediction losses. Logit bias is a sound proposal, not a validated result — say so.
  7. A static bias hurts in free space. Make it state-conditioned — and condition the gate on a signal that is not itself drowned, or you relocate the problem into the gate.
  8. Rate mismatch destroys information irrecoverably by aliasing. Two-rate architectures are the consensus answer, and the best ones make tactile use structurally unavoidable.
Part IV

Case Studies

Four architectures, read for their reasoning rather than their results. Each chapter states the tensor contract explicitly, gives the network as a block diagram with shapes on every wire, writes the loss out in full, and works backwards from the deployment constraint to the design that answers it. Two of the four are traced across their whole line of papers, because the variable each successive paper moved is more informative than any one of them alone.

9Case study: T-Rex

Core ideas

T-Rex[Niu et al., arXiv:2606.17055, 15 Jun 2026] is worth studying in full because it is a clean instance of every principle in this Part. Its central architectural move — asynchronous cascaded flow matching — is the most elegant answer yet to the rate-mismatch problem: split the flow trajectory at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​, let a heavy vision-conditioned expert do the coarse part once per chunk, and let a light tactile-conditioned expert finish the fine part four times per chunk against a cached prefix. Both experts regress the same velocity target on disjoint sub-intervals, which is what makes the split coherent rather than a hack. It achieves 65% average success across 12 contact-rich tasks against 35% for the strongest baseline.

9.1The setup

Bimanual Dexmate Vega-1 (7 actuated joints per arm; wheels, torso and head fixed) with two 22-DoF Sharpa Wave dexterous hands. Three RGB streams at 640×360640\times360640×360: a head ZED X Mini and two wrist-mounted ZED X One S. Ten fingertip tactile sensors, each providing a deformation depth map and a 6-axis net wrench. Relative end-effector delta control for the arms via differential IK (Pink / Pinocchio), absolute joint control for the fingers, low-pass filtered into a 300 Hz cascade PID loop. Teleoperation by Manus gloves (fingertip positions, retargeted) plus VIVE trackers (wrist SE(3)SE(3)SE(3)), with a 30 Hz high-level thread and a 300 Hz low-level thread.

Three experts on a Qwen3VL-2B backbone: a latent expert (1.41B, 28 layers, hidden 2048) predicting future visual representations; an action expert (1.41B, action dim 62, chunk 16, 6 inference timesteps); and a tactile expert (0.62B, FFN intermediate size 1536, 4 inference timesteps). Trained on 24 H100s, AdamW, peak LR 1×10−41\times10^{-4}1×10−4, cosine schedule, bf16, DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 1.

Stated as a tensor contract, in the same form as the three chapters that follow:

Table 9.0 — The T-Rex tensor contract. The two output ports are the point: one expert produces a boundary state and the other finishes it, on disjoint parts of the same flow interval. Source: T-Rex §4 and App. A.
PortShapeWhat it is

9.2Asynchronous cascaded flow matching

Standard conditional flow matching, in T-Rex's convention (x0x_0x0​ = clean action, x1x_1x1​ = noise):

Now the idea. Split [0,1][0,1][0,1] at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​. The action expert integrates the upper segment τ∈[τsplit,1]\tau\in[\tau_{\text{split}},1]τ∈[τsplit​,1] — from pure noise down to a partially-denoised intermediate state. The tactile expert integrates the lower segment τ∈[0,τsplit]\tau\in[0,\tau_{\text{split}}]τ∈[0,τsplit​] — from that intermediate state to the final executable action.

With N=10N=10N=10 total Euler steps, τsplit=0.4\tau_{\text{split}}=0.4τsplit​=0.4, Kslow=6K_{\text{slow}}=6Kslow​=6, Kfast=4K_{\text{fast}}=4Kfast​=4, and chunk length Ta=16T_a=16Ta​=16, the fast stream is "triggered frequently at offsets {0,4,8,12}\{0,4,8,12\}{0,4,8,12} within the chunk, which bypasses the heavy visual network".

Why this is the right place to split. This is the conceptual core and worth articulating carefully. In a flow model, the trajectory from noise to data resolves structure coarse-to-fine: early integration steps (high τ\tauτ) decide the gross shape of the motion — which object, which direction, which strategy — and late steps (low τ\tauτ) decide precise values. The gross shape is a vision-and-language question and it changes slowly. The precise values are a contact question and they change fast. So the split is not an arbitrary computational division; it aligns the trajectory's own coarse-to-fine structure with the physical coarse-to-fine structure of the task, and gives each half to the modality that can actually answer it.

9.3Training the two experts

Each expert is trained on its own τ\tauτ range, with the action expert deliberately covering the full interval:
