Four implementation details in the appendix that are easy to miss and each of which matters:

  1. The action expert trains over the full (0,1](0,1](0,1], not just its deployment interval. The paper's reason: "training the action expert across the full (0,1](0,1](0,1] domain ensures it retains standalone competency of action generation and keeps consistency with the pretraining paradigm." So the model degrades gracefully — if tactile sensing fails, the action expert can still produce a complete action. That is a robustness property bought for free by a choice of sampling range.
  2. The KV cache is detached. "KVτsplit\mathrm{KV}_{\tau_{\text{split}}}KVτsplit​​ is extracted from a detached slow-stream pass" run under torch.no_grad. The tactile expert therefore cannot backpropagate into the vision tower. This prevents the tactile objective from corrupting the pretrained visual representation — the exact failure mode that sank the naive baseline.
  3. The cache is re-encoded at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​. It is composed as KVτsplit=[KVlat∣KVτsplitact]\mathrm{KV}_{\tau_{\mathrm{split}}}=[\mathrm{KV}^{\mathrm{lat}} \mid \mathrm{KV}^{\mathrm{act}}_{\tau_{\mathrm{split}}}]KVτsplit​​=[KVlat∣KVτsplit​act​], so the action positions are re-encoded at the split time rather than at the initial noise time. "This re-encoding ensures the tactile expert attends to a coherent, partially-denoised contextual manifold rather than the initial noise-time encoding."
  4. Delay augmentation. Because fast ticks run asynchronously, there is real staleness between the frozen visual cache and the live tactile stream. T-Rex draws δ∼Uniform{0,4,8,12}\delta\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{0,4,8,12\}δ∼Uniform{0,4,8,12} during training to shift the tactile frame indices relative to the visual ones, "strictly matching the deployment-time staleness distribution". This is a lovely piece of engineering discipline: train on the distribution you will deploy under, including its timing artefacts.
L_act 1.0661 | L_tac 1.0644 | total 2.1305
slow tick (K=6, tau 1.0->0.4) -> x_split (4, 16, 62)
4 fast ticks (K=4, tau 0.4->0) off ONE slow tick | action std across ticks 0.0074
slow 10.36M params vs fast 3.10M (3.3x cheaper) -> fast loop is affordable at high rate

The last line is the point of the whole design: the fast expert is 3.3× cheaper in this scaled-down reproduction (0.62B vs 1.41B in the real system, ~2.3×), and the per-control-step cost "is therefore dominated exclusively by the KfastK_{\text{fast}}Kfast​ Euler steps of the lightweight tactile expert". The visual tower, latent expert and action expert do not re-execute during a fast tick at all.

Thread safety, which papers rarely discuss

T-Rex's deployment runtime uses "a single-threaded request socket combined with an explicit execution lock" that "serializes the two experts, guaranteeing that no high-frequency fast tick initiates until any in-flight slow tick has fully committed its KVτsplit\mathrm{KV}_{\tau_{\text{split}}}KVτsplit​​ cache and intermediate boundary state x^τsplit\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{\tau_{\text{split}}}x^τsplit​​ to the shared memory space." Without this you get a torn read: a fast tick using a half-updated cache paired with the previous boundary state, producing an action from an inconsistent context. It is the kind of bug that manifests as rare, unreproducible jerks and takes a week to find. If you are asked to design an asynchronous policy runtime, mentioning the lock is a strong signal.

Two conclusions the authors draw, both important. First, large-scale pretraining dominates: ViTacFormer and RDP, trained from scratch on 100 task demonstrations, score 3 and 6 — they are excellent architectures starved of data. EgoScale, with no tactile at all but massive egocentric pretraining, reaches 35 and is the strongest baseline. If you take one thing from this table, it is that tactile architecture cannot substitute for pretraining scale. Second, tactile is nonetheless necessary: EgoScale "still fails at precise contact adjustment and force-sensitive behaviors", and the 35 → 65 gap is what tactile-grounded mid-training plus reactive control buys.

w/o Tactile42 (−23)Value of the modality as a whole

The recipe ablation is the most instructive number in the paper. Pretraining alone gives +27, mid-training alone +16, but together they give +47 — more than the sum (+43). The stages are synergistic: human video pretraining supplies broad visuomotor priors that have no grounding in robot-executable contact dynamics, and tactile mid-training supplies grounding that has nothing to generalise over without the priors. Neither is useful alone in the way it is useful together.

On τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​, the paper reports an interior optimum and gives the mechanism both ways: "When τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​ is too small, the action expert provides insufficient visuomotor priors for downstream refinement; when τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​ is too large, the tactile expert has limited capacity to incorporate tactile feedback." That is exactly the trade the coarse-to-fine argument in §9.2 predicts.

9.5The dataset design

The dataset is a contribution in its own right and its organising principle is worth stealing. Rather than collecting narrow task-specific demonstrations, T-Rex builds a taxonomy by crossing 207 household objects with 22 motor primitives, pruning physically infeasible pairs (pouring a solid block, twisting a non-articulated object) via a manual per-primitive feasibility checklist. Of 207×22=4,554207\times22=4{,}554207×22=4,554 candidates, 502 survive, yielding 7,755 episodes and 100 hours, with ~16 demonstrations per pair, median episode 29.8 s (IQR 21.0–41.1 s), collected over 10 weeks. Six tabletop backdrops, 0–5 distractors drawn from a pool of 210+ non-target items, randomised initial object pose every episode. Language annotations generated by a commercial VLM from 4–6 sampled head-camera frames plus the recorded object and primitive labels, then human-verified "to filter out hallucinations".

The controlled comparison is the compelling part: against a 100-hour task-specific dataset collected from 11 tasks — a matched data budget — the primitive-organised dataset "achieves stronger generalization and zero-shot transfer". And in the low-data regime, tactile-grounded mid-training "substantially improves performance", reducing the downstream demonstrations required. The lesson generalises well beyond tactile: at a fixed collection budget, coverage of compositional primitives beats depth on target tasks. This is a strong thing to say in a data-strategy discussion.

9.6What still fails

T-Rex's failure analysis is unusually candid and each mode maps onto a concept from earlier chapters:

Table 9.3 — T-Rex failure modes (App. H) and their conceptual home.
FailureObservedMaps to
Object collisionBulb collides with socket before insertionInsufficient fine visual alignment; excessively rapid execution
Slipping offKey grasped, then droppedFine in-hand dexterity limited by "the data distribution of the teleoperated data" — §2.5 retargeting
Imprecise positionEgg grasped intact but mis-placed in trayExplicitly attributed to "the inherent distribution shift characteristic of Behavioral Cloning" — §1.2

The stated limitations point at the next research directions: reinforcement learning or online interaction for long-horizon precise-contact tasks where teleoperation itself is difficult (Chapter 17), and hardware — "sensor distortion, calibration drift across devices, and the absence of dense palm sensing", motivating "unified representations across heterogeneous tactile sensors". That last phrase is precisely RDP's 3D-deformation-field abstraction (§7.4) applied at scale, and it is a good answer to "what would you work on next?"

Key takeaways
  1. Cascaded flow matching splits one trajectory at τsplit=0.4\tau_{\text{split}}=0.4τsplit​=0.4 between two experts regressing the same target v⋆v^\starv⋆ on disjoint intervals. Coherent by construction, not a hack.
  2. The split aligns the flow's natural coarse-to-fine structure with the task's: gross motion is a slow vision question, precise values are a fast contact question.
  3. Kslow=6K_{\text{slow}}{=}6Kslow​=6, Kfast=4K_{\text{fast}}{=}4Kfast​=4, fast ticks at offsets {0,4,8,12}\{0,4,8,12\}{0,4,8,12} in a 16-step chunk. Per-step cost is dominated by the small tactile expert; the visual tower never re-runs.
  4. Four details that make it work: full-range τ\tauτ training for graceful degradation; a detached KV cache so tactile cannot corrupt vision; re-encoding the cache at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​; and delay augmentation matching deployment staleness.
  5. 65% vs 35% for the strongest baseline. Ablations: tactile worth 23, temporal force encoding 7, deformation 6, asynchrony 5.
  6. Pretraining (+27) and mid-training (+16) are synergistic, together giving +47.
  7. Primitive-organised data beats task-specific data at matched budget — 207 objects × 22 primitives, pruned to 502 feasible pairs.
  8. Remaining failures are fine visual alignment, in-hand dexterity, BC distribution shift, finger coordination, and temporal tactile conditioning.

10Case study: the π\piπ line, π0\pi_0π0​ through π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​

Core ideas

π0\pi_0π0​[Black et al. 2024] is the reference implementation of the pattern §4.1 describes in the abstract: a pretrained vision-language model carries the semantics, a small separately-parameterised action expert carries the continuous control, and a block-causal mask is what lets the two share one attention stack without the action side polluting the language side. Everything after it is a modification of that skeleton rather than a replacement for it, and the four modifications are each answering a different failure. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ changes what the model is trained on and as. π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ changes where the training data comes from, by letting the robot generate it. π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ changes what the model is told, by turning the prompt into a structured bundle of instructions, quality targets, control modes and predicted future images. Read in sequence, the line is the clearest available demonstration that in a VLA the architecture is the cheap part — it barely moves across four papers — and the data and the conditioning are the expensive ones.

This chapter is written against the papers and against openpi, the released implementation. Where the two disagree, both are given, because the disagreements are instructive.

10.1The problem the architecture is answering

Before the architecture, the constraint. A generalist manipulation policy has to satisfy four requirements that pull against each other, and every structural decision in π0\pi_0π0​ is a response to one of them.

  1. Semantic generality it cannot learn from robot data. There is no robot dataset large enough to teach a policy what a colander is. That knowledge has to be inherited from web-scale vision-language pretraining, which fixes the backbone as a VLM and fixes its interface as tokens.
  2. Continuous, high-frequency, multimodal actions. Dexterous tasks need smooth commands at tens of hertz, and the conditional action distribution is genuinely multimodal — the problem Chapter 1 calls chunk-level multimodality. A discrete next-token head answers the first requirement and fights the second; a regression head answers the second and collapses on the third.
  3. Heterogeneous embodiments. Single arms, dual arms, and mobile manipulators have different action dimensionalities, and a single set of weights has to serve all of them.
  4. Latency. A 3B VLM forward pass per control step is not affordable at 50 Hz. Whatever runs fast must be small, and whatever is large must run rarely.

Read in that order, the architecture is almost forced. Requirement 1 gives a VLM backbone. Requirement 2 gives a generative continuous head. Requirement 3 gives a padded action space. Requirement 4 gives the asymmetric parameter split and the block-causal mask that makes a prefix cacheable. The rest of this chapter checks each step against what the paper and the code actually do.

10.2Inputs and outputs, exactly

The single most useful thing to hold about any VLA is its tensor contract. For π0\pi_0π0​:

Table 10.1 — The π0\pi_0π0​ tensor contract. Batch dimension BBB suppressed in the prose, shown in the shapes. Paper column from π0\pi_0π0​ §III and App. B; code column from openpi/src/openpi/models/pi0.py and pi0_config.py.
PortShapeWhat it is
Images(B, n, 224, 224, 3)n∈{2,3}n\in\{2,3\}n∈{2,3} camera views depending on the platform — "with 2 or 3 images per robot". The code fixes three named slots, base_0_rgb, left_wrist_0_rgb, right_wrist_0_rgb, each accompanied by a boolean image_mask, so a platform with two cameras supplies a masked third rather than a shorter sequence. Resolution is a module constant, IMAGE_RESOLUTION = (224, 224).

The paper says that number is 18 — "the configuration vector qt\mathbf q_tqt​ and action vectors at\mathbf a_tat​ always have the dimensionality of the largest robot in the dataset (18 in our case)". The released code sets action_dim: int = 32. One linear projection, one token.

Paper 18, code 32

Both numbers are real and neither is a typo. 18 is what the paper reports for the corpus it was written about; 32 is the default the released implementation ships, sized for the platforms openpi has since had to serve. The transferable point is that the padded width is a property of the training corpus, not of the architecture — it is a number you re-choose when your fleet changes, and nothing else in the model has to move when you do. Quote whichever one you can point at; do not quote one as if it were the other.

Three further details repay attention. The state is one token, not eighteen or thirty-two — a single linear map from R32\mathbb R^{32}R32 to the expert's width, which is why proprioception cannot dominate attention here in the way Chapter 8 warns about, and also why it cannot carry much. The action chunk is fifty tokens, one per timestep, so the action expert's sequence length is set by the horizon rather than by the action dimension. And the padding is not cosmetic: it is the mechanism by which one set of weights serves a 7-DoF single arm and a 14-DoF bimanual platform, at the cost of the network spending capacity on dimensions that are identically zero for most of the data.

10.3The whole network, in one diagram

The table gives the ports. What it does not give is the widths in between, and those are where the design is legible. Everything in Figure 10.1 is either a shape from the config or an arithmetic consequence of one.

Two things in that diagram are worth reading twice. First, there is no cross-attention anywhere. Images, language, proprioception and the noised action chunk are all tokens in a single sequence, and the only thing that distinguishes them is which weight set processes them and what the mask permits. That is the extreme end of the fusion spectrum in §8.1, and it is a bet: it assumes the mask is enough to stop 816 perceptual tokens from drowning one state token, an assumption §8.2 shows is not automatically safe.

Second, the flow timestep enters through an MLP that also consumes the action tokens, so the network sees "which action, at what noise level" as one fused representation rather than as an additive embedding. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ changes exactly this, and §10.6 explains what it changes it to.

Where each embedding in this diagram was introduced

Nothing in Figure 10.1 is new machinery; every box has a section earlier in the manual that explains why it has the shape it has.

  • The image tokens — patch embedding, why patch size fixes token count, and the semantic-versus-geometric trade-off that decides which tower you pick: §4.4.
  • The 32-dimensional action and state layout — joint versus end-effector space, delta versus absolute, and the rotation representation that must not be a quaternion: §2.1, §2.2, §2.3.
  • The normalisation that happens before the state ever reaches state_proj — per-dimension statistics, and why quantile normalisation beats mean/std here: §2.4.
  • The single state token, and the attention-mass argument for why one token of proprioception among 816 perceptual tokens is a real risk: §8.2.
  • The velocity field and its integration — the derivation, the sign conventions, and why ten steps rather than fifty: §3.1, §3.2.
  • The masked third camera, and what a policy learns to do when a modality is sometimes absent: §13.1.

10.4The loss, written out

Chapter 3 argued the general case: when the conditional action distribution has several valid modes, a regression head averages them into something invalid, and a generative head does not. π0\pi_0π0​ is where that argument meets a deadline. The training objective is a single mean-squared error and it fits on one line, but the line has three conventions buried in it that each cause confusion, so it is worth writing in full.

Sample a flow time, and note that it is not uniform:

τ  ∼  0.999⋅Beta(1.5, 1)+0.001,τ∈(0.001, 1.0)\tau \;\sim\; 0.999\cdot\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,\,1) + 0.001, \qquad \tau\in(0.001,\,1.0)τ∼0.999⋅Beta(1.5,1)+0.001,τ∈(0.001,1.0)
(10.1)

Interpolate between the clean action chunk A\mathbf AA and a Gaussian sample ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε, in the direction where τ=0\tau=0τ=0 is data:

Aτ  =  τ ε+(1−τ) A,u  =  ε−A\mathbf A^\tau \;=\; \tau\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon + (1-\tau)\,\mathbf A, \qquad \mathbf u \;=\; \boldsymbol\varepsilon - \mathbf AAτ=τε+(1−τ)A,u=ε−A
(10.2)

and regress the network's output onto that constant velocity:

L(θ)  =  Eτ, ε, (o,A)∼D[  ∥ vθ(Aτ, τ, o)−(ε−A) ∥22  ]\mathcal L(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb E_{\tau,\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\,(\mathbf o,\mathbf A)\sim\mathcal D} \Big[\;\big\lVert\, v_\theta(\mathbf A^\tau,\,\tau,\,\mathbf o) - (\boldsymbol\varepsilon - \mathbf A) \,\big\rVert_2^2 \;\Big]L(θ)=Eτ,ε,(o,A)∼D​[​vθ​(Aτ,τ,o)−(ε−A)​22​]
(10.3)

Sampling integrates the same field in the opposite direction, from noise at τ=1\tau=1τ=1 down to data at τ=0\tau=0τ=0, with a fixed step:

Aτ+Δ  =  Aτ+Δ vθ(Aτ, τ, o),Δ=−1K,K=10\mathbf A^{\tau + \Delta} \;=\; \mathbf A^{\tau} + \Delta\, v_\theta(\mathbf A^\tau,\,\tau,\,\mathbf o), \qquad \Delta = -\tfrac{1}{K},\quad K = 10Aτ+Δ=Aτ+Δvθ​(Aτ,τ,o),Δ=−K1​,K=10
(10.4)

The three conventions, in the order they trip people up.

  • The direction of τ\tauτ is the diffusion one, not the paper's. In (10.2), τ=1\tau=1τ=1 is pure noise. The π0\pi_0π0​ paper writes the interpolant the other way round. The openpi source carries an unusually candid comment about this: "we use the convention more common in diffusion literature, where t=1 is noise and t=0 is the target distribution. yes, this is the opposite of the pi0 paper, and I'm sorry." §3.2 gives the general translation rule; the practical consequence is that Δ\DeltaΔ is negative in (10.4), and a sign error here produces a policy that integrates away from the data and outputs noise.
  • The Beta sampling is deliberately lopsided. Beta(1.5,1)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1)Beta(1.5,1) puts most of its mass near 1, which under this direction convention is the noisy end. That is where the velocity field is hardest to learn and where an error compounds through the most remaining integration steps, so it gets the most training samples. §3.4 works through why that asymmetry exists rather than being an arbitrary schedule choice.
  • The loss is unweighted. No signal-to-noise reweighting, no vvv-prediction, no auxiliary consistency term — one mean-squared error over 50 × 32 numbers. Everything else in the system is doing work so that this can stay simple.

The inference cost follows directly. Ten evaluations of a 300M expert is the entire per-chunk cost above the single 3B prefix pass, and that ratio — ten small passes against one large one — is what buys 50 Hz. Note also that the cost is fixed and schedulable: exactly ten passes, every time, which is a property an autoregressive decoder of variable length does not have and which matters more for a real-time control loop than the average latency does. §14.1 makes that argument in budget terms.

The comparison that is easy to get backwards

π0\pi_0π0​-FAST[Pertsch et al. 2025] is the same backbone with a discrete head: DCT-then-BPE tokens and a cross-entropy loss instead of a velocity field. It is not a weaker model; it is a different point on the training-simplicity/inference-latency curve, and §3.5 covers the tokeniser itself. Autoregressive decoding over a variable-length token string is simpler to train and slower to run; a fixed ten-step integration is harder to train and predictable to run. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ then uses both, in sequence — which only makes sense once you see them as two heads on one representation rather than two competing models.

10.5The data mixture, which is the real contribution

The architecture section of the π0\pi_0π0​ paper is short. The data section is not, and the ordering reflects where the difficulty actually lives. Pre-training uses "over 10,000 hours of robot data"; the in-house portion covers "7 different robot configurations and 68 different tasks", combined with the open cross-embodiment corpus. What that buys is not a better velocity field but a policy whose language conditioning means something outside the training scenes.

π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​[Physical Intelligence et al. 2025] makes the point sharper by measuring it. Of the data in its first training phase, 97.6% "do not come from mobile manipulators performing household tasks" — the target domain is a 2.4% slice, and the rest is other robots, other labs, web captioning, visual question answering and object localisation. The claimed result is generalisation to entirely new homes, doing "long-horizon and dexterous manipulation skills, such as cleaning a kitchen or bedroom".

Epistemic status

The π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ home evaluations are small-nnn demonstrations in a handful of residences, not a benchmark with error bars, and the comparison against π0\pi_0π0​ is not a controlled ablation of the data mixture alone. The 97.6% figure is solid and comes from the paper; the causal claim that co-training caused the generalisation is the paper's interpretation, and a reasonable one, but it is an interpretation.

10.6π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​: two architectural changes and one training change

π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ is usually described purely as a data-and-curriculum paper, and the headline result is indeed about the mixture. But the released implementation carries two genuine architectural differences, both small enough to state in a sentence and both consequential enough to be worth knowing. The Pi0Config docstring names them itself: "Pi05 has two differences from Pi0: the state input is part of the discrete language tokens rather than a continuous input that is part of the suffix; the action expert uses adaRMSNorm to inject the flow matching timestep."

The training change is the one the paper leads with, and it is a two-stage curriculum rather than a modification of any layer.

Table 10.2 — π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ against π0\pi_0π0​, and the constraint each change answers. Sources: π0\pi_0π0​, π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​, and openpi/src/openpi/models/pi0_config.py.
π0\pi_0π0​π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​Why
Pre-training headFlow matching throughoutDiscrete FAST tokens Discrete tokens give "simple, scalable, and efficient training" — one cross-entropy loss over a heterogeneous mixture that includes non-robot data, where a velocity field has no meaning.
Post-training headsameFlow-matching action expert added afterwards Real-time inference. The discrete head is trained first and the continuous one is attached to the representation it produced.
State inputContinuous, one suffix token, own mask block Discretised into the language prefix So the state exists during a text-only pre-training stage, and so it lands inside the cached prefix instead of being recomputed ten times per chunk.
Timestep injectionConcatenated to each action token, then MLP adaRMSNorm scale on every suffix layer One conditioning path instead of fifty copies of a time embedding, and a stronger one: it modulates the whole layer rather than adding to the input.
Language budgetmax_token_len = 48max_token_len = 200 Room for the serialised state and for high-level subtask strings.
InferenceInstruction → chunkInstruction → subtask → chunk "The model first produces a high-level subtask for the robot to perform and then, conditioned on this subtask, predicts the low-level actions." A long-horizon task is decomposed by the same weights that execute it.
DataRobot data, 10k+ hoursRobot + web VQA + captioning + detection + subtask labelsOpen-world generalisation. See the 97.6% figure above.

The hierarchical inference step deserves a second look, because it is the part most often described loosely. It is not a separate planner model. It is the same VLA, run twice: once autoregressively in language space to emit a short subtask string, then once more in action space with that string appended to its own prompt. The cost is one extra language decode per high-level step; the benefit is that the difficult credit-assignment problem of long-horizon tasks is partly handed to a representation that was pretrained on language, where it is much better conditioned.

10.7π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​: the same policy, trained on its own experience

Every model so far in this chapter learns from demonstrations, and demonstrations have a ceiling: they show the policy what success looks like and never what recovery looks like, because a teleoperator rarely makes the mistakes the policy will make. Chapter 17 treats the general problem of putting reinforcement learning on top of a VLA, and derives why the obvious routes — policy-gradient fine-tuning, learned reward models — are so awkward here. π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ [Physical Intelligence et al. 2025] is the architecture that results from taking the least awkward route seriously, and the reason it belongs in this chapter rather than only in Chapter 17 is that it is a second model, with its own tensor contract, bolted alongside the policy.

The value model's objective is a cross-entropy over discretised returns rather than a regression, which is the distributional-RL choice and is there for the same reason the action head is generative: a scalar regression onto a return whose distribution is multimodal — sometimes the grasp works, sometimes it does not — converges to the mean of outcomes that never happen.

min⁡ϕ    Eτ∼D[∑ot∈τH(RtB(τ),  pϕ(V∣ot, ℓ))],pϕ(V∣⋅)∈ΔB,  B=201\min_{\phi}\;\; \mathbb E_{\tau\sim\mathcal D}\Big[\textstyle\sum_{\mathbf o_t\in\tau} H\big(R^B_t(\tau),\; p_\phi(V\mid \mathbf o_t,\,\ell)\big)\Big], \qquad p_\phi(V\mid\cdot)\in\Delta_B,\; B = 201ϕmin​Eτ∼D​[∑ot​∈τ​H(RtB​(τ),pϕ​(V∣ot​,ℓ))],pϕ​(V∣⋅)∈ΔB​,B=201
(10.5)

The policy's objective is then two likelihood terms — one unconditional, one conditioned on the advantage indicator ItI_tIt​ — which is how a single set of weights learns both what the data does and what the good part of the data does:

min⁡θ    ED[−log⁡πθ(at∣ot, ℓ)  −  αlog⁡πθ(at∣It, ot, ℓ)]\min_{\theta}\;\; \mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\Big[-\log \pi_\theta(\mathbf a_t\mid \mathbf o_t,\,\ell) \;-\; \alpha \log \pi_\theta(\mathbf a_t\mid I_t,\,\mathbf o_t,\,\ell)\Big]θmin​ED​[−logπθ​(at​∣ot​,ℓ)−αlogπθ​(at​∣It​,ot​,ℓ)]
(10.6)

At inference the indicator is set to positive. Optionally the two branches are combined by classifier-free guidance with a weight β>1\beta>1β>1, which extrapolates away from the unconditional behaviour — the same mechanism image generators use to sharpen a prompt, applied to "be the competent version of yourself". Reported gains on the hardest tasks are more than a doubling of throughput and roughly a halving of failure rate.

Epistemic status

The throughput and failure-rate figures are from a single self-improvement iteration on the authors' own tasks and hardware, with the baseline being their own supervised model. They are not a benchmark result and there is no comparison against another lab's RL post-training. The architectural facts — 4B backbone, 860M expert, 670M critic, 201 bins, 30th-percentile threshold — are stated directly in the paper.

10.8π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​: the prompt becomes a structured bundle

By π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​[Physical Intelligence et al. 2026] the architecture has stopped moving: the paper says plainly that it "builds on the existing VLA architecture from π0.6\pi_{0.6}π0.6​", a Gemma 3 4B backbone including a 400M vision encoder, plus an 860M flow-matching action expert, about 5B parameters in total, producing a 50-step chunk of which 15 or 25 steps are executed. What changes is what the model is conditioned on, and the change is large enough to reorganise the input contract.

The concept first, independent of this paper. A policy trained on a large heterogeneous corpus faces a problem that has nothing to do with capacity: the corpus contains episodes that were fast and episodes that were slow, episodes that succeeded cleanly and episodes that recovered from a fumble, episodes recorded in joint space and episodes recorded in end-effector space. Averaged together these are contradictory supervision. There are three things you can do about it. Filter the corpus, and lose most of it. Add a separate model per regime, and lose the sharing. Or tell the model which regime each episode came from, and ask for the regime you want at test time. The third is strictly more informative than the first two, and it is what π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ already did with a single advantage bit. π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ generalises that bit into a structured context.

The training objective for the policy is the same conditional likelihood it has always been; only the conditioning set has grown:

max⁡θ    ED[log⁡πθ(at:t+H  ∣  ot−T:t,  Ct)],Ct={ ℓ^t,  mt,  Gt,  c }\max_{\theta}\;\; \mathbb E_{\mathcal D}\Big[\log \pi_\theta\big(\mathbf a_{t:t+H} \;\big|\; \mathbf o_{t-T:t},\; \mathcal C_t\big)\Big], \qquad \mathcal C_t = \{\,\hat\ell_t,\; m_t,\; G_t,\; c\,\}θmax​ED​[logπθ​(at:t+H​​ot−T:t​,Ct​)],Ct​={ℓ^t​,mt​,Gt​,c}
(10.7)

with ℓ^t\hat\ell_tℓ^t​ the subtask instruction, mtm_tmt​ the episode metadata, GtG_tGt​ the multi-view visual subgoals and ccc the control-mode identifier. The subgoal generator is trained separately, by flow matching, against ground-truth future frames.

Two observations that transfer beyond this paper. First, dropout rates are the real interface specification. A field dropped 30% of the time is a field the deployed system may omit; a field never dropped — here, the control mode — is one the deployed system must always supply, and discovering that at integration time rather than from the table is an expensive way to learn it. Second, a quality score in the prompt turns data curation into inference-time steering. The low-quality episodes are not discarded; they are labelled, learned from as examples of what a 2-out-of-5 execution looks like, and then never requested. That is the same manoeuvre as advantage conditioning in §10.7, generalised from one bit to several fields, and it is the single most portable idea in this chapter.

Epistemic status

The architecture numbers, dropout probabilities, test-time metadata values and guidance weights are stated in the paper. The evaluations are largely head-to-head against the authors' own π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ and π0.6\pi_{0.6}π0.6​ on their own task suites, with success rates read from figures rather than from a table of means and intervals; the cross-embodiment shirt-folding comparison against experienced teleoperators (80% versus 80.6%) is a single task on a single platform. Treat the direction as well supported and the magnitudes as demonstrations.

10.9Reading the line end to end

Table 10.3 — Four papers, one skeleton. Every row that does not change is as informative as every row that does.
π0\pi_0π0​π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​
VLM backbonePaliGemma 3BPaliGemma 3BGemma 3 4BGemma 3 4B
Action expert300M300M860M860M
HeadFlow matchingFAST tokens, then flowFlow matchingFlow matching
Chunk50505050, execute 15 or 25
Images2–3 at 224²2–3 at 224²3 at 224²up to 4 at 448², with history
Extra conditioning—high-level subtaskadvantage indicatorsubtask + metadata + subgoal images + control mode
Second model——670M value model14B subgoal generator
Where the data comes fromteleoperationteleoperation + web+ the robot's own rollouts and interventions+ human video, autonomous episodes, evaluations

Four transferable conclusions, none of which depend on liking this particular family.

  • The expert split is about caching, not capacity. A 300M action expert is not there because 300M parameters are needed to regress a velocity. It is there because a block-causal mask plus a small suffix means the expensive tower runs once per chunk instead of once per integration step. §4.2 gives the mask algebra; this is what it is worth.
  • Padding is the cross-embodiment mechanism. There is no clever adapter. There is a fixed-width vector — 18 in the paper, 32 in the code — and a convention about which slots a given robot uses. Heterogeneity is often solved by an agreed layout rather than by architecture, which Chapter 11 shows RDT taking considerably further.
  • The head is a deadline decision as much as a distribution decision. Flow matching wins over discrete tokens here partly because ten fixed steps is a schedulable cost and a variable-length autoregressive decode is not.
  • Conditioning is where the last two papers spent their effort, and it is cheap. An advantage bit, a quality score, a control-mode string and a predicted future image are all prompt-side changes. None of them required a new layer. Both papers report their largest gains from them.
Key takeaways
  1. π0\pi_0π0​ = PaliGemma 3B prefix + 300M action expert in one attention stack, joined by a blockwise causal mask with three blocks: [images, language], [state], [actions]. Both halves are depth 18 with 8 heads of dimension 256; only the width (2048 versus 1024) and the MLP size (16384 versus 4096) differ, which is what lets them interleave layer-for-layer.
  2. Contract: 3 image slots at 224² giving 256 tokens each, 48 language tokens, one state token from a vector padded to 18 (paper) or 32 (code), and 50 action tokens. Prefix 816 tokens, suffix 51. Output is a velocity field of shape (B, 50, 32), integrated in 10 Euler steps to give the chunk, executed at up to 50 Hz.
  3. The loss is a plain unweighted MSE onto ε−A\boldsymbol\varepsilon-\mathbf Aε−A, with τ\tauτ drawn from 0.999⋅Beta(1.5,1)+0.0010.999\cdot\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1)+0.0010.999⋅Beta(1.5,1)+0.001 and — in the code — τ=1\tau=1τ=1 meaning noise, the opposite of the paper's convention.
  4. Pre-training is 10,000+ hours; the in-house dexterous portion is 7 robot configurations and 68 tasks. For π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​, 97.6% of first-phase data is not the target domain.
  5. π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ moves the state into the discrete language prefix, injects the flow timestep by adaRMSNorm instead of concatenation, raises the language budget from 48 to 200 tokens, trains discrete-then-continuous, and splits inference into a high-level subtask decode followed by a low-level action decode.
  6. π0.6∗\pi^*_{0.6}π0.6∗​ adds a 670M distributional value model over 201 bins, thresholds its advantage at the 30th percentile into a single text token, and trains the policy by ordinary likelihood on demonstrations plus rollouts plus interventions. At test time it asks for "positive".
  7. π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​ keeps that architecture and restructures the prompt into four separately-droppable fields — subtask, episode metadata, visual subgoals, control mode — with a 14B BAGEL-initialised generator producing the subgoals every 4 seconds. At deployment it requests 15th-percentile speed, quality 5, and no mistakes.
  8. Across four papers the backbone changes once, the expert size changes once, and the chunk length never changes. Everything else that moved was data and conditioning. That ratio is the finding.

11Case study: RDT-1B

Core ideas

RDT-1B[Liu et al. 2024] answers the same generalist-policy question as the π\piπ line and answers it differently at almost every branch, which is exactly what makes the pair instructive. There is no vision-language backbone carrying the action head: the encoders are frozen and the policy is a diffusion transformer trained from scratch. Conditioning enters by cross-attention rather than by sharing one sequence, so the action stream is 67 tokens long no matter how many pixels are watching it. There is no padded 18- or 32-vector: there is a 128-slot physically interpretable unified action space in which every slot has a fixed meaning across every robot in the corpus. And the target is specifically bimanual — two arms, a multimodal action distribution that a unimodal head provably cannot represent, and 1M+ trajectories of pre-training to make the diffusion head's sample complexity affordable. Reading it against Chapter 10 separates what is essential to a VLA from what is one team's taste.

As in the previous chapter, the numbers here come from the paper and from the released implementation, thu-ml/RoboticsDiffusionTransformer. The configuration file configs/base.yaml is unusually complete and settles several questions the paper leaves open.

11.1Two problems, one of which is not about architecture

The paper states its difficulty in one sentence worth taking literally: bimanual manipulation is hard "due to the inherent complexity of coordinating two robot arms (leading to multi-modal action distributions) and the scarcity of training data". Those are two different problems with two different solutions, and conflating them is the commonest misreading of this line of work.

Multimodality is a representational problem, and it is the one Chapter 1 and Chapter 3 already solved in general: use a generative head. RDT uses diffusion rather than flow matching, which — as §3.2 shows — is a choice of parameterisation and schedule rather than a change of kind.

Scarcity is a data problem, and no head fixes it. The response has to be to make data from different robots mutually intelligible, so that a trajectory recorded on one platform is training signal for another. That is what the unified action space is for, and it is the contribution the title does not mention.

11.2The unified action space, in detail

π0\pi_0π0​'s answer to heterogeneity is to pad every action to the width of the largest robot and let the network work out what the slots mean from context. RDT's answer is to fix the meaning of every slot in advance. The action vector is 128-dimensional — state_dim: 128 in the config, with a comment insisting it "MUST be equal to configs/state_vec.py" — and the index ranges are a published table rather than a learned convention:

Table 11.1 — Part of RDT's 128-slot unified action space. Each physical quantity has a reserved index range; a robot that lacks a quantity leaves those slots masked rather than repurposing them. Source: RDT-1B, App. C, Tab. 4, and configs/state_vec.py.
Index rangePhysical quantity
[0, 10)Right arm joint positions
[10, 15)Right gripper joint positions
[15, 25)Right arm joint velocities
[25, 30)Right gripper joint velocities
[30, 33)Right end-effector position
[33, 39)Right end-effector 6D pose
[50, 60)Left arm joint positions — the left block mirrors the right
[103, 128)Reserved

The consequences are worth spelling out, because this design has a real cost as well as a real benefit.

  • A single-arm robot is a masked bimanual robot. Its trajectory occupies the right block and leaves the left block masked. No conversion, no adapter, no per-dataset head. The paper's phrase for the goal is "preserving the physical meanings of original actions", and the point of preserving them is that the network can transfer a fact about gripper velocity from one embodiment to another because it lands on the same coordinates.
  • The mask is an input, not a preprocessing step. This is the detail the paper underplays and the code makes obvious. The state adaptor is built with in_features = state_token_dim * 2, and the comment says why: "state + state mask (indicator)". Every state and every action step is presented to the network as a 256-vector — 128 numbers and 128 validity flags side by side — so the model is told explicitly which slots are meaningful rather than having to infer it from the zeros. §13.1 argues for exactly this: a zero is ambiguous between "absent" and "genuinely zero", and a separate flag removes the ambiguity.
  • The 6D rotation representation is in the layout, not bolted on. Slots [33, 39) are six numbers for orientation, which is the continuous representation §2.3 argues for at length. Choosing it once, in the shared layout, means no dataset in the corpus can silently introduce a quaternion discontinuity.
  • Most slots are zero most of the time. 128 dimensions, of which any one platform populates perhaps 20. That is a large amount of representational capacity spent on emptiness, and it is the price of the layout being fixed rather than learned. π0\pi_0π0​ pays a smaller version of the same price at 18 or 32 dimensions.

11.3Inputs and outputs, exactly

Table 11.2 — The RDT-1B tensor contract. Sources: RDT-1B §4, the released model card, and configs/base.yaml, models/rdt_runner.py.
PortShapeWhat it is
Images(B, 3, 2, 3, 384, 384)Three views — "exterior, right-wrist, and left wrist cameras", num_cameras: 3 — each with two frames of history, img_history_size: 2. Encoded by a frozen siglip-so400m-patch14-384. Aspect ratio handled by padding, not cropping: image_aspect_ratio: pad.
Image tokens(B, 4374, 1152)The code computes img_cond_len = img_history_size × num_cameras × num_patches. SigLIP-so400m/14 at 384² gives ⌊384/14⌋2=272=729\lfloor 384/14 \rfloor^2 = 27^2 = 729⌊384/14⌋2=272=729 patches, so 2×3×729=43742\times3\times729 = 43742×3×729=4374 conditioning tokens. These are keys and values only — never queries.
Language(B, ≤1024, 4096)Instruction embedded by a frozen T5-XXL (t5-v1_1-xxl), tokenizer_max_length: 1024. Not a backbone that also carries the action head — an encoder whose output is cross-attended.
State(B, 1, 256)Current proprioception in the unified layout concatenated with its 128-wide validity mask, so 256 numbers in, one token out. The released bimanual configuration fills 14 of the 128 slots (7 + 7) before scattering.
Noised chunk(B, 64, 256)The diffusion interpolant, again with the mask appended to every timestep. action_chunk_size: 64 — the model predicts "the next 64 robot actions".
Control frequency(B,)The hertz of the source dataset, embedded as its own token. See §11.7; this port has no analogue in π0\pi_0π0​ and it is the most easily overlooked input in the model.
Diffusion step kkk(B,)An integer in [0,1000)[0, 1000)[0,1000), embedded as its own token.
Output(B, 64, 128)The clean action chunk, from a nonlinear MLP decoder rather than a linear one — see §11.5 for why "clean" and not "noise".
Executed(B, Hexec, 14)Gathered back out of the 128 slots onto the platform's real joints, at 6 action chunks per second.

Two numbers in that table are the whole latency story, and they pull in opposite directions. The chunk is 64 steps — longer than π0\pi_0π0​'s 50 and four times T-Rex's 16 — so each inference commits to a long horizon. And inference is "an action chunk inference frequency of 6 Hz (action chunks per second)", achieved after the sampler is accelerated from 100 denoising steps down to 5. A 64-step chunk regenerated 6 times a second means each chunk is replaced long before it is exhausted, which is the same receding-horizon pattern Chapter 14 analyses — and it makes the chunk-stitching discontinuity of §14.4 a live concern rather than a theoretical one.

11.4The whole network, in one diagram

Where each embedding in this diagram was introduced
  • The frozen SigLIP tower, and what a language-supervised encoder does and does not give you compared with a self-supervised one: §4.4.
  • The 128-slot layout — joint versus end-effector, delta versus absolute, and why slots [33, 39) hold six numbers instead of four: §2.1, §2.3.
  • The validity mask travelling alongside the values, rather than being encoded as zeros: §13.1.
  • Per-dataset normalisation, which is what makes 46 corpora commensurable once the slots agree: §2.4.
  • Cross-attention as a fusion mechanism, its cost, and when it beats concatenation: §8.1, §8.2.
  • The diffusion formulation and its relationship to flow matching: §3.3.

11.5The loss, and the parameterisation choice inside it

RDT's objective looks like the plainest thing in this Part, and it contains one decision that is easy to miss and changes the meaning of every other number in the model. The forward process is standard DDPM: sample an integer step kkk uniformly from {0,…,999}\{0,\dots,999\}{0,…,999} and corrupt the clean chunk A\mathbf AA with Gaussian noise according to the schedule's cumulative signal ratio αˉk\bar\alpha_kαˉk​,

Ak  =  αˉk A  +  1−αˉk  ε,ε∼N(0,I)\mathbf A^{k} \;=\; \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,\mathbf A \;+\; \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\;\boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf 0,\mathbf I)Ak=αˉk​​A+1−αˉk​​ε,ε∼N(0,I)
(11.1)

The network is then trained to output — and this is the decision — the clean chunk itself, not the noise:

L(θ)  =  Ek, ε, (o,A)∼D[  ∥ fθ(Ak, k, ν, o)−A ∥22  ]\mathcal L(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb E_{k,\,\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\,(\mathbf o,\mathbf A)\sim\mathcal D} \Big[\;\big\lVert\, f_\theta(\mathbf A^{k},\,k,\,\nu,\,\mathbf o) - \mathbf A \,\big\rVert_2^2 \;\Big]L(θ)=Ek,ε,(o,A)∼D​[​fθ​(Ak,k,ν,o)−A​22​]
(11.2)

where ν\nuν is the control frequency of §11.7. In the released code this is one line — prediction_type: sample in the config, and target = action_gt; loss = F.mse_loss(pred, target) in the runner — but the choice between x0\mathbf x_0x0​-prediction and ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε-prediction is not cosmetic, and §3.3 sets out the general trade-off. Three consequences here in particular.

  • The loss is uniform in importance across noise levels. Under ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε-prediction, an equal error in ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε costs wildly different amounts in action space depending on kkk; under x0\mathbf x_0x0​-prediction the error is measured in the units you care about — metres and radians — at every step. For a signal with a hard physical tolerance, that is the right place to put the metric.
  • It is stable at low noise, which is where a 5-step sampler spends its time. ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε-prediction has the well-known problem that as αˉk→1\bar\alpha_k\to1αˉk​→1 the recovery of A\mathbf AA divides by a vanishing quantity. Cutting 1000 training steps to 5 sampling steps means every sampling step is a large jump, and x0\mathbf x_0x0​-prediction degrades far more gracefully under those jumps.
  • The masked slots cost nothing. Because the target is the padded action vector and the output is multiplied by action_mask, the empty slots of §11.2 contribute a constant zero rather than a noise-shaped target the network must learn to reproduce.

The beta_schedule: squaredcos_cap_v2 and clip_sample: False settings are the two remaining config lines with teeth. The cosine schedule keeps more of the trajectory at usefully intermediate noise levels than a linear one, which matters when only five of them will ever be visited; and clipping is disabled because the unified action space is normalised but not guaranteed to lie in [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1], so clamping would silently truncate valid commands.

11.6The four repairs, and why they are not small

A diffusion transformer built for images does not survive contact with robot data unmodified. The paper names three changes, each a response to a property of the signal rather than a general improvement, and the code adds a fourth that the paper describes but does not emphasise.

  • QKNorm. "We add QKNorm to avoid numerical instability." Robot observations arrive on wildly different scales — joint angles in radians, velocities in radians per second, forces in newtons — and unnormalised query–key dot products on such inputs produce attention logits with enormous dynamic range. In the code this is qk_norm=True with norm_layer=RmsNorm on both the self-attention and the cross-attention of every block, which is worth noting: the cross-attention is where the scale mismatch is worst, because the queries come from radians and the keys come from a frozen vision encoder. §7.2 makes the same argument about per-modality normalisation from the sensor side; QKNorm is the same defect caught one layer later.
  • RMSNorm for LayerNorm. Cheaper and, more importantly, it does not re-centre. When zero is a physically meaningful value — as it is for a velocity or a wrench — subtracting a batch mean destroys information that mean-free normalisation preserves. Every normalisation in the block is RmsNorm(hidden_size, eps=1e-6); there is no LayerNorm anywhere in the model.
  • A nonlinear MLP decoder instead of a linear one. The stated reason is to "capture the nonlinearity and high frequency of robotic data". A linear decoder makes the final output an affine function of the last hidden state, which is a strong smoothness prior — exactly the wrong prior for a signal containing contact transients. The code's FinalLayer is RMSNorm followed by a two-layer GELU MLP, 2048 → 2048 → 128, with the last linear zero-initialised so that the model starts as an exact no-op and learns away from it.
  • Alternating condition injection. "We strategically alternate between injecting image and text tokens in successive layers' cross-attention", and in the code this is literally conds[i % 2] over a list of [lang, img]: even-numbered blocks attend to language, odd-numbered blocks to images, 14 of each. The alternative — concatenating image and text tokens and cross-attending to the union — would put a few dozen language tokens in direct competition with 4374 image tokens for a single softmax. That is modality drowning, in the exact form §8.2 derives, and alternation sidesteps it by never making the two compete in the same attention distribution. It halves the cross-attention FLOPs as a side effect.

One structural detail the paper does not mention at all: the block's feed-forward network has hidden_features = hidden_size, an expansion ratio of one, where a standard transformer uses four. The parameter budget was spent on depth and on two attention operations per block rather than on the MLP — a reasonable allocation for a model whose job is conditioning-heavy and whose query sequence is only 67 tokens long, but an unusual one, and worth knowing before you copy the block into something else.

11.7Control frequency as an input

Start with the concept, because it generalises well beyond this model. A cross-embodiment corpus is not only heterogeneous in what is recorded — that is what the unified action space solves — it is heterogeneous in how fast it was recorded. A 10 Hz dataset and a 50 Hz dataset describing the identical physical motion produce action chunks whose per-step deltas differ by a factor of five. To a model that is not told the rate, those are simply two different and contradictory behaviours for the same observation, and the best it can do is average them — which is the multimodality failure of §1.3 arriving through a side door. There are only three responses available: resample everything to a common rate and accept the interpolation artefacts, train one model per rate, or tell the model the rate.

RDT takes the third. ctrl_freqs is a per-sample input, passed through its own TimestepEmbedder — the same sinusoid-then-MLP machinery used for the diffusion step — and inserted as a dedicated token at position 1 of the query sequence, immediately after the diffusion step and before the state. The model is therefore conditioned on the hertz of its own output in the same way it is conditioned on the noise level, and the learnable positional embedding is initialised with a multimodal layout that names the four segments explicitly: ('timestep', 1), ('ctrl_freq', 1), ('state', 1), ('action', 64).

The deployment consequence is direct and is the kind of thing that is discovered painfully. Changing the control rate of your robot changes the meaning of a number the model is reading, so a policy that behaved correctly at 25 Hz will produce systematically wrong-magnitude deltas at 30 Hz unless the input is changed too. §14.6 treats control-rate and dtdtdt matching as a deployment concern; RDT is the clearest example of a model that promotes it to an architectural one.

11.8Scale, and what it was spent on

Pre-training covers "46 datasets, with a total size of 1M+ trajectories and 21TB", and the model is "1.2B parameters, which is the largest diffusion-based foundation model for robotic manipulation". Fine-tuning is a self-collected bimanual set of "6K+ trajectories". The config's own comment on the RDT block — "1B: num_head 32 hidden_size 2048" — suggests the 1.2B headline includes the adaptors, which is consistent with the runner printing the total over the model plus all three.

Put beside π0\pi_0π0​'s 10,000+ hours, the interesting comparison is not which number is larger — they measure different things and are not directly commensurable — but where the two teams spent their generality budget. π0\pi_0π0​ bought generality from a pretrained VLM and spent its robot data on dexterity. RDT bought generality from breadth of embodiment and spent its capacity on a from-scratch diffusion model. The unified action space is what made the second strategy possible at all; without a shared coordinate meaning, 46 datasets are 46 separate problems.

Table 11.3 — The two designs side by side, restricted to decisions where they disagree. Neither column is the correct answer; the pair is the useful object.
Decisionπ0\pi_0π0​RDT-1B
Semantic knowledge fromA pretrained VLM that is also the policyFrozen encoders that are not the policy
Conditioning mechanismOne sequence, block-causal maskCross-attention, alternating by layer
Action stream length51 tokens inside an 867-token sequence67 tokens, separate from 5398 conditioning tokens
Cross-embodimentPad to the widest robot, meaning learned128 slots, meaning fixed and published
Missing dimensions marked byZerosAn explicit mask concatenated to every vector
Generative headFlow matching, 10 stepsDDPM trained, DPM-Solver++ sampled, 5 steps
What the head predictsVelocity ε−A\boldsymbol\varepsilon-\mathbf Aε−AThe clean chunk A\mathbf AA
Control rateImplicit in the dataAn explicit input token
NormalisationGemma's RMSNorm, inheritedRMSNorm throughout, chosen; QK-norm added
MLP expansion8× (2048 → 16384), 4× in the expert1× (2048 → 2048)
Epistemic status

The 6 Hz figure is a chunk rate on the authors' hardware and software stack, not a property of the architecture, and it is not measured against π0\pi_0π0​'s 50 Hz on comparable hardware. Any cross-paper latency comparison in this area is between different GPUs, different batch shapes and different amounts of engineering, and should be treated as an order of magnitude rather than a measurement. The 4374 image-token count is arithmetic from the code and the SigLIP patch geometry, not a figure printed in the paper.

Key takeaways
  1. RDT-1B is a 1.2B diffusion transformer trained from scratch — 28 blocks, width 2048, 32 heads of 64, MLP expansion 1× — conditioned by frozen SigLIP-so400m/14-384 and T5-XXL encoders through cross-attention, not a VLM backbone with an action head attached.
  2. Contract: 3 camera views × 2 frames at 384² giving 4374 image tokens, up to 1024 T5 language tokens, a 128-slot state, and a (B, 64, 128) noised chunk. The query sequence is only 67 tokens: [diffusion step, control frequency, state, 64 actions]. Out comes a (B, 64, 128) chunk, executed at 6 chunks per second after the sampler is cut from 1000 training steps to 5 DPM-Solver++ steps.
  3. The head predicts the clean chunk, not the noise — prediction_type: sample — which puts the loss in physical units and survives a five-step sampler far better than ε\boldsymbol\varepsilonε-prediction would.
  4. The 128-dimensional physically interpretable unified action space gives every physical quantity a fixed index range, so a single-arm dataset is a masked bimanual one and 46 datasets become one corpus. Every state and every action step carries its 128-wide validity mask concatenated alongside it, so the adaptor sees 256 numbers, and "absent" is never confused with "zero".
  5. Four repairs, each answering a property of robot data: QKNorm on both attentions for scale heterogeneity, RMSNorm everywhere because zero is meaningful, a zero-initialised nonlinear decoder because contact is high-frequency, and strictly alternating image/text cross-attention — literally conds[i % 2] — so 4374 image tokens and a few dozen language tokens never compete in one softmax.
  6. Control frequency is an input token, embedded like the diffusion step. That is how one model serves corpora recorded at different rates, and it means changing your robot's control rate changes an input the model reads.
  7. Pre-training: 46 datasets, 1M+ trajectories, 21TB. Fine-tuning: 6K+ bimanual trajectories.
  8. Against π0\pi_0π0​: same problem, opposite bets. Pretrained-VLM generality versus breadth-of-embodiment generality; shared attention stack versus cross-attention; 18 or 32 padded dimensions versus 128 fixed ones; velocity prediction versus sample prediction.

12Case study: the OpenVLA line, RT-1 to OFT

Core ideas

This is the oldest continuous line of work in the Part and the most conservative, which is exactly why it is the most useful baseline. Its central claim, held constant from 2022 to 2025, is that a robot action is a short string: quantise each dimension, spend a handful of vocabulary entries on the bins, and the entire apparatus of a pretrained sequence model — weights, optimiser recipe, loss, serving stack — transfers unchanged. RT-1 established the encoding with a 35M bespoke transformer. RT-2 replaced the bespoke transformer with a web-pretrained vision-language model and thereby invented the VLA as the field now uses the term. OpenVLA[Kim et al. 2024] reproduced RT-2's argument at a size and a licence that let everyone else build on it, which is why it is the number every subsequent paper reports against. OpenVLA-OFT[Kim et al. 2025] then changed exactly three things on that fixed backbone and measured each separately — the closest thing the field has to a controlled experiment on what the generative machinery is actually buying. The punchline is that the line's founding assumption was half right: the pretrained sequence model was the good idea, and decoding one dimension at a time was the bad one.

12.1The line, and what each step in it was for

Four papers, and each one changes a single load-bearing component while holding the others fixed. Read as a sequence they are a better argument than any of them is alone.

12.2The argument for discretisation

Start with the concept rather than the model. A pretrained language model is a machine for predicting the next element of a discrete sequence. If actions can be made into such a sequence, the entire apparatus — the pretrained weights, the optimiser recipe, the loss, the serving stack — comes across unchanged. No new head, no new loss, no new failure mode. That is a serious argument, and it is why discretisation was the first thing anyone tried.

What it costs is everything §3.1 describes. Quantisation puts a floor under precision; per-dimension binning cannot represent correlations between dimensions within a timestep; and a per-timestep token stream is long, highly autocorrelated and low in entropy, which is a poor diet for an autoregressive model — the observation that motivates FAST's frequency-domain tokeniser in §3.5. This line accepts all of that. The question the chapter answers is how much it matters, and the honest answer turns out to be: less than expected for accuracy, much more than expected for speed.

It is worth separating two decisions that the line bundles together and that are usually conflated, because OFT eventually unbundles them.

  • Discretisation is about the output space: a softmax over bins rather than a real number. It costs precision and inter-dimension correlation, and it buys a categorical likelihood that can represent a multimodal distribution over a single dimension without any generative machinery at all.
  • Autoregression is about the decoding order: emitting dimension ddd conditioned on dimensions 1…d−11\dots d-11…d−1. It costs one full forward pass per dimension, and it buys the ability to represent correlations between dimensions that per-dimension binning destroys.

Both are inherited from language modelling, where they are inseparable. In robotics they are not, and the whole result of §12.7 follows from noticing that the second one is paying a very large bill for a benefit that chunking supplies more cheaply.

12.3Inputs and outputs, exactly

Table 12.1 — The OpenVLA tensor contract, and what OpenVLA-OFT changes. Sources: OpenVLA §4, OpenVLA-OFT §3, and prismatic/vla/action_tokenizer.py in the released repository.
PortOpenVLAOpenVLA-OFT
Image(B, 3, 224, 224), one third-person view same resolution; ALOHA configuration adds two wrist views, so three at 224²
Vision tokens(B, 256, 2176) — DINOv2 and SigLIP run separately and "the resulting feature vectors are concatenated channel-wise", then a 2-layer MLP projects into the decoder's embedding space. The released checkpoint names the two towers exactly: vit_large_patch14_reg4_dinov2.lvd142m at width 1024 and vit_so400m_patch14_siglip_224 at width 1152, and 1024+1152=21761024+1152 = 21761024+1152=2176. unchanged; optionally FiLM-modulated inside both towers

The 256 vision tokens follow from the encoders' patch size rather than being stated directly: both towers use patch-14 at 224², and 224/14=16224/14 = 16224/14=16 per side gives 16×16=25616\times16 = 25616×16=256 patches. The channel-wise concatenation means the token count is unchanged by having two encoders — the cost is width, not sequence length, which is why a dual encoder is nearly free in attention terms. That is worth contrasting with adding a second camera, which does multiply the sequence length and does dilute attention in the way §8.2 quantifies, and it is why the ALOHA configuration of OFT is measurably slower than the LIBERO one.

12.4The whole network, in one diagram

The training objective is worth writing down precisely because it is so ordinary. With a=(a1,…,a7)\mathbf a = (a^1,\dots,a^7)a=(a1,…,a7) the normalised action, q(⋅)q(\cdot)q(⋅) the binning map of §12.5 and o\mathbf oo the observation:

L(θ)  =  − E(o,a)∼D[  ∑d=17log⁡pθ( q(ad)  ∣  o,  ℓ,  q(a1),…,q(ad−1))]\mathcal L(\theta) \;=\; -\,\mathbb E_{(\mathbf o,\mathbf a)\sim\mathcal D} \left[\;\sum_{d=1}^{7} \log p_\theta\big(\,q(a^d) \;\big|\; \mathbf o,\;\ell,\; q(a^1),\dots,q(a^{d-1})\big)\right]L(θ)=−E(o,a)∼D​[d=1∑7​logpθ​(q(ad)​o,ℓ,q(a1),…,q(ad−1))]
(12.1)

That is next-token prediction with the sum restricted to the seven action positions. There is no auxiliary term, no value head, no reconstruction loss. The conditioning on q(a1),…,q(ad−1)q(a^1),\dots,q(a^{d-1})q(a1),…,q(ad−1) inside the logarithm is the autoregression — it is what allows the model to express that a large Δx\Delta xΔx implies a particular Δy\Delta yΔy, and it is also the term that forces seven serial passes.

Where each embedding in this diagram was introduced
  • The dual vision tower, and the semantic-versus-geometric complementarity that motivates it, with the channel-concatenation trick that makes it nearly free: §4.4.
  • Prepending vision tokens to text tokens as the simplest point on the fusion spectrum, and what it assumes: §8.1.
  • The 7-dimensional end-effector delta action — why delta rather than absolute, why end-effector rather than joint, and what the three rotation numbers actually are: §2.1, §2.2, §2.3.
  • Quantile normalisation, which is what the 1st and 99th percentiles in §12.5 are doing and why outlier clipping matters more than variance matching: §2.4.
  • Action tokenisation in general, including the frequency-domain alternative that this line eventually needed: §3.4, §3.5.
  • FiLM, which OFT adds and which is a gate rather than a competitor for attention mass: §8.1.

12.5How a continuous action becomes a language token

256 bins, 255 intervals

The paper says 256 bins and the code agrees, but the code is the place to look if you ever have to reimplement this. ActionTokenizer builds its boundaries with np.linspace(-1, 1, 256) — that is 256 edges, which delimit 255 intervals — and then takes bin_centers as the midpoints, giving 255 of them. np.digitize returns indices in [1,256][1, 256][1,256], and the decoder clips the top index down so it lands on the last centre. The repository's own comment spells the off-by-one out at length. It changes nothing about the argument and it is an eighth of a percent of the action range, but "256 bins" and "256 distinguishable output values" are not the same statement, and a reimplementation that assumes they are will be silently off by half a bin everywhere.

The clipping range in the tokeniser is a fixed [−1,+1][-1, +1][−1,+1]; the 1st-and-99th-quantile step happens upstream, in the dataset normalisation, which maps each dimension's corpus statistics into that interval. Two separate stages, and it is the upstream one that carries the per-dataset information — which is also why a fine-tuning corpus with different action statistics needs its own normalisation computed rather than inherited. §2.4 covers the general failure.

One more thing lives in that upstream stage and is easy to miss: the released checkpoint ships norm_stats per dataset, and each carries a seven-element boolean mask whose last entry is false. The gripper dimension is deliberately excluded from quantile normalisation, because it is a binary open/close command rather than a continuous displacement, and rescaling it by corpus percentiles would map "closed" onto an arbitrary interior value. A per-dimension normalisation policy, not a global one — exactly the point §2.4 makes about treating heterogeneous action dimensions heterogeneously.

12.6What the training cost, and why that number matters

OpenVLA was "trained on a cluster of 64 A100 GPUs for 14 days, or a total of 21,500 A100-hours", at "a batch size of 2048", for "27 epochs" over "970k robot demonstrations from the Open X-Embodiment dataset" — filtered to "manipulation datasets with at least one 3rd person camera" using "single-arm end-effector control".

Two things follow. First, that filter is why the action space is seven-dimensional and why everything in this chapter is single-arm: the corpus was chosen to be homogeneous, which is the opposite of RDT's bet in Chapter 11 and a legitimate alternative to it. Where RDT spends 128 slots and a published layout to make heterogeneous data commensurable, OpenVLA discards the data that does not fit. Both are answers to §11.1's scarcity problem; the second is cheaper and buys a narrower model.

Second, 21,500 A100-hours is the pre-training number that makes the fine-tuning number interesting. LoRA at "rank=32", "fine-tuning only 1.4% of the parameters", needs "59.7 GB" of VRAM — one 80 GB accelerator. The pre-training is a lab-scale expense; the adaptation is not. That gap is the entire practical argument for open VLA checkpoints, and it is why this model became the baseline everyone else reports against.

12.7OFT as a controlled experiment

OpenVLA-OFT is best read not as a new model but as an ablation of the previous chapters' claims, run on a fixed backbone. Three axes, changed one at a time.

Table 12.2 — The three OFT changes, and which earlier argument each one tests. Source: OpenVLA-OFT.
ChangeWhat it replacesThe claim it tests
Parallel decodingAutoregressive token-by-token emission That autoregression, not representation, is the latency bottleneck. Empty action embeddings differing only in positional encoding are fed in, the causal mask is switched to bidirectional, and one pass produces the whole chunk.
Action chunkingOne timestep per inference §1.4's argument that chunking suppresses temporal multimodality and compounding error. Free here, because parallel decoding already emits many slots.
Continuous L1L_1L1​ head256-way softmax per dimension Whether a generative head is necessary at all. A four-layer ReLU MLP on the decoder's own hidden states, regressing into [−1,+1][-1,+1][−1,+1].

The continuous head's objective is the simplest in the Part, and its simplicity is the finding:

L(θ)  =  E(o,A)∼D[1KD∑k=1K∑d=1D∣ a^kd(o,ℓ)−akd ∣]\mathcal L(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb E_{(\mathbf o,\mathbf A)\sim\mathcal D} \left[\frac{1}{KD}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{d=1}^{D} \big|\, \hat a^{d}_{k}(\mathbf o,\ell) - a^{d}_{k} \,\big|\right]L(θ)=E(o,A)∼D​[KD1​k=1∑K​d=1∑D​​a^kd​(o,ℓ)−akd​​]
(12.2)

No sampling, no noise schedule, no integration, no softmax. The paper also reports a diffusion variant of the same head — a 4-layer MLP noise predictor, DDIM with 50 steps and a squared-cosine schedule — which reaches 95.4% against the L1L_1L1​ head's 95.3%, statistically indistinguishable while costing fifty forward passes of the head instead of one. That null result is more informative than the headline.

Reconciling this with Chapter 3

It does not contradict Chapter 3; it locates its boundary. Chapter 3's claim is that a regression head fails when the conditional action distribution is genuinely multimodal after conditioning and after chunking. Chunking removes temporal multimodality. LIBERO's demonstrations are scripted and comparatively unimodal, so once chunked there is little residual multimodality left for a generative head to represent, and its extra capacity buys nothing while its sampling loop costs everything. The correct reading is not "diffusion was unnecessary" but "match the head to the residual multimodality of your data" — and that residual is an empirical property of the demonstrations, which means it is measurable before you choose. Contact-rich, human-teleoperated, multi-solution tasks are the regime where the generative head earns its cost; Chapter 9's task suite is that regime, and LIBERO is not. Note also that the L1L_1L1​ head is not quite a mean regressor: L1L_1L1​ recovers the conditional median, which on a bimodal distribution lands on one mode's side rather than in the empty middle. That is a weaker failure than the L2L_2L2​ averaging §1.3 describes, and part of why the result is as good as it is.

FiLM is the fourth change and is deliberately reported as conditional rather than universal: it is applied inside every block of both vision towers, after self-attention and before the feed-forward, with a separate projector per block, and it was needed in the ALOHA real-world experiments and not in LIBERO, "whose policies follow instructions well enough without it". A result reported as situational is more trustworthy than one reported as universal, and §4.4 treats the mechanism itself.
