Chunk50641, then K=8K=8K=8 or 2516
Rateup to 50 Hz6 chunks/s4.2 → 108.8 Hzasynchronous, two rates
Where the last paper spent its effortConditioning: metadata, subgoals, control mode The unified action layoutDeleting the decode loopSplitting the head by rate

The row that varies least is the one that matters most: all four chunk, and all four condition on a pretrained visual representation they did not train from scratch. The rows that vary most — head, conditioning path, cross-embodiment scheme — are the ones where the literature genuinely has not converged, and where a paper's choice is better explained by its deployment constraint than by an argument that its choice is superior.

Key takeaways
  1. The line is RT-1 (35M bespoke transformer, 256 bins, 3 Hz) → RT-2 (the same encoding on a web-pretrained PaLI-X or PaLM-E, 1–5 Hz) → OpenVLA (the same idea, open, 7B, ~6 Hz) → OFT (the same model without the autoregressive decode, 108.8 Hz). Each step moves one variable.
  2. OpenVLA is Llama 2 7B + fused DINOv2/SigLIP (patch-14 at 224², so 256 tokens, concatenated channel-wise to width 2176, projected by a 2-layer MLP), with actions discretised into 256 bins per dimension between the 1st and 99th quantile, written over the 256 least-used tokenizer entries by indexing backwards from the end of the vocabulary. In the code the 256 edges give 255 usable intervals.
  3. Contract: one 224² image and an instruction in; (B, 7) out, as seven sequential decodes, trained by plain cross-entropy masked to the action positions. OFT changes the output to (B, K, 7) in one pass with a mean-L1L_1L1​ objective.
  4. Training cost 21,500 A100-hours (64 A100s × 14 days, batch 2048, 27 epochs) over 970k Open X-Embodiment demonstrations filtered to single-arm end-effector control. LoRA rank 32 adapts it in 59.7 GB — one accelerator. That gap is the practical argument for open checkpoints.
  5. OFT isolates three changes and measures each: parallel decoding and chunking take 76.5% → 90.2% and 4.2 → 108.8 Hz; the continuous L1L_1L1​ head takes it to 95.3%; adding a wrist camera and proprioception reaches the headline 97.1%, at 71.4 Hz. A diffusion head scores 95.4% — indistinguishable from L1L_1L1​ at fifty times the sampling cost.
  6. Discretisation and autoregression are separable decisions that this line bundled. Autoregression was the expensive half, and chunking supplies the inter-dimension correlation it was buying.
  7. The L1L_1L1​ result bounds Chapter 3 rather than refuting it: once chunking has absorbed temporal multimodality, scripted benchmark data has little residual multimodality left, and a generative head buys nothing. Measure the residual before choosing the head.
  8. Across all four case studies, chunking and pretrained visual features are universal; the head, the conditioning path and the cross-embodiment scheme are not.
Part V

Deployment

Everything between "the checkpoint evaluates well" and "the robot works". This is where most VLA projects actually fail, and it is what separates people who have trained a policy from people who have shipped one.

13Robustness: dropout, missing modalities, and calibration drift

Core ideas

A multimodal policy has more ways to fail than a unimodal one, because every sensor is a dependency. Three distinct problems: the policy may over-rely on one modality and learn a shortcut; a sensor may fail at deployment and the policy must survive it; and sensors drift and get replaced, so the input distribution moves under you. The unifying answer is to make the failure modes part of the training distribution — dropout for over-reliance and sensor loss, sensor-agnostic intermediate representations for drift.

13.1Modality dropout

Dropping whole modalities during training is different from dropping individual tokens and the distinction matters. Token dropout teaches the network to interpolate over missing patches — a smoothness prior. Modality dropout teaches it to solve the task without that sensor at all, which is a genuinely different capability and the one you need when a wrist camera's cable comes loose mid-episode.

The learned null embedding per modality matters: zeroing a token is not the same as signalling absence, because zero is a valid value in a normalised feature space and the network cannot distinguish "the force is zero" from "there is no force sensor". A dedicated null token says missing unambiguously.

Modality dropout buys three things at once:

  • Robustness to sensor failure at deployment. The obvious one.
  • A cure for causal confusion. This is the important one. Proprioception dropout breaks the shortcut at≈g(qt)\mathbf{a}_t \approx g(\mathbf{q}_t)at​≈g(qt​) by making qt\mathbf{q}_tqt​ unavailable a fraction of the time, so the policy cannot rely on it and must learn the visual pathway. GR00T's fine-tuning recipe applies state dropout at p=0.2p=0.2p=0.2; the same logic motivates historical-frame dropout against the copycat problem.
  • Implicit modality balancing. Dropping vision with some probability forces the network through the force pathway on those batches — which is, in weakened form, what FACTR does deliberately with its corruption curriculum.

Two cautions. First, the published literature is clear that modality dropout "improves robustness, but it fails to fully recover the lost performance" — it is a mitigation, not a solution, and a policy trained with 20% vision dropout still degrades noticeably when vision is actually gone. Second, dropout probability is a real hyperparameter with a real trade: too high and you are training a weaker unimodal policy most of the time.

Dropout treats every modality as equally likely to be missing, at a fixed rate, throughout training. That is a strong assumption and often a wrong one: a policy does not fail because a camera vanishes, it fails because vision is good enough that the harder modalities never earn any gradient. If that is the diagnosis, the remedy is not to remove the dominant modality at random but to degrade it on a schedule — hard at the start, when the weak modalities need room to become useful, and progressively less as training proceeds. Degradation as a curriculum rather than as noise.

13.2The FACTR curriculum, and why it is better than dropout

FACTR[Liu et al. 2025] makes the balancing explicit and schedules it: corrupt the visual input with decreasing intensity across training. Early on vision is heavily degraded, so the only usable signal is force and the force pathway must learn. As training proceeds the corruption anneals away and the policy integrates both. Reported: +43% generalisation to unseen objects versus no curriculum, on box lifting, prehensile pivoting, fruit pick-and-place and dough rolling.

Why a curriculum beats stochastic dropout: dropout is i.i.d., so on any given batch the network can still rely on vision with probability 1−p1-p1−p, and gradient descent — which is greedy — will preferentially exploit that. A curriculum removes the easy pathway for a sustained period, long enough for the hard pathway to become competent. It is the same reason curriculum learning beats random task sampling generally: it changes what the optimiser can exploit, not merely what it occasionally cannot.

Note the shape of the argument matches §8.2 exactly. The problem is that gradient descent will not find the force-using solution, not that it cannot represent it. A curriculum is an intervention on the optimisation path.

13.3Sensor drift, replacement, and heterogeneity

This is the set of problems that separates a paper from a product, and T-Rex names it as a primary limitation: "tactile-reactive manipulation remains bottlenecked by hardware, including sensor distortion, calibration drift across devices, and the absence of dense palm sensing."

Table 13.1 — Deployment-time distribution shifts specific to contact sensing, and the defence for each.
ShiftCauseDefence
Bias driftTemperature, creep, hours of operationPeriodic re-taring during known no-contact phases; discretisation (T-Rex's VQ-VAE deadbands small drift)
Gel wear / replacementOptical sensor elastomer degrades and is swappedMarker-field PCA rather than raw pixels (RDP); background subtraction against a fresh reference (Sparsh)
Unit-to-unit variationTen fingertips, ten calibrationsPer-sensor normalisation statistics; shared encoder weights + per-sensor identity embeddings (T-Rex)
Sensor model changeYou upgrade the hardwareA sensor-agnostic intermediate representation (RDP's 3D deformation field) with a per-sensor adapter into it
Lighting / texture changeOptical sensor illuminationBackground subtraction; latent-space SSL rather than pixel-space (Sparsh's finding)

The general principle is worth stating abstractly because it is the reusable idea: put a calibrated, physically-meaningful, sensor-agnostic representation between the hardware and the policy, and absorb hardware change in the adapter. RDP demonstrates this concretely — the same 3D deformation field VtV_tVt​ describes a 549-USD GelSight Mini, a 50-USD lab-fabricated MCTac, and a robot's built-in joint torque estimate, and the same policy architecture works across all three. Compare with a policy trained on raw GelSight pixels, which is coupled to one gel, one illumination geometry, and one marker pattern.

Sparsh's contribution is the learned version of the same idea: one encoder family spanning DIGIT, GelSight 2017 and GelSight Mini, with 10-shot adaptation to a new sensor reported in its appendix. If asked how to support a new tactile sensor without retraining the policy, "adapt into the existing representation with a small amount of paired data" is the answer, and both the hand-designed (RDP) and learned (Sparsh) versions are citable.

13.4A checklist

Before deploying a multimodal policy, run these. Each catches a failure that is otherwise found on the robot, expensively.

  1. Ablate each modality at evaluation time. If removing a modality does not change performance, the policy is not using it — you have paid for a sensor and an encoder for nothing. This is the single most informative diagnostic and almost nobody runs it.
  2. Swap the language instruction, hold the scene fixed. If behaviour is unchanged, language is being ignored (§5.3).
  3. Freeze proprioception at a constant. If performance barely drops, you have causal confusion — or proprioception was never needed.
  4. Inject a constant offset into the force reading. Simulates drift. A policy that collapses has no drift tolerance and needs discretisation or re-taring.
  5. Log VQ codebook utilisation every epoch if you use a discrete tactile tokeniser (§7.3). Collapse is silent.
  6. Evaluate under deployment-time staleness, not perfectly synchronised inputs. T-Rex's delay augmentation exists because the two differ.
  7. Test with a dead sensor. Physically unplug one wrist camera and one fingertip. This is what the field does to you eventually.
Key takeaways
  1. Drop whole modalities, not tokens, and replace them with a learned null embedding per modality — zero is a valid value and does not signal absence.
  2. Modality dropout buys sensor-failure robustness, breaks causal confusion (state dropout p=0.2p{=}0.2p=0.2 in GR00T), and weakly balances modalities. It mitigates but does not fully recover.
  3. FACTR's annealed vision-corruption curriculum beats i.i.d. dropout (+43% on unseen objects) because it removes the easy pathway for long enough that the hard one becomes competent.
  4. Put a sensor-agnostic physical representation between hardware and policy. RDP's 3D deformation field spans a 549-USD sensor, a 50-USD sensor, and joint-torque estimates.
  5. Discretisation is a drift defence, not just compression — a quantiser is a deadband.
  6. Run the ablation checklist before deployment. "Remove the modality and see if anything changes" is the highest-information test you can run, and it is nearly free.

14Deploying a VLA on a real robot

Core ideas

Physics does not pause while your model thinks. That single constraint generates every deployment problem: a 3B-parameter model takes 100–300 ms to produce an action chunk, the robot needs a command every 3 ms, and the gap between those two numbers must be bridged architecturally rather than wished away. The bridge has three layers: action chunking gives you a buffer of commands to execute while thinking, asynchronous inference overlaps thinking with executing, and chunk-boundary handling (RTC and its successors) stops the seams from producing jerks. On top of that sit the unglamorous things that decide whether a system survives an eight-hour shift: control-rate matching, thread safety, runtime monitoring, and a failure detector.

14.1The latency budget

Start by writing the budget down, because most deployment arguments are really disagreements about which row dominates.

Table 14.1 — A representative end-to-end latency budget for a bimanual dexterous VLA. Figures are order-of-magnitude for a 2–3B model on a single modern GPU; the point is the relative sizes and where the leverage is.
StageTypicalScales withHow to attack it
Camera exposure + transfer10–30 msResolution, number of cameras, busLower resolution; hardware-timestamp everything
Image preprocessing2–5 msCamerasGPU-side resize/normalise; avoid CPU round-trips
Vision encoder15–40 msTokens × camerasToken pruning, smaller encoder, cache across the chunk
VLM backbone prefix40–150 msParameters × contextRun once per chunk (block masking, §4.2); quantise
Action expert, KKK steps5–30 msKKK × expert sizeFewer NFEs (flow > diffusion); smaller expert; cascade (§9.2)
Post-processing + IK1–5 msDoFWarm-start IK from the previous solution
Network / IPC1–20 msTopologyCo-locate; avoid a Python GIL hop on the hot path
Total inference~75–280 ms
Low-level control period3.3 ms (300 Hz)—Fixed by the hardware

The ratio is the whole problem: inference is 20–80× slower than the control period. A published reference point for the low end — LiteVLA-Edge reports 150.5 ms mean end-to-end latency (~6.6 Hz) running entirely offline in a ROS 2 pipeline with 4-bit quantisation via llama.cpp on an embedded GPU[LiteVLA-Edge]. Even aggressively optimised, you are two orders of magnitude from a servo loop.

14.2The control stack

The consensus architecture is a strict separation into a slow policy thread and a fast control thread, with an asynchronously-updated shared target. T-Rex states it plainly: "a T-Rex policy inference thread runs concurrently with a high-frequency low-level control thread operating at 300 Hz. The policy outputs action chunks, which asynchronously update the targets tracked by the low-level controller."

Rules that are learned painfully:

  • The control thread must never block on the policy thread. If a chunk is late, the controller continues tracking the last target — it does not wait. A blocked servo loop on a robot holding an object is a safety event.
  • Low-pass filter the policy output before it reaches the controller. T-Rex does this explicitly. Policy outputs contain step discontinuities at chunk boundaries; a PID loop fed a step commands a torque spike.
  • Use a watchdog on chunk staleness. If no new chunk arrives within nnn chunk durations, decelerate to a stop rather than replaying the tail of an increasingly stale plan.
  • Hardware-timestamp every stream and align on timestamps, not arrival order. A USB camera's frames arrive with variable delay; treating arrival order as temporal order silently corrupts your observation history.
  • Serialise access to shared state with an explicit lock. See §9.3 — T-Rex's runtime guarantees no fast tick starts until an in-flight slow tick has committed both its KV cache and its boundary state. A torn read between the two produces an action from an inconsistent context.

14.3The chunk-boundary problem

Action chunking creates a specific, visible artefact. You execute chunk iii; meanwhile you compute chunk i+1i+1i+1 from an observation taken at the start of chunk iii. By the time chunk i+1i+1i+1 begins executing, the world has moved on by the inference latency, and the first action of the new chunk was planned for a state that no longer holds. The symptom is a jerk at every boundary — and at worst, an out-of-distribution state that compounds.

The naive fixes both fail. Wait for the new chunk before continuing gives you a pause at every boundary — the robot stutters, and stopping mid-contact changes the physics (static friction differs from kinetic). Just start executing the new chunk gives you the discontinuity. The framing from the literature is precise: chunking "does not fully address the latency problem, leading to pauses or out-of-distribution jerky movements at chunk boundaries"[RTC].

Given that artefact, there are three things you can do. Blend the two chunks and accept a trajectory that is smooth but belongs to neither. Execute the old chunk to exhaustion and accept a policy that cannot react. Or make the new chunk aware, at generation time, of the actions that are already committed — so that it is not stitched to them afterwards but generated to continue them. The third is a constraint on sampling rather than a post-hoc filter, and a generative head is exactly the kind of model that can accept such a constraint: fixing part of the output and sampling the rest conditioned on it is inpainting, which diffusion and flow models already do.

14.4Generating into the boundary: Real-Time Chunking

RTC[Black et al. 2025, Physical Intelligence] reframes the boundary as an inpainting problem, and it is an elegant reframing. While the robot executes chunk iii, generate chunk i+1i+1i+1 under a constraint: the actions that are guaranteed to have already executed by the time the new chunk takes over are frozen, and the rest is generated to be consistent with them. You are not generating a fresh chunk; you are filling in the unknown portion of a partially-specified one.

The key property is that it "is applicable to any diffusion- or flow-based VLA out of the box with no re-training" — it is an inference-time algorithm, so you can add it to an existing checkpoint.

Two mechanisms in that weight vector, and understanding both is the substance of the method. The hard freeze on the first ddd steps is a correctness constraint: those actions will execute regardless of what the model wants, so generating anything else there is fiction. The soft decay over the following β\betaβ steps is the smoothness constraint: it pulls the new chunk toward the old one immediately after the handover and releases it progressively, so the trajectory is continuous in value and approximately in derivative, while the policy regains full freedom further out. The frozen prefix matches the committed actions exactly.

The reported behaviour is "a surprising amount of resilience even to high inference delays", which makes sense — as latency grows, ddd grows, and RTC simply freezes more of the chunk, degrading toward open-loop execution rather than toward incoherence.

When inference-time RTC is not enough

RTC propagates its constraint through the denoising process. With ~10 integration steps there is room for the constraint to influence the whole trajectory. Under a very tight budget of 1–2 steps — which is where you end up with fast actions and a hard real-time deadline — there is not: a model never trained to inpaint cannot propagate the consistency constraint in one or two steps. The published successor makes this explicit and moves the conditioning into training: Training-Time Action Conditioning for Efficient Real-Time Chunking[Black et al. 2025]. The general lesson is worth stating: inference-time constraints work when you have compute to propagate them; when you do not, the constraint must be trained in. Being able to name both the RTC paper and its training-time successor, and to say why the second exists, is a strong signal.

A related line attacks the same seam differently: VLASH uses future-state-aware asynchronous inference to plan for where the robot will be when the chunk lands rather than where it was when the observation was taken[VLASH]. Conceptually this is latency compensation by forward prediction, the same idea as a Smith predictor in classical control, and it composes with RTC rather than replacing it.

14.5Making the model fast

Four levers, roughly in order of payoff per unit of effort.

1. Cache the prefix — the biggest single win

Covered in §4.2, but it belongs here because it is a deployment decision as much as an architectural one. If vision never attends to action tokens, the VLM prefix is computed once per chunk and the KKK integration steps cost only the action expert. Going from "run 3B parameters 10 times" to "run 3B once and 300M ten times" is roughly a 7× reduction in the dominant term — larger than anything quantisation will give you, and it is lossless.

T-Rex extends this one level further. Its fast ticks reuse KVτsplit\mathrm{KV}_{\tau_{\text{split}}}KVτsplit​​, so "the visual tower, the latent expert, and the action expert do not re-execute during a fast tick. The per-control-step computational cost is therefore dominated exclusively by the KfastK_{\text{fast}}Kfast​ Euler steps of the lightweight tactile expert." Four reactive updates per chunk at the cost of four small-network passes.

2. Reduce the number of function evaluations

Every integration step is a full forward pass of the expert. The levers: flow matching instead of diffusion (~10 steps instead of 50–100, §3.3); a cascade that spends its cheap steps where reactivity is needed (T-Rex: 6 slow + 4 fast rather than 10 slow); and adaptive step counts driven by predicted variance (AdaFlow, §18.4) — spend more steps where the action distribution is genuinely multimodal and fewer where it is nearly deterministic. Note that a plain L1L_1L1​ head (OpenVLA-OFT) has K=1K=1K=1 by construction, which is a large part of its 25–50× speedup.

3. Quantisation

Post-training quantisation to 8-bit is close to free in quality terms and roughly halves memory bandwidth, which is what actually bounds you on a transformer at batch size 1. Four-bit is more aggressive but demonstrated: LiteVLA-Edge fine-tunes in FP32, applies post-training 4-bit GGUF quantisation, and runs through llama.cpp with full GPU offload, reporting that aggressive 4-bit quantisation "can be effectively applied to compact VLA models for robotic control while maintaining sufficient representational density for stable and precise motor command generation".

The caution specific to robotics: quantisation error in a language model costs you a slightly worse word. Quantisation error in an action head is a position error in metres. Always evaluate a quantised policy on the real robot, and pay attention to precision-critical tasks (insertion, threading) rather than averages — the loss is not uniformly distributed across tasks.

4. Token pruning and smaller encoders

Vision tokens dominate context length and therefore attention cost. Pruning visually redundant tokens is an active 2025–26 line, with the robotics-specific caveat that the tokens a classifier finds redundant are not the same as those an action head needs — the relevant work explicitly frames this as bridging a "semantic–action gap"[token pruning for VLA]. Pruning by generic saliency can delete exactly the fine geometric detail near the gripper that the policy depends on.

14.6Control-rate and dtdtdt matching

A quiet, extremely common bug. A chunk of actions carries an implicit timestep: if it was recorded at 30 Hz, consecutive actions are 33 ms apart and their magnitudes encode velocities at that spacing. Execute the same chunk at 50 Hz and every implied velocity is 1.67× too fast.

vexecuted=Δadtdeploy=vdemo⋅dttraindtdeploy\mathbf{v}_{\text{executed}} = \frac{\Delta \mathbf{a}}{dt_{\text{deploy}}} = \mathbf{v}_{\text{demo}}\cdot\frac{dt_{\text{train}}}{dt_{\text{deploy}}}vexecuted​=dtdeploy​Δa​=vdemo​⋅dtdeploy​dttrain​​
(14.1)

Symptoms of a mismatch are distinctive and worth recognising: uniformly too-fast or too-slow motion; overshoot on every reach; and — the confusing one — a policy that appears to work in simulation and fails on hardware because the simulator stepped at the training rate. Rules:

  • Record the control rate in the dataset metadata and assert it at load time. Do not infer it.
  • If you must deploy at a different rate, resample the chunk temporally (interpolate) rather than executing it faster.
  • Note that the chunk rate and the servo rate are different things. T-Rex's 30 Hz high-level thread feeds a 300 Hz low-level controller which interpolates between targets — that is a rate conversion, done deliberately, not a mismatch.

14.7Runtime monitoring and failure detection

A deployed policy needs to know when it is failing, because a policy that fails silently for eight hours is worse than one that stops. The methods are developed in Chapter 18; what belongs here is the deployment framing of what to monitor and what to do about it.

Table 14.2 — What to instrument at runtime, and the action each signal should trigger.
SignalSourceCostTrigger
Chunk-boundary discontinuity∥a0(i+1)−ad(i)∥\|\mathbf{a}^{(i+1)}_0 - \mathbf{a}^{(i)}_{d}\|∥a0(i+1)​−ad(i)​∥FreeSpike ⇒ RTC is failing or latency grew; degrade to slower motion
Temporal consistency (STAC)Disagreement between overlapping chunksFree — you already sample themHigh disagreement ⇒ policy is uncertain; slow down or ask for help
Observation-space density (logpZO)A small flow model over observation embeddingsOne small forward passLow density ⇒ out of distribution; stop
Sensor liveness + stalenessTimestamps per streamFreeStale beyond threshold ⇒ treat as missing modality (§13.1) or halt
Force limitsWrench magnitudeFreeOver limit ⇒ immediate compliance or stop. This is a safety interlock, not a metric
Cycle-time histogramPolicy thread timingFreeTail latency growth ⇒ thermal throttling or memory pressure, before it becomes a jerk

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are nearly free. STAC compares the action distributions of overlapping consecutive chunks — you are already generating overlapping chunks if you run the policy faster than the chunk duration, so the disagreement measure costs nothing beyond a distance computation. Chunk-boundary discontinuity is a single norm and is the most direct available proxy for "is my deployment actually working", since it measures the exact artefact §14.3 is about. If you instrument nothing else, instrument these two.

14.8Evaluation that predicts deployment

Offline validation loss is a weak predictor of real-robot success, with one important caveat: at sufficient scale it becomes a good one. EgoScale's contribution is partly the observation that validation loss "strongly correlates with downstream real robot performance", which is what makes their log-linear scaling law actionable. But that is a statement about a pretraining corpus's scale, not about your fine-tune's checkpoint selection.

Protocol details that determine whether your numbers mean anything:

  • Randomise initial conditions every trial. T-Rex randomises object positions and rotations across all 16 trials per task. A fixed start position measures memorisation.
  • Use progress-based rubrics for multi-stage tasks. Binary success on an 11-stage task is a very high-variance estimator; T-Rex uses "progress-based rubrics for multi-stage tasks to capture partial completion", and distinguishes additive rubrics (independent credit per sub-step) from progress rubrics (how far along a hierarchy).
  • Report enough trials. 16 trials gives a standard error of about 12 percentage points at p=0.5p=0.5p=0.5. Differences under ~10 points on a single task are not meaningful; this is why averages across 12 tasks are the headline number and single-task numbers are not.
  • Evaluate consecutive-repetition reliability, not just per-trial success. This is the axis industrial labs emphasise — folding 50 novel items, 200 consecutive repetitions, hours of uninterrupted operation. A policy at 90% per-trial success fails within the first ten reps of a hundred-rep run with near certainty. Reliability is a different and harder metric than success rate, and saying so is a mark of deployment experience.
  • Evaluate under the deployment-time staleness distribution, not with perfectly synchronised inputs (§9.3).

14.9A deployment checklist

  1. Measure the end-to-end latency distribution — the tail, not the mean. A p99 of 400 ms with a p50 of 120 ms is a system that jerks once a minute.
  2. Confirm the VLM prefix is genuinely cached across integration steps. Profile it; do not assume.
  3. Assert the training control rate matches the deployment rate, or resample explicitly.
  4. Enable RTC or a training-time-conditioned equivalent; measure boundary discontinuity before and after.
  5. Low-pass filter policy output before the controller.
  6. Watchdog on chunk staleness → decelerate, never freeze holding an object.
  7. Hard force and velocity limits below the policy, in the control thread, non-bypassable.
  8. Instrument STAC and boundary discontinuity; define the action each threshold triggers.
  9. Test with a physically disconnected camera and a dead fingertip sensor.
  10. Run a long consecutive-repetition test before claiming a success rate.
Key takeaways
  1. Inference is 20–80× slower than the servo period (75–280 ms vs 3.3 ms). That ratio generates every deployment problem.
  2. Three tiers: policy (2–10 Hz), optional reactive (20–100 Hz), control (300–1000 Hz), over lock-protected shared state. The control thread never blocks on the policy thread.
  3. Chunk boundaries produce jerks because the new chunk was planned from a stale observation. Waiting causes stutter; not waiting causes discontinuity.
  4. RTC reframes this as inpainting: hard-freeze the committed prefix, soft-decay the overlap, generate the rest. Training-free, works on any flow/diffusion VLA, resilient to high delay.
  5. Under a 1–2 step budget, inference-time RTC cannot propagate its constraint — hence the training-time conditioning successor. Constraints need compute to propagate, or they must be trained in.
  6. Speed levers in order: cache the prefix (largest, lossless), cut NFEs, quantise (evaluate on hardware — error here is metres, not words), prune tokens (carefully; action-relevant ≠ semantically salient).
  7. Control-rate mismatch scales every velocity by dttrain/dtdeploydt_{\text{train}}/dt_{\text{deploy}}dttrain​/dtdeploy​. Assert the rate; never infer it.
  8. Instrument STAC and chunk-boundary discontinuity — both are essentially free and both measure what actually goes wrong.
  9. Randomise initial conditions, use progress rubrics, report enough trials, and measure consecutive-repetition reliability — it is a different and harder metric than per-trial success.
Part VI

Beyond Imitation

World models, reinforcement learning, and knowing when the policy is about to fail — the three directions that push past the demonstrator's ceiling. The reinforcement-learning chapters are built to be read by someone who has not touched the subject in years: the theory first, each equation mapped to the idea it encodes, and then every published attempt at putting RL on top of a robot policy, sorted by what it did with the trajectories that went wrong.

15World models and JEPA

Core ideas

A world model predicts the future. The field splits on what it predicts: generative models (the Dreamer line) predict future observations through a decoder, while joint-embedding models (the JEPA line) predict future representations and have no decoder at all. The trade is sharp. Reconstruction forces the latent to retain information so it cannot collapse, but spends capacity modelling unpredictable pixel detail. Latent prediction discards that detail by construction, but must be defended against representation collapse — the degenerate solution where the encoder outputs a constant and prediction becomes trivially perfect.

15.1The taxonomy

Table 15.1 — The two families.
Generative / pixel (Dreamer, GR-2)Joint-embedding / latent (JEPA)
PredictsFuture observations (pixels)Future representations
Has a decoderYesNo
Collapse riskNone — reconstruction anchors the latentCentral problem
Capacity spendTexture, lighting, leaf motion — much of it irreducibly unpredictableOnly predictable structure
InspectableYes — you can watch its dreamsNo
PlanningDirectly in imagination; RL inside the modelLatent-space planning against a goal embedding

The argument for JEPA compresses to one sentence: much of the pixel content of a future video frame is inherently unpredictable — the exact texture of a fold, the precise specular highlight — so a model forced to predict it spends most of its capacity on noise, whereas a model predicting a representation can discard exactly the components that are unpredictable. Notice this is the same argument Sparsh arrives at independently for tactile images (§7.5): latent-space SSL beats pixel-space because gel texture and illumination are nuisance variables.

15.2JEPA and collapse

A JEPA encodes a context xxx and a target yyy with encoders fθf_\thetafθ​ and fθˉf_{\bar\theta}fθˉ​, and trains a predictor gϕg_\phigϕ​ to map the context embedding to the target embedding, conditioned on some transformation descriptor zzz (a mask location, an action, a time offset):

LJEPA=∥gϕ(fθ(x), z)−sg[fθˉ(y)]∥2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{JEPA}} = \big\| g_\phi\big(f_\theta(x),\, z\big) - \mathrm{sg}\big[f_{\bar\theta}(y)\big] \big\|^2LJEPA​=​gϕ​(fθ​(x),z)−sg[fθˉ​(y)]​2
(15.1)

The failure is immediate and total: if fθ≡cf_\theta \equiv \mathbf{c}fθ​≡c for a constant c\mathbf{c}c, the loss is exactly zero. The representation carries no information and the objective is perfectly satisfied. Everything interesting about JEPA training is the machinery preventing this.

It is worth seeing this happen rather than taking it on faith. Training a small JEPA on synthetic data under four regimes, 400 steps each:

Table 15.2 — Measured with code/d_jepa.py. A 16-dimensional embedding; "effective rank" is exp⁡\expexp of the entropy of the normalised covariance spectrum, so 16 means all directions are used equally.
Objectiveprediction lossembedding stdeffective rank / 16What happened
naive symmetric (no predictor, no stop-grad)3.3e−070.05811.79Collapsed. Loss is essentially zero because the encoder became nearly constant
stop-gradient + asymmetric predictor1.4e−021.29811.04No scale collapse, but fewer directions in use
+ VICReg2.9e−021.49315.88Spectrum spread across nearly all dimensions
+ SIGReg2.9e−020.98715.12Spread and scaled to unit variance — it is matching N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I)N(0,I), not merely spreading

Three observations, one of them a caution about the metric itself.

The first row is collapse, and the prediction loss rewards it. Loss 3.3×10−73.3\times10^{-7}3.3×10−7 is four to five orders of magnitude better than every other row, achieved by an encoder whose output standard deviation fell to 0.058. A monitoring dashboard tracking only the training loss would report this run as by far the most successful.

Effective rank alone does not detect it. The collapsed run scores 11.79 — higher than the stop-gradient run's 11.04. That is because effective rank is computed from the normalised eigenvalue spectrum, so it measures the shape of the covariance and is blind to its overall scale. A cloud shrunk uniformly by 20× keeps its spectral shape perfectly. If you monitor JEPA training, track embedding norm and effective rank together; either one alone can be fooled.

Stop-gradient plus an asymmetric predictor genuinely works — the second row shows no scale collapse at all, which is exactly why those heuristics are ubiquitous. But it uses noticeably fewer effective dimensions than either explicit regulariser. This is the gap LeJEPA argues should be closed by a principled objective rather than by architectural asymmetry, and note that SIGReg is the only row landing near unit variance, because that is literally what it optimises for.

Table 15.3 — Anti-collapse mechanisms, in increasing order of principle.
MechanismHowCharacter
Stop-gradient + EMA teacherTarget encoder is a slowly-updated copy; no gradient flows to itHeuristic; empirically essential in BYOL/DINO-style training
Asymmetric predictorPredictor exists on the context branch only, breaking the symmetry that makes constants optimalHeuristic
Variance/covariance penalty (VICReg)Explicitly penalise low per-dimension variance and off-diagonal covarianceConstrains the first two moments only
SIGReg (LeJEPA)Match the embedding distribution to an isotropic Gaussian via random 1-D projectionsPrincipled; constrains the full distribution

15.3I-JEPA and V-JEPA: the masking is the method

§15.2 left the architecture with a hole in it: predict the representation of what you cannot see, and nothing in the loss stops the encoder from making every representation identical. The regularisers in the next two sections close that hole from the loss side. I-JEPA and V-JEPA close a different part of it from the data side, and the mechanism is worth understanding on its own, because it is the part that decides whether the learned features are any use to a robot.

The claim is narrow and concrete: what you mask determines what the representation encodes. Mask a few scattered pixels and the cheapest way to predict them is local texture interpolation, which is a low-level statistic and generalises to nothing. Mask a large, contiguous, semantically coherent region and texture interpolation no longer works — the only way to predict it is to know what kind of thing is there. The two papers below are the image and video instances of that single idea.

I-JEPA: large blocks, informative context

I-JEPA[Assran et al. 2023] states the design as a requirement rather than a hyperparameter: it is "crucial to (a) sample target blocks with sufficiently large scale (semantic), and to (b) use a sufficiently informative (spatially distributed) context block". The concrete recipe behind those two words:

  • Targets. "Typically, we set MMM equal to 4, and sample the blocks with a random aspect ratio in the range (0.75,1.5)(0.75, 1.5)(0.75,1.5) and random scale in the range (0.15,0.2)(0.15, 0.2)(0.15,0.2)." Four blocks, each 15–20% of the image — large enough that no local filter can fill them in.
  • Context. "We first sample a single block x\mathbf xx from the image with a random scale in the range (0.85,1.0)(0.85, 1.0)(0.85,1.0) and unit aspect ratio", and then "we remove any overlapping regions from the context block". The removal is the essential step: without it the task is partly copying.
  • Predictor. A deliberately narrow ViT — "we fix the embedding dimension of the predictor to 384", with depth 6 for a ViT-B/16 backbone and 12 for the larger ones. It is a bottleneck on purpose; a predictor with the capacity of the encoder would let the encoder do less work.
  • Target encoder. An exponential moving average of the online encoder: "we use a momentum value of 0.9960.9960.996, and linearly increase this value to 1.01.01.0 throughout pretraining."
  • Loss. "The average L2L_2L2​ distance between the predicted patch-level representations."

V-JEPA: the same idea with time attached

V-JEPA[Bardes et al. 2024] carries the recipe to video and changes exactly one structural thing, which happens to be the thing that matters for robotics. A clip is 16 frames at temporal stride 4, patchified into tubelets of 16×16×216\times16\times216×16×2 — so each token already spans two frames. Masks come in two flavours: short-range, "8 randomly sampled target blocks covering 15% of each frame", and long-range, "2 randomly sampled target blocks covering 70% of each frame", with aspect ratios again "randomly chosen in the range (0.75,1.5)(0.75, 1.5)(0.75,1.5)". The loss is an L1L_1L1​ regression in latent space.

The structural change is that a mask extends through the entire temporal dimension. A masked region is not a hole in one frame; it is a tube, absent from every frame of the clip. That single decision is what forces the representation to be about dynamics rather than appearance, and the reasoning is short enough to state completely: if a region were visible in frame 1 and masked in frame 8, the model could predict it by copying frame 1 — an appearance task solved by a nearest-neighbour lookup in time. Masking the tube removes that shortcut, and the only remaining route to a prediction is a model of how the visible part of the scene evolves.

Why any of this belongs in a robotics manual

The connection is not that a robot should run I-JEPA. It is that three separate decisions elsewhere in this manual are the same decision as the one above, and seeing them as one thing is worth more than the individual results.

  1. Latent prediction is the reason a world model is affordable. A generative world model spends capacity on pixels that no controller will ever read — specular highlights, sensor noise, the texture of the floor. §15.1 made this argument abstractly; I-JEPA is where it was first shown to produce competitive features without it. For a policy running at 30 Hz the difference is not aesthetic, it is whether the model fits the budget.
  2. The same objective transfers to non-visual sensors, and has. §7.5 reports a direct comparison on tactile images: MAE (pixel-space), DINO, I-JEPA and V-JEPA trained on the same data, with the latent-space objectives beating the pixel-space one — "indicating the merits of learning in latent space". The per-task split is the useful part, and it follows from the masking rather than from the acronym: DINO wins on force regression, V-JEPA wins on slip detection, because slip is intrinsically temporal and V-JEPA is the only one of the four whose pretext task cannot be solved without modelling time. A tactile image sequence has exactly the property the tube mask was designed for.
  3. It is the pretraining stage of an actual planner. V-JEPA 2 in the next section is this encoder, scaled, with an action-conditioned predictor attached — and the reason the attachment works on 62 hours of robot data is that the representation was already about dynamics before any action was ever supplied.
What a JEPA does not give you

A JEPA encoder predicts in its own latent space, which means its predictions are not directly inspectable and its errors are not directly interpretable. You cannot look at an imagined future and see that the model thinks the mug is floating; you can only observe that a distance in an abstract space is large. That is a real cost relative to a generative world model, and it is the honest reason the pixel-space line of work in §15.7 has not gone away. A latent world model is cheaper and a generative one is auditable, and no result so far has made that a settled trade.

15.4VICReg, and exactly what it cannot see

LVIC=λ 1d∑jmax⁡ ⁣(0, γ−Var(zj)+ε)⏟variance: no dimension may collapse  +  μ 1d∑j≠kCjk2⏟covariance: no redundancy\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VIC}} = \lambda\,\underbrace{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j}\max\!\big(0,\,\gamma - \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(z_j)+\varepsilon}\big)}_{\text{variance: no dimension may collapse}} \;+\; \mu\,\underbrace{\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j\neq k} C_{jk}^2}_{\text{covariance: no redundancy}}LVIC​=λvariance: no dimension may collapsed1​j∑​max(0,γ−Var(zj​)+ε​)​​+μcovariance: no redundancyd1​j=k∑​Cjk2​​​
(15.2)

The variance term forbids any single dimension from becoming constant; the covariance term forbids dimensions from duplicating one another. Together they exclude the obvious collapses, and they are cheap. The limitation is exactly stateable: VICReg constrains only the first two moments. A distribution can have unit variance in every coordinate, zero covariance between every pair, and still be pathological.

This is not a hypothetical. Below, a distribution that satisfies both VICReg terms to three decimal places while being obviously degenerate.

§15.4 ended with a gap: matching the first two moments does not pin down a distribution, and an embedding cloud can satisfy a variance and covariance criterion while being badly shaped. The obvious repair is to test the whole distribution rather than two of its moments. The obvious objection is cost — a distributional test in a 1000-dimensional embedding space is not something you can afford inside a training loop. So the question becomes: is there a distributional test whose cost is linear in the batch and independent of the embedding width? There is, and it comes from a classical result: a high-dimensional distribution is determined by all of its one-dimensional projections, so testing enough random projections tests the distribution.

15.5SIGReg: sketching a distribution test

LeJEPA[Balestriero & LeCun 2025] starts from a different question: what is the optimal embedding distribution? Their answer is the isotropic Gaussian, on the grounds that it minimises downstream linear-probe risk. The objective then becomes: match the embedding distribution to N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I)N(0,I). The obstacle is that testing distributional equality in d≈1024d\approx1024d≈1024 dimensions is intractable.

The Cramér–Wold escape. A probability distribution is uniquely determined by the set of all its one-dimensional projections. So "is this cloud N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I)N(0,I)?" is equivalent to "is every 1-D projection N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1)?" Testing all directions is impossible, so SIGReg sketches: draw a modest set A\mathbb{A}A of random unit directions, run a univariate goodness-of-fit test on each projection, and resample the directions every iteration. The paper's Definition 2:

SIGRegT(A,{fθ(xn)}n=1N)  ≜  1∣A∣∑a∈AT({a⊤fθ(xn)}n=1N)\mathrm{SIGReg}_T\big(\mathbb{A}, \{f_\theta(x_n)\}_{n=1}^N\big) \;\triangleq\; \frac{1}{|\mathbb{A}|}\sum_{\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{A}} T\big(\{\mathbf{a}^\top f_\theta(x_n)\}_{n=1}^{N}\big)SIGRegT​(A,{fθ​(xn​)}n=1N​)≜∣A∣1​a∈A∑​T({a⊤fθ​(xn​)}n=1N​)
(15.3)

Two details in that equation are deliberate. It is an average over directions, not a maximum — the paper replaces the max "to avoid sparse gradient over the directions in A\mathbb{A}A", since a max would send gradient through only one direction per step. And the directions are resampled, so isotropy is enforced in expectation rather than along a fixed basis.

Which univariate test?

The paper evaluates three families and the reasoning is worth carrying, because it is a good example of choosing a loss for its optimisation properties rather than its statistical power alone.

Table 15.4 — Why Epps–Pulley. Source: LeJEPA §4.2.
FamilyExampleVerdict
Moment-basedJarque–Bera; extended JB adding the first two momentsUnstable. Moments are polynomial in the data, so "raising values to a power of kkk can quickly lead to exploding gradients" — and they only match finitely many moments anyway
CDF-based (cumulative distribution function)Cramér–von Mises, Anderson–DarlingImpractical. They require sorting the samples, which is awkward to differentiate and to distribute
Characteristic-functionEpps–PulleyChosen. The empirical CF is a mean of complex exponentials: bounded, smooth, O(N)\mathcal{O}(N)O(N), and trivially distributed via all_reduce

with ϕ(t)=e−t2/2\phi(t)=e^{-t^2/2}ϕ(t)=e−t2/2 the characteristic function of N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1) and σ\sigmaσ typically 1. The stability claim is made precise in the paper's Theorem 4: the gradient and curvature are bounded,

∣∂EP(a)∂zi∣≤4σ2N,∣∂2EP(a)∂zi2∣≤Cπ σ32N\left|\frac{\partial \mathrm{EP}(\mathbf{a})}{\partial z_i}\right| \le \frac{4\sigma^{2}}{N}, \qquad \left|\frac{\partial^{2} \mathrm{EP}(\mathbf{a})}{\partial z_i^{2}}\right| \le \frac{C\sqrt{\pi}\,\sigma^{3}}{2N}​∂zi​∂EP(a)​​≤N4σ2​,​∂zi2​∂2EP(a)​​≤2NCπ​σ3​
