which is the property that lets SIGReg replace stop-gradient, teacher–student setups, and elaborate learning-rate schedules. The reported payoff: linear time, low memory, multi-GPU scaling, a single tunable hyperparameter, and 79% top-1 linear-probe accuracy on ImageNet-1k with a ViT-H/14.

What the two objectives actually see

Running both on the same five distributions, each with 4096 samples in 2-D:

Table 15.5 — Measured with code/d_jepa.py. The VICReg column is the variance + covariance terms; SIGReg is the mean Epps–Pulley statistic over 256 random directions.
Distributionstd xxxstd yyycov xyxyxyVICRegSIGRegVerdict
isotropic Gaussian0.9891.015−0.0070.0110.47both satisfied — this is the target
collapsed0.0300.0300.0001.936536.6both catch it
correlated1.0011.0040.9661.868126.9both catch it
Laplace (unit variance)0.9940.977−0.0190.03013.6VICReg blind to heavy tails
"X" distribution1.0081.008−0.0200.000815.3VICReg completely blind

The last row is the paper's own counterexample and it is the one to remember. The "X" distribution places all its mass on two crossing lines, yet its marginals are standard Gaussian and its covariance is the identity — so VICReg scores it 0.0008, essentially perfect. Every statistic VICReg computes is satisfied by a distribution that is manifestly not isotropic Gaussian. Sweeping the projection direction shows how SIGReg finds it:

direction   0 deg : Epps-Pulley =  0.64
direction  30 deg : Epps-Pulley = 22.68
direction  45 deg : Epps-Pulley = 41.43   <-- spike
direction  60 deg : Epps-Pulley = 22.71
direction  90 deg : Epps-Pulley =  0.94
direction 135 deg : Epps-Pulley = 52.57   <-- spike

Along the axes the projection is a standard Gaussian, so the statistic is near zero — which is exactly why a coordinate-wise method sees nothing. Along the diagonals, where the two lines project onto a spike at zero and a spread-out remainder, the statistic explodes. Random directions find those diagonals with high probability, and resampling every step means they are found repeatedly.

Everything so far has been about learning a representation from passive observation. To control something you need one more ingredient: a predictor that takes an action as an argument. Once you have that, a policy becomes optional. Given a goal state and a model of how actions move the world, you can search over action sequences for one that lands near the goal, and the search replaces the learned policy entirely. This is planning, and its appeal in robotics is economic: the expensive part — the world model — can be learned from video that no robot produced, and only the cheap part, the action conditioning, needs interaction data.

15.6V-JEPA 2 and action-conditioned planning

V-JEPA 2[Assran et al. 2025] is the staged instantiation: first build a general observation-based world model from over 1 million hours of internet video, then post-train it for action-conditioned planning using only 62 hours of robot data. That ratio is the headline — four orders of magnitude more passive video than interaction data.

V-JEPA 2-AC plans by treating prediction as an energy function. Given a goal image, search for an action sequence minimising the L1L_1L1​ distance between the imagined future representation and the goal representation, optimised with the cross-entropy method:

a1:T⋆=arg⁡min⁡a1:T ∥s^T(a1:T)−sgoal∥1\mathbf{a}^\star_{1:T} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{a}_{1:T}}\ \big\| \hat{s}_{T}(\mathbf{a}_{1:T}) - s_{\text{goal}} \big\|_1a1:T⋆​=arga1:T​min​ ​s^T​(a1:T​)−sgoal​​1​
(15.6)

Deployed zero-shot on Franka arms in two labs it had never seen, with no data from those environments and no task-specific training or reward, it reaches 65–80% success on reach, grasp, and pick-and-place. The significance is that a world model plus a goal image can substitute for a policy, which is a genuinely different paradigm from everything in Parts I–IV.

The case against everything in this chapter is worth stating properly rather than dismissing. If a world model predicts pixels, you can look at what it imagined, and so can a reviewer, a safety case, and a debugging session at two in the morning. A latent model offers none of that. It is also true that the "wasted capacity" argument against pixel prediction is an argument about efficiency, not about achievability — with enough compute, predicting pixels works, and it produces a model that can be trained by reinforcement learning inside its own imagination because the imagined states are complete.

15.7Dreamer 4 and the generative counterpoint

Dreamer 4[Hafner, Yan & Lillicrap 2025] is the current state of the generative line: an agent that learns control by reinforcement learning inside its own world model. It is the first agent to obtain diamonds in Minecraft purely from a standard offline dataset with no environment interaction — a task requiring sequences of over 20,000 mouse and keyboard actions from raw pixels. It achieves real-time interactive inference on a single GPU through a "shortcut forcing" objective and an efficient transformer.

The data result is the transferable one: 100 hours of action-paired video out of 2,500 total hours reached 85% of full performance, and it outperforms VPT with 100× less data. Most world knowledge extracts from unlabelled footage; actions are only needed to ground it. That is precisely T-Rex's thesis in a different domain — pretrain broadly on cheap passive data, ground narrowly with expensive labelled interaction — and noticing the parallel is a good observation to make.

15.8How world models are actually used in manipulation

  1. Representation learning. Use the encoder as a frozen visual backbone. DINO-WM's route: build the world model on a frozen pretrained encoder rather than learning one.
  2. Planning. Search over action sequences in latent space against a goal embedding (V-JEPA 2-AC).
  3. Policy training in imagination. Run RL inside the model, avoiding real-world sample cost (Dreamer 4).
  4. Auxiliary objective inside a VLA. The most practically relevant for this manual. Add future-latent prediction as a loss term alongside the action loss. T-Rex does exactly this — λfuture=0.5\lambda_{\text{future}}=0.5λfuture​=0.5 on a future-visual-latent prediction loss, with its latent expert dedicated to it — and states the purpose plainly: "to align this tactile modality with the broader visual context during mid-training". GR00T N1.5 similarly trains "jointly with flow matching and world-modeling objectives".

Use 4 is worth dwelling on because it reframes what a world model is for in a VLA. It is not there to plan. It is there as a dense auxiliary signal that forces the encoder to represent physical dynamics rather than just enough appearance to regress the next action. An action loss is a weak signal for representation learning — a 62-dimensional target per chunk. "Predict the next visual latent" is enormously denser, and it is a signal that a tactile encoder can meaningfully contribute to, which is exactly why it helps with modality grounding.

Key takeaways
  1. Generative world models predict pixels (no collapse, wasted capacity); JEPAs predict latents (efficient, collapse-prone). The same argument favours latent-space SSL for tactile images.
  2. Collapse is the JEPA failure: a constant encoder achieves zero loss. A naive symmetric JEPA reaches prediction loss 3.3e−07 with embedding std 0.058. The loss function rewards the failure.
  3. Effective rank alone cannot detect collapse, because it uses the normalised covariance spectrum and is blind to scale. Monitor embedding norm and effective rank.
  4. Stop-gradient + asymmetric predictor genuinely prevents scale collapse (that is why it is everywhere) but uses fewer effective dimensions than an explicit regulariser.
  5. VICReg constrains variance and covariance — the first two moments only.
  6. SIGReg exploits Cramér–Wold (a distribution is determined by all its 1-D projections): sketch random directions, run a univariate test on each, average rather than maximise to avoid sparse gradients. The test is Epps–Pulley, comparing empirical and target characteristic functions — chosen over moment tests (polynomial ⇒ exploding gradients) and CDF tests (need sorting). Its gradient is bounded by 4σ2/N4\sigma^2/N4σ2/N.
  7. The counterexample that settles it: the "X" distribution has standard-Gaussian marginals and identity covariance, so VICReg scores it 0.0008 — essentially perfect — while SIGReg scores 15.3, with the statistic spiking at exactly 45° and 135°.
  8. V-JEPA 2: >1M hours of video + 62 hours of robot data; V-JEPA 2-AC plans by minimising L1L_1L1​ distance to a goal embedding, 65–80% zero-shot in unseen labs.
  9. Dreamer 4 mines Minecraft diamonds fully offline; 100 of 2,500 hours action-paired reaches 85% of performance — actions ground knowledge that video supplies.
  10. In a VLA, the world model's real job is as a dense auxiliary objective (λfuture=0.5\lambda_{\text{future}}{=}0.5λfuture​=0.5 in T-Rex), not as a planner.

16Reinforcement learning: the essentials

Core ideas

Reinforcement learning replaces a per-step target with a late scalar, and everything else in the subject follows from that one substitution. You need four objects — the return, the value function, the action-value function and the advantage — and one structural distinction, on-policy versus off-policy, which decides how many robot-hours a gradient step costs. This chapter builds those intuitively and maps each equation to the idea it encodes; derivations are deliberately omitted, because none of the arguments in Chapter 17 turn on them. What those arguments do turn on is knowing precisely what a value function is a function of, and why a policy gradient has to measure every action against a baseline — a term §16.3 makes precise.

16.1What changes when the target disappears

Every loss in this manual so far has had a target in it. Behavioural cloning has the demonstrator's action; flow matching has the velocity u=ε−au = \varepsilon - au=ε−a; the OpenVLA cross-entropy has a bin index. In each case the supervision arrives at the same time and place as the prediction, and the gradient is local: this output was wrong, here is the direction that makes it less wrong.

Reinforcement learning removes that. What arrives instead is a scalar reward, usually late, often once, that says how well things went and nothing about what should have been done instead. The arithmetic of the gap is worth doing explicitly, because it is what makes robot RL hard rather than merely inconvenient. A policy running at 50 Hz on a sixty-second task emits three thousand actions and, under a sparse success reward, receives one bit. Figure 16.1 draws the two regimes side by side.

The formal object is a Markov decision process: states sss, actions aaa, a transition law P(s′∣s,a)P(s'\mid s,a)P(s′∣s,a), a reward r(s,a)r(s,a)r(s,a) and a discount γ∈[0,1)\gamma\in[0,1)γ∈[0,1). A policy πθ(a∣s)\pi_\theta(a\mid s)πθ​(a∣s) induces a distribution over trajectories τ\tauτ, and the quantity being maximised is the expected discounted return:

Gt=∑k=0∞γkrt+k,J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ[G0]G_t = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^{k} r_{t+k}, \qquad J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}\big[G_0\big]Gt​=k=0∑∞​γkrt+k​,J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ​​[G0​]
(16.1)

The discount is usually presented as a mathematical convenience that keeps the sum finite. Treat it instead as a statement about horizon: γ\gammaγ sets an effective horizon of roughly 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma)1/(1−γ) steps, beyond which rewards are invisible to the learner. At the conventional γ=0.99\gamma=0.99γ=0.99 that is a hundred steps, which at 50 Hz is two seconds. A manipulation task that takes thirty seconds is therefore not, under that discount, a single problem the agent can see the end of. This is one of the reasons the RL formulations in Chapter 17 so often operate over chunks rather than control steps: a chunk of 50 actions at 50 Hz is one second of behaviour, and an MDP whose steps are chunks has a horizon thirty to fifty times shorter in step count for the same physical task.

A subtlety worth pinning down

"State" in the MDP means a quantity from which the future is conditionally independent of the past. A robot's camera image is not that — velocity is not visible in one frame, occluded objects are not represented, and the contents of a closed drawer are not observable at all. Everything in practice is a partially observed MDP dressed as an MDP, which is why observation histories, proprioception and the modality work of Chapters 5–8 matter as much to an RL formulation as to an imitation one. When a value function behaves erratically, an unobservable state variable is a more common cause than a bad optimiser.

16.2Value, action-value, advantage

Three functions do all the work, and they are routinely conflated. Each answers a different question about the same situation:

Vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣st=s],Qπ(s,a)=Eπ[Gt∣st=s, at=a]V^{\pi}(s) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[G_t \mid s_t = s\big], \qquad Q^{\pi}(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[G_t \mid s_t = s,\ a_t = a\big]Vπ(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s],Qπ(s,a)=Eπ​[Gt​∣st​=s, at​=a]
(16.2)
Aπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s)A^{\pi}(s,a) = Q^{\pi}(s,a) - V^{\pi}(s)Aπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s)
(16.3)

In words, and these phrasings are worth keeping:

  • Vπ(s)V^\pi(s)Vπ(s) — how good is this situation, given that I will go on behaving as I currently do.
  • Qπ(s,a)Q^\pi(s,a)Qπ(s,a) — how good is this situation if I do this one specific thing now, and then go on behaving as I currently do.
  • Aπ(s,a)A^\pi(s,a)Aπ(s,a) — was this particular action better or worse than my own average in this situation.
Actor, critic, and what a critic is for

Two words for two networks, worth fixing now because the rest of the chapter leans on them. The actor is the policy πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ — the thing that looks at a state and emits an action. In this manual the actor is the VLA itself. The critic is a second, separately trained network whose only job is to estimate one of the value functions above, usually VVV or QQQ, for the actor as it currently behaves. It never chooses anything; it answers "how well is this going?" The two names come from the actor–critic family of algorithms (§16.8), and "value network" means the same thing as critic.

You need one for two distinct reasons, and keeping them apart makes the rest of the chapter much easier to read:

  • To supply the baseline. Eq. (16.5) reinforces actions that turned out better than expected, and something has to estimate "expected". That something is VπV^\piVπ, and the critic is what produces it. Without it the policy gradient still points the right way on average, but so noisily that it is unusable. §16.3 defines the baseline precisely, and says why subtracting one costs nothing.
  • To make the signal local. Figure 16.1's problem is that the reward arrives once, at the end. A critic's prediction is available at every state, so the change between consecutive predictions — Eq. (16.7) — is a learning signal that exists long before the episode is over. A critic is a learned stand-in for the future, which is precisely what converts the sparse global scalar back into something that looks like supervision.

The cost is real: the critic is a second large network to fit, its training data keeps shifting underneath it as the actor changes, and when it is wrong it corrupts the actor directly rather than merely slowing it down. That expense is why the group-relative methods of §16.7 exist. If all you needed was the baseline, KKK rollouts from the same starting state will supply one for free, and the critic can be dropped entirely — which is what "no value network" means in Table 17.1.

Only the third carries a sign that tells you what to change. VVV and QQQ are both large in a good situation regardless of whether the action taken was any good, which is exactly the failure mode that makes an unbaselined policy gradient useless: it reinforces every action taken in a lucky episode, including the ones that nearly lost it. Figure 16.2 puts numbers on all three at a single state.

A critic is a function of the policy, not of the world

All three functions carry a superscript π\piπ, and it is load-bearing. There is no such thing as "the value of this state". A critic fitted to demonstration data estimates the value of the demonstrator, and will be systematically optimistic about a policy that is worse — it predicts returns the current policy cannot actually achieve. That is the root of two otherwise unrelated problems: the instability of actor–critic methods, where the target moves because the policy moves, and the extrapolation failure of offline RL in §16.9. Every time you change the policy, you have partly invalidated the critic.

The Bellman equation is the consistency condition linking a value to the values that follow it:

Qπ(s,a)=Es′[ r(s,a)+γ Ea′∼π[Qπ(s′,a′)]]Q^{\pi}(s,a) = \mathbb{E}_{s'}\Big[\, r(s,a) + \gamma\, \mathbb{E}_{a'\sim\pi}\big[Q^{\pi}(s',a')\big]\Big]Qπ(s,a)=Es′​[r(s,a)+γEa′∼π​[Qπ(s′,a′)]]
(16.4)

It is not a formula for computing QQQ; it is a constraint that the true QQQ satisfies, and every value-based algorithm is a way of enforcing it approximately by regression. Read the right-hand side carefully and the discipline's central hazard is visible: the regression target contains the function being fitted. You are training a network on labels it produced itself one step earlier. Target networks, twin critics, layer normalisation and conservative penalties are all responses to that self-reference, not incidental tricks.

16.3From measuring to improving: the policy gradient

Everything so far has been description. VVV, QQQ and AAA say how well things are going; not one of them changes the policy. This section is the step from measurement to improvement, and it is worth being clear about where the difficulty lies, because it is not where a reader coming from supervised learning expects.

The quantity to be maximised is J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ[G0]J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}[G_0]J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ​​[G0​] from Eq. (16.1). The obstacle is that θ\thetaθ appears in the distribution being averaged over, not merely in the thing being averaged. Changing the policy changes which trajectories happen at all, and the map from a policy to the trajectories a robot produces runs through contact, friction and a physical arm. There is nothing there to differentiate.

The score-function identity — classically called REINFORCE, the name that survives in the variants of §16.7 — evades this by moving the derivative off the environment and onto the policy's own log-probability, which is a neural network and so differentiable by construction:

∇θJ(θ)=Eτ∼πθ ⁣[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st)  A^t]\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}\!\left[\sum_{t} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\; \hat{A}_t\right]∇θ​J(θ)=Eτ∼πθ​​[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)A^t​]
(16.5)

Read it as: increase the log-probability of actions that turned out better than expected, in proportion to how much better. Notice what it does not require. No model of the environment, no derivative of the reward, no knowledge of how the robot moves — only the actions you took, the log-probabilities your own network assigned them, and one number per action saying how it turned out. That is the whole reason this identity is the foundation of the subject.

Two phrases in that sentence carry the rest of the chapter, and it is worth taking them separately.

"Better than expected" is a baseline. A baseline b(s)b(s)b(s) is any quantity subtracted from the return before it weights the log-probability, subject to exactly one condition: it may depend on the state, but not on the action taken there. Written out, the estimator is

∇θJ(θ)=E ⁣[∑t∇θlog⁡πθ(at∣st) (Gt−b(st))],Ea∼πθ ⁣[∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s) b(s)]=0\nabla_\theta J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\,\big(G_t - b(s_t)\big)\right], \qquad \mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_\theta}\!\big[\nabla_\theta \log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)\, b(s)\big] = 0∇θ​J(θ)=E[t∑​∇θ​logπθ​(at​∣st​)(Gt​−b(st​))],Ea∼πθ​​[∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s)b(s)]=0
(16.6)

The second identity is the entire justification, and it is worth reading rather than deriving: because b(s)b(s)b(s) does not vary with the action, its contribution averages to zero over the actions the policy might have taken. Subtracting it therefore changes nothing about where the gradient points. What it changes is the variance, and by a great deal. Take b(s)=Vπ(s)b(s) = V^\pi(s)b(s)=Vπ(s) — the critic's estimate of the policy's own average from that state — and Gt−b(st)G_t - b(s_t)Gt​−b(st​) becomes precisely the advantage of Eq. (16.3), which is why A^t\hat A_tA^t​ and not GtG_tGt​ stands in Eq. (16.5). Every other baseline in this chapter is a cheaper way of approximating that same choice: the group mean of §16.7, or the leave-one-out mean beside it.

That this matters is not an optimisation nicety. Set b=0b = 0b=0 and every action in a successful episode is reinforced — the recovery from a near-miss and the wasted motion that preceded it alike — while in a failed episode every action is suppressed, including the correct ones. The estimator is still unbiased. It is simply dominated by which episodes happened to succeed rather than by what made them succeed, and no quantity of data repairs an estimator whose every individual sample points somewhere unhelpful.

"τ∼πθ\tau \sim \pi_\thetaτ∼πθ​" is the expectation's subscript, and it is a much sharper restriction than it looks. The identity holds for trajectories drawn from the policy being differentiated — that policy, not one close to it. Take a single gradient step and θ\thetaθ has moved, so the batch still sitting in memory was produced by a policy that no longer exists.

Two gaps, and where each is closed

Equation (16.5) is now the target of the chapter, and it has two holes in it. The next two sections close them in order.

  • It is written in terms of A^t\hat A_tA^t​, but the advantage is exactly what you do not have. What you have is sampled returns, which are noisy, and a critic, which is wrong. §16.4 is about building A^t\hat A_tA^t​ out of those two flawed materials.
  • Its expectation is over trajectories from the current policy, which makes every batch perishable. §16.5 is about what that costs — and on a robot, it is the most consequential sentence in this chapter.

16.4Where the advantage estimate comes from

Equation (16.5) wants a number at every timestep saying how much better than expected that action turned out. There are exactly two honest ways to produce one, they fail in opposite directions, and everything used in practice is a dial between them.

Wait and see. Let the episode finish and use the return that actually occurred. This is a Monte Carlo estimate, and it is unbiased for the best possible reason: it is a sample of precisely the quantity being estimated. It is also a sample of everything else that happened in that episode. In a three-thousand-step manipulation task, the return credited to the grasp at step 40 contains the consequences of every decision from step 41 to step 3,000, nearly all of which had nothing to do with that grasp. The estimate is correct on average and close to uninformative in any one episode.

Ask the critic. Instead of waiting, substitute the critic's prediction of the return still to come — using an estimate to build an estimate, which is what bootstrapping means wherever the word appears in these two chapters. The noise largely disappears, because a critic's prediction is a smooth function of the state rather than one noisy rollout. It is replaced by bias: the estimate is wrong by however wrong the critic is, and §16.2 has already established that the critic is always somewhat wrong, because the policy it describes keeps moving.

The smallest version of the second idea — one real reward, one real transition, and the critic's opinion on either side of it — has a name, and it does most of the work in what follows:

δt=rt+γV(st+1)−V(st)\delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1}) - V(s_t)δt​=rt​+γV(st+1​)−V(st​)
(16.7)

Read δt\delta_tδt​ as the amount by which the world turned out better than the critic expected. If the critic were exactly right and the policy fixed, its expectation would be zero everywhere, so a non-zero δt\delta_tδt​ is always one of two things: news about the world, or evidence that the critic needs correcting. Both are useful, which is why the same quantity trains the critic and weights the actor.

Between the two extremes lies an obvious family. You can take one real step and then bootstrap, or two real steps and then bootstrap, or three — each additional real step buys a little less bias and costs a little more variance. Generalised advantage estimation [Schulman et al. 2015] takes that entire family and averages it with geometric weights, which collapses to a single line:

A^tGAE(γ,λ)=∑l=0∞(γλ)l δt+l\hat{A}^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}_t = \sum_{l=0}^{\infty} (\gamma\lambda)^{l}\,\delta_{t+l}A^tGAE(γ,λ)​=l=0∑∞​(γλ)lδt+l​
(16.8)

λ\lambdaλ is the dial. At λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 only δt\delta_tδt​ survives: maximum bias, minimum variance. At λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 the sum telescopes, every bootstrapped term cancels against its neighbour, and what remains is the Monte Carlo advantage: no bias, maximum variance. Practice sits near 0.950.950.95 — closer to the unbiased end than most people assume, because over a long episode the bias of a wrong critic is paid at every step it is trusted for, while the variance is paid once.

One consequence is specific to robotics and is rarely stated. Under a sparse reward — nothing at all until the episode succeeds or fails — every δt\delta_tδt​ before the final step is rt=0r_t = 0rt​=0 plus the critic's disagreement with itself. A small λ\lambdaλ therefore does not merely add bias; there is almost no signal in it until the critic has learned to carry the terminal reward backwards across hundreds of steps, which takes many episodes that a real robot does not have. That leaves two exits: run at high λ\lambdaλ and pay the variance, or abandon per-step credit assignment altogether and give every action in an episode the same number. The second sounds like a retreat. It is what the methods that dominate the VLA literature actually do, and §16.7 explains why it works.

Table 16.1 — Advantage estimators, and what each costs you.
EstimatorBiasVarianceNeeds a criticNeeds the episode to end
Monte Carlo returnnonevery highonly for the baselineyes
One-step TD (λ=0\lambda=0λ=0)high while the critic is wronglowyesno
GAE, λ≈0.95\lambda\approx0.95λ≈0.95smallmoderateyesno
Episode-level, group-relative (§16.7)none about the episode; no per-step credit at allmoderate, falls as the group growsnoyes

16.5Where the data may come from: on-policy, off-policy, offline

Now the second gap. Equation (16.5) is an expectation over trajectories from πθ\pi_\thetaπθ​ — the policy currently being differentiated — so taken literally, every sample you hold expires the instant you use it. How seriously a method takes that constraint is what decides where its training data may come from, and on hardware that decision is the difference between an experiment that fits in an afternoon and one that does not fit in a year.

Three regimes sit on that spectrum. On-policy methods obey the constraint: collect with the current policy, take a few gradient steps, discard the batch, collect again. Off-policy methods sidestep it by not using Eq. (16.5) at all — a critic fitted by regression onto Bellman targets does not care which policy produced a transition, so every transition ever collected stays usable indefinitely. Offline methods go further and never interact with the world at all. Figure 16.3 draws the three, priced in the only currency that matters on a real robot.

If you do want to keep using Eq. (16.5) on data that is slightly stale, the bridge is the importance ratio, which reweights a sample drawn from an old policy so that it counts as though it had come from the current one:

rt(θ)=πθ(at∣st)πθold(at∣st)r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t\mid s_t)}rt​(θ)=πθold​​(at​∣st​)πθ​(at​∣st​)​
(16.9)

The correction is exact in expectation and useless in practice once the two policies differ much, because the ratio's variance grows without bound — a single action the old policy rarely took and the new one likes can dominate an entire batch. That leaves two families of response, and between them they account for every algorithm in the rest of this chapter: keep the two policies close enough that the ratio stays near 1, which is PPO in §16.6, or never form a ratio at all, which is what learning a QQQ-function buys you in §16.8.

The inversion that explains the literature

On-policy methods are sample-inefficient by construction, which sounds disqualifying for robotics. It is — on hardware. In simulation the calculus inverts completely: with thousands of parallel environments, samples are nearly free and what is scarce is stability, which is exactly what on-policy methods sell. This is why the simulation-based VLA papers of §17.5 — SimpleVLA-RL, πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}πRL​, TGRPO — reach for PPO and GRPO, while every paper that trains on a real arm — SERL, HIL-SERL, ConRFT — reaches for an off-policy actor–critic. Neither group is unaware of the other's methods. They are answering different scarcity constraints.

16.6PPO: keeping the policies close

This is the first of the two escape routes §16.5 ended on: keep the new policy close enough to the one that collected the data that Eq. (16.9)'s ratio stays near 1, and in exchange get to reuse the batch for more than a single gradient step. PPO [Schulman et al. 2017] importance-weights the batch across several epochs and stops the ratio drifting by clipping:

LCLIP=E[min⁡(rt(θ) A^t,  clip(rt(θ), 1−ϵ, 1+ϵ) A^t)]\mathcal{L}^{\mathrm{CLIP}} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\min\big(r_t(\theta)\,\hat A_t,\ \ \mathrm{clip}(r_t(\theta),\, 1-\epsilon,\, 1+\epsilon)\,\hat A_t\big)\Big]LCLIP=E[min(rt​(θ)A^t​,  clip(rt​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t​)]
(16.10)

The min⁡\minmin is doing something specific and often described imprecisely. It makes the objective pessimistic. When the advantage is positive, the clipped branch caps how much the objective can improve by increasing rtr_trt​, so past 1+ϵ1+\epsilon1+ϵ there is no longer any gradient pushing the probability up. When the advantage is negative, the same construction caps how much is gained by pushing rtr_trt​ down. In both directions the policy loses its incentive to move far from the policy that collected the data, which is precisely the condition under which the importance weights remain trustworthy.

What the clip does not do is bound the update — a single large step can still leave the region, since the clip only removes the incentive, it does not impose a constraint. That distinction is why PPO implementations also carry an early-stopping criterion on the measured Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence — a standard measure of how far one probability distribution has moved from another — and why the method that preceded it, TRPO [Schulman et al. 2015], enforced a genuine trust region at considerably greater cost per step. PPO is best understood as the cheap approximation to TRPO that turned out to be good enough, and it is the reason a single algorithm now spans Atari, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) for language models, and flow-based robot policies.

16.7Throwing the critic away: group-relative baselines

A critic is expensive. For a 7B-parameter VLA it means a second network of comparable size, with its own optimiser state, its own failure modes and its own warm-up schedule. And on a task whose only reward is binary success at the end of the episode, notice what the critic is actually being asked for: not per-step credit assignment, which a sparse reward cannot support anyway, but a baseline — a number to subtract so the advantage has a meaningful sign.

There is a way to get that baseline for free: roll the same start state out KKK times and let the group's own outcomes supply it. Two variants dominate. GRPO [Shao et al. 2024] standardises the returns within the group; RLOO [Ahmadian et al. 2024] uses each sample's leave-one-out mean, which is the unbiased choice:

A^iGRPO=Ri−mean(R1:K)std(R1:K),A^iRLOO=Ri−1K−1∑j≠iRj\hat A_i^{\mathrm{GRPO}} = \frac{R_i - \mathrm{mean}(R_{1:K})}{\mathrm{std}(R_{1:K})}, \qquad \hat A_i^{\mathrm{RLOO}} = R_i - \frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{j \neq i} R_jA^iGRPO​=std(R1:K​)Ri​−mean(R1:K​)​,A^iRLOO​=Ri​−K−11​j=i∑​Rj​
(16.11)

Both say the same thing in different words: an episode is good insofar as it beat this policy's other attempts at the same problem. No value network, no bootstrapping, no TD error, and no γ\gammaγ — the advantage is a property of the whole episode and is applied identically to every action in it.

The requirement hiding in "roll the same start state out KKK times" is a reset. In simulation that is one function call. On a real robot it means physically restoring the scene KKK times per gradient sample, which is the reset problem of §16.11 and is why this entire family lives in simulation.

16.8The off-policy family, and the overestimation problem

§16.7 removed the critic because it was expensive. This section takes the opposite bet — make the critic the centre of the method rather than an accessory to it — and the reason is the second escape route from §16.5. A policy gradient can only consume data its own policy produced. A QQQ-function cannot tell the difference, and that single property is what makes learning on a real robot affordable at all.

The actor–critic line — DDPG [Lillicrap et al. 2015] → TD3 [Fujimoto et al. 2018] → SAC [Haarnoja et al. 2018] — learns a QQQ-function from a replay buffer and extracts a policy from it. Because the critic is trained by regression onto Bellman targets rather than by a policy-gradient expectation, it does not care which policy produced a transition, and every transition can be reused indefinitely. That is the sample efficiency, and it is what makes real-robot RL possible at all.

Three ideas carry most of the weight.

Overestimation, and twin critics. The Bellman target for a deterministic policy involves a maximisation over actions. A maximum over noisy estimates is biased upwards — whichever action happened to be overestimated is the one selected — and because the target feeds back into the critic, the error compounds rather than averaging out. TD3's response is to keep two critics and take the minimum of the pair in the target, trading a known downward bias for an unbounded upward one, and to update the actor less often than the critic so that the policy is not chasing a target that is still moving.

Entropy, and SAC. SAC maximises reward and policy entropy together:

JSAC(π)=∑tE[ r(st,at)+α H(π(⋅∣st))]J_{\mathrm{SAC}}(\pi) = \sum_{t}\mathbb{E}\Big[\,r(s_t,a_t) + \alpha\,\mathcal{H}\big(\pi(\cdot\mid s_t)\big)\Big]JSAC​(π)=t∑​E[r(st​,at​)+αH(π(⋅∣st​))]
(16.12)

The entropy term is usually explained as "principled exploration", which is true but undersells it. It also keeps the policy from collapsing onto whichever action the critic currently overrates, which is a stability mechanism, and it makes the method strikingly insensitive to hyperparameters — the practical reason SAC became the default for continuous control. Modern implementations tune α\alphaα automatically against a target entropy rather than fixing it.

Prior data, and RLPD. The recipe that actually runs on hardware is RLPD [Ball et al. 2023], which shows that an off-policy algorithm needs surprisingly few changes to exploit offline demonstrations: draw half of every batch from the demonstration buffer and half from online data regardless of their relative sizes, normalise the critic's layers, use an ensemble of critics rather than one, and take many gradient steps per collected transition — a high update-to-data ratio, which is how a small amount of robot experience is made to go a long way. It reports a 2.5× improvement over prior approaches at no additional computational cost, and it is the algorithm underneath both SERL and HIL-SERL in §17.6. The symmetric-sampling detail is the one to remember: it is what stops a growing online buffer from drowning the twenty or thirty demonstrations that made learning possible.

16.9Offline RL and the extrapolation problem

Offline RL removes interaction entirely: a fixed dataset, no environment, one policy at the end. For robotics this is the most attractive setting imaginable — it is the setting you are already in, because every deployed policy is logging rollouts — and it contains one hard problem that all of its machinery addresses.

The problem is that the Bellman target in Eq. (16.4) evaluates QQQ at actions a′a'a′ drawn from the current policy, and in an offline dataset those actions were never taken, so nothing in the data constrains the critic's answer there. A neural network asked to extrapolate will confidently report large values for actions no one has tried. The policy, whose job is to maximise the critic, then walks directly towards them. The failure is not slow degradation; it is divergence, and it happens reliably.

Every offline method is a way of refusing to trust the critic off-support, and they differ in where the refusal is inserted:

  • CQL [Kumar et al. 2020] adds a penalty that explicitly pushes QQQ down on actions sampled from the policy and up on actions that appear in the data, so out-of-distribution values are pessimistic by construction.
  • IQL [Kostrikov et al. 2021] takes the cleaner route of never querying an unseen action at all. It fits VVV by expectile regression on the dataset's own actions, which approximates a maximum over the actions present without ever evaluating one that is absent, and then extracts the policy by advantage-weighted regression:
L2κ(u)=∣κ−1(u<0)∣ u2,u=Q(s,a)−V(s)L_{2}^{\kappa}(u) = \big|\kappa - \mathbb{1}(u < 0)\big|\,u^{2}, \qquad u = Q(s,a) - V(s)L2κ​(u)=​κ−1(u<0)​u2,u=Q(s,a)−V(s)
(16.13)

Read the expectile loss as an asymmetric squared error: at κ=0.5\kappa=0.5κ=0.5 it is ordinary regression and VVV learns the mean; as κ→1\kappa\to1κ→1 underestimates are penalised far more heavily than overestimates and VVV is pulled towards the upper tail of the QQQ values that the data contains. It is a maximum taken by weighting rather than by searching, which is exactly what makes it safe offline.

This matters for VLAs more than its position in this chapter suggests. A VLA fine-tuned on its own logged rollouts — the situation every fleet operator is in — is an offline RL problem whether or not it is described as one, and the choice between "filter to the successes and do behavioural cloning" and "run a conservative offline algorithm" is the subject of §17.4.

16.10Where the reward comes from

In benchmark RL the reward function is given. In manipulation it is a design problem, and usually the hardest one in the system. The available sources, with what each costs:

Table 16.2 — Reward sources for manipulation, and how each fails.
SourceWhat it isCostHow it goes wrong
Simulator predicateA hand-written success test on ground-truth stateFree, if you have a simulatorOnly exists in simulation; inherits the sim-to-real gap wholesale
Binary success classifierA small network trained on labelled images of success and failureA few hundred labels per taskExploitable — the policy optimises the classifier's idea of success, not yours
Human in the loopAn operator who intervenes, and whose intervention is itself the signalOperator time, continuouslyDoes not scale past a small fleet; operator fatigue changes the labels
VLM or process reward modelA vision-language model asked to judge progressInference cost; a model to fine-tuneJudges appearance, not achievement; drifts on unfamiliar scenes
Learned world modelRoll out inside a video predictor and score against a goalA world model, and its errorsThe policy learns to exploit the world model's mistakes
Dense shaped rewardHand-designed distances, alignments, contact termsEngineering per taskThe classic hacking surface; shaping determines the solution more than the goal does

The pattern across §17.5 is that sparse and verifiable beats dense and informative. A binary success signal is hard to satisfy accidentally; a shaped reward for a contact-rich task is a specification of how to do it, and the optimiser will find the cheapest way to satisfy the specification rather than the task. When a dense signal is unavoidable, the defensible structure is a sparse ground truth plus a learned value function that densifies it — which is precisely what RECAP does in §17.7.

Reward hacking is physical here

Robot policies hack rewards in ways language models cannot. The recorded patterns are worth knowing: exploiting a simulator's contact solver to gain energy from a collision; pushing an object out of the camera's field of view so that a misplacement detector stops firing; satisfying a success classifier's viewpoint without achieving the task; and oscillating against a dense alignment term to accumulate shaping reward without ever completing the motion. None of these are visible in a reward curve, which rises smoothly throughout. They are visible in a video. Watch the video.

16.11Why robot RL is hard

Table 16.3 — The five problems, and what the field actually does about each.
ProblemWhyPractical response
Sample costReal time does not accelerate; hardware wears outOff-policy methods; simulation; start from an imitation policy
SafetyExploration breaks robots and objectsConstrained action spaces, impedance limits, human oversight, learn in simulation first
ResetEvery episode needs the scene restoredAutonomous reset policies; reset-free formulations; human operators (expensive)
RewardContact-rich success is hard to specify denselySparse binary success + learned reward models + VLM judges (§16.10)
Sim-to-realContact, friction and deformation are exactly what simulators model worstDomain randomisation, system identification, real-data fine-tuning

The reset row deserves more weight than it usually gets, because it silently determines which algorithms are available. Group-relative methods (§16.7) need KKK rollouts from an identical state; episodic on-policy methods need a clean start every episode. Both assumptions are free in simulation and expensive on hardware, and that single fact — not any property of the optimiser — is why the hardware papers in §17.6 are built on replay buffers and human interventions instead.

The sim-to-real row deserves emphasis because it is the reason this manual is mostly about imitation. The gap is not uniform across physics: rigid-body kinematics simulate well, and contact dynamics, friction and deformation simulate badly. Those are precisely the phenomena that define the tasks in Chapter 9 — flipping a page, splitting stacked cups, extracting a card from a tight slot. You cannot simulate your way to a tactile policy today, which is why T-Rex collected 100 hours of real teleoperation.

The sim-to-real playbook, stated compactly: randomise what you cannot measure (masses, frictions, latencies, textures), identify what you can (link inertias, motor constants), keep the observation space as close to sim-invariant as possible (depth and point clouds transfer better than RGB — another argument for Chapter 6), and reserve real data for the final adaptation stage.

Key takeaways
  1. RL replaces a per-step target with a late scalar. Value functions exist to convert that global signal back into a local one; everything else is a consequence.
  2. VVV says how good a situation is, QQQ how good a situation-plus-action is, AAA whether that action beat the policy's own average. Only AAA has a sign worth acting on, and all three are functions of the policy — change the policy and the critic is partly invalid.
  3. The Bellman equation is a constraint, not a formula, and its self-reference — the target contains the function being fitted — is the source of every stability mechanism in the field.
  4. The policy gradient works by moving the derivative off the environment and onto the policy's own log-probability, so no model of the world is needed. A baseline — any quantity that depends on the state but not on the action — can be subtracted for free, because its contribution averages to zero; subtracting VπV^\piVπ is what turns the return into the advantage.
  5. GAE's λ\lambdaλ dials between a biased one-step estimate and an unbiased Monte Carlo one. Under sparse rewards a small λ\lambdaλ leaves almost no signal, which pushes the field towards episode-level advantages.
  6. On-policy, off-policy and offline differ in where a gradient step's data may come from, and on hardware that difference is measured in robot-hours. Simulation inverts the trade, which is why simulation papers use PPO and GRPO while hardware papers use SAC and RLPD.
  7. PPO's clipped min⁡\minmin makes the objective pessimistic — it removes the incentive to move the ratio far from 1, but does not bound the step.
  8. Group-relative methods replace the critic with KKK rollouts from one reset. Failures become the baseline, and a group whose outcomes all agree gives no gradient at all — which is why RL post-training must start from a policy that already sometimes succeeds.
  9. Offline RL's central problem is critic extrapolation onto actions nobody took. CQL penalises those values; IQL never queries them.
  10. Sparse and verifiable beats dense and informative. Physical reward hacking does not show up in the reward curve — watch the video.
  11. Robot RL is hard for five specific reasons: sample cost, safety, reset, reward, sim-to-real. The gap is worst exactly where manipulation lives, which is why imitation dominates and real tactile data is irreplaceable.

17Reinforcement learning on top of a VLA

Core ideas

The standard shape of a frontier system is pretrain → supervised fine-tune → RL post-training, and RL is the stage where the policy stops being bounded by its demonstrator. Four obstacles stand between Chapter 16 and a working system: a flow or diffusion action head has no cheaply computable likelihood, so Eq. (16.5) cannot be evaluated; an action chunk is not an MDP step; optimising a narrow reward destroys broad pretrained competence; and on real hardware there is no reward function at all until someone builds one. This chapter takes those in turn, sorts the published methods by which obstacle they attack, and gives the paper map — what each system did, to which base policy, with what reward, and what it produced.

17.1What post-training RL is actually for

Three specific things, and it is worth being precise about them because "RL makes it better" is not a design argument.

Exceeding the demonstrator. Behavioural cloning has a ceiling at the data, and §1.2 establishes that it does not even reach it. A demonstrator who succeeds eighty per cent of the time produces a policy that succeeds less often than that. RL optimises the outcome directly, so its ceiling is set by the reward rather than by the operator — which is an improvement exactly insofar as the reward is a good description of the task.

Recovery. This is the structurally interesting one. A teleoperator rarely makes the mistakes the policy will make, so demonstration data contains almost no examples of being in trouble and getting out. The states where a deployed policy most needs guidance are precisely the states least represented in its training set — the compounding-error argument of §1.2 stated from the data side. Any method that trains on the policy's own rollouts fixes this by construction, regardless of which optimiser it uses, and that alone accounts for a large fraction of the gains reported in §17.5.

Reliability over hours. A policy with 95% per-episode success fails roughly once every twenty attempts, which for a task repeated hundreds of times in a shift means constant intervention. The metric that matters in deployment is throughput and uninterrupted run length, not per-trial success (§14.8), and those are dominated by the tail of rare failure modes rather than by the typical case. RL post-training attacks the tail, because the tail is where the low-advantage states are.

17.2The four obstacles

No tractable likelihood. Equation (16.5) needs ∇θlog⁡πθ(a∣s)\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)∇θ​logπθ​(a∣s). For a flow or diffusion policy the action is the endpoint of a KKK-step integration of a learned velocity field, and with a deterministic ODE sampler the policy is a delta function at that endpoint — the density is defined only through a change-of-variables formula that is expensive to evaluate and worse to differentiate. Nothing in Chapter 16's on-policy machinery applies unmodified. §17.3.

A chunk is not a step. Every architecture in this manual emits a chunk of HHH actions at once — 50 for π0\pi_0π0​, 64 for RDT, 8 for OpenVLA-OFT. The MDP whose actions are chunks has a horizon HHH times shorter, which is a gift, but its "action" is a (H×d)(H \times d)(H×d)-dimensional object and its transition takes HHH control steps to resolve. Treating each control step as an MDP step instead means the policy that produced step t+3t{+}3t+3 is not conditioned on the state at t+3t{+}3t+3 at all, which breaks the Markov assumption the gradient rests on. The clean answer is to define the MDP over chunks and learn a critic over chunks too — the construction of Q-chunking [Li et al. 2025], which trains both actor and critic on hhh consecutive actions and gains unbiased nnn-step backups and temporally coherent exploration as a result.

Catastrophic forgetting. The base model has broad competence from web-scale and robot-scale pretraining. Optimising it against a narrow task reward will trade all of that for a few points on the target task, and the loss is invisible unless you measure it on tasks you are not training on. The generic answer is a KL anchor to the reference policy:

L=− E[A^t]  +  β DKL ⁣(πθ ∥ πref)\mathcal{L} = -\,\mathbb{E}\big[\hat A_t\big] \;+\; \beta\, D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\big)L=−E[A^t​]+βDKL​(πθ​∥πref​)
(17.1)

with πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}πref​ the frozen supervised fine-tuning (SFT) checkpoint. The intuition is a trust region in behaviour space rather than parameter space: you may improve, but you must remain recognisably the policy that already worked. This is the same device as RLHF for language models, and carries the same tuning problem — β\betaβ too large and nothing improves, too small and you get reward hacking plus collapse. It is worth noting that several VLA papers report better results with the KL term removed entirely: SimpleVLA-RL drops it, on the reasoning that a binary task reward is not hackable enough to need the anchor, and that the clip alone suffices. Whether that generalises beyond simulation benchmarks with verifiable success predicates is not established.

No reward exists. In simulation the benchmark supplies a success predicate. On hardware somebody has to build one, and §16.10 lists what that costs. This obstacle is the one that most strongly determines system design, and it is why the hardware cluster of §17.6 looks so different from the simulation cluster.

17.3The likelihood problem, and its four answers

The obstacle is narrow and precisely stated: policy gradients need log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log\pi_\theta(a\mid s)logπθ​(a∣s), and a flow-matching head does not provide one. There are exactly four families of response in the published work, and they are ordered here by how much of Chapter 16 each keeps.

One — keep the actions discrete. An autoregressive VLA that emits action tokens (Chapter 12) already produces a categorical distribution per token, so the log-likelihood is a sum of logits and every method in Chapter 16 applies unchanged. This is not a workaround; it is the main reason the OpenVLA line, rather than the π\piπ line, hosts most of the RL post-training literature. RIPT-VLA, SimpleVLA-RL, VLA-RL and TGRPO all sit here.

Two — make the denoising chain an MDP. If the sampler is stochastic, each denoising step is a Gaussian transition with a tractable density, and the chain's total log-likelihood is a sum over steps:

log⁡πθ(a0∣s)  =  ∑k=1Klog⁡N ⁣(ak−1; μθ(ak,k,s), σk2I)\log \pi_\theta\big(a^{0}\mid s\big) \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \mathcal{N}\!\big(a^{k-1};\ \mu_\theta(a^{k},k,s),\ \sigma_k^{2} I\big)logπθ​(a0∣s)=k=1∑K​logN(ak−1; μθ​(ak,k,s), σk2​I)
(17.2)

This is the DPPO construction [Ren et al. 2024]: the denoising process becomes an MDP in its own right, nested inside the environment's MDP, and PPO is applied to the inner chain. The cost is that one environment step now contains KKK policy steps, so the effective horizon is multiplied by the number of denoising iterations. The benefit DPPO reports is unexpected — exploration becomes structured and on-manifold, because perturbing a denoising trajectory produces another plausible action rather than noise.

πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}πRL​ [Chen et al. 2025] carries this into flow-matching VLAs with two variants. Flow-Noise models the denoising process as a discrete-time MDP with a learnable noise network, which makes the log-likelihood exact rather than approximated. Flow-SDE converts the sampling ODE into an equivalent stochastic differential equation (SDE) — the standard construction that leaves the marginals unchanged while making the path stochastic — and interleaves it with environment interaction as a two-layer MDP.

Three — use a method that never forms a ratio. Value-based off-policy learning needs QQQ, not log⁡π\log\pilogπ. ConRFT [Chen et al. 2025] takes this route, combining behavioural cloning with QQQ-learning under a unified consistency-policy objective — a consistency model reaches its output in one or two steps rather than ten, which is what makes the critic's gradient tractable through the sampler at all. Q-chunking is the same instinct applied to the chunk structure.

Four — do not do RL. Convert the reward signal into a supervised label and train by likelihood. Advantage conditioning (RECAP, §17.7) labels each state with its advantage and conditions the policy on it; preference optimisation (GRAPE, §17.4) turns pairs of trajectories into a classification problem; distillation (RLDG) runs RL somewhere the likelihood is tractable and then clones the result into the VLA. All three sidestep the obstacle rather than solving it, and two of the three currently hold the strongest results in the field.

A tempting shortcut that does not work

The obvious idea — take the deterministic ODE output, treat the policy as a Gaussian centred on it with some fixed variance, and compute a likelihood from that — quietly replaces the model you trained with a different one. The flow head's whole purpose (§3.1) is to represent a multimodal action distribution; a Gaussian surrogate has exactly one mode, so the ratio in Eq. (16.9) is computed for a policy that is not the policy being executed. The result is a gradient that is not wrong in an obvious way, which is worse than one that is.

17.4What to do with a trajectory that went wrong

A fleet of robots running a deployed policy produces, every day, a large pile of trajectories most of which succeeded and some of which did not. The question of what to do with the failures is the single most consequential design decision in post-training, and the published answers span a wide range. They are best sorted not by their mathematics but by how far the lesson travels — whether what is learned from one bad trajectory applies only to that trajectory, to trajectories like it, or to every state in its neighbourhood.

1. Discard it. Filter to the successful rollouts and run supervised fine-tuning on them. This is the default in practice, it is trivially safe, and it is strictly worse than it looks: the states it discards are exactly the states where the policy is wrong, which are exactly the states where supervision is worth the most. It also has a ratchet problem — filtering to what the policy already does well reinforces the current behaviour rather than improving it.

2. Let it set the bar. In a group-relative method (§16.7) a failure lowers the group mean, which is what gives its successful siblings a positive advantage. The failures are not merely retained, they are structurally necessary: Figure 16.4 shows that a group with no failures produces no gradient at all. RIPT-VLA [Tan et al. 2025] makes this explicit with dynamic rollout sampling, which discards groups whose outcomes all agree before the update, and a leave-one-out advantage estimator that needs no critic whatsoever.

3. Pair it with a success. Given one good and one bad trajectory from the same initial condition, the improvement direction can be learned as a binary classification rather than as a policy gradient. This is the DPO construction [Rafailov et al. 2023] applied to whole trajectories, which is what GRAPE [Zhang et al. 2024] calls trajectory-wise preference optimisation:

LTPO=− E(τw,τl)[log⁡σ ⁣(βlog⁡πθ(τw)πref(τw)−βlog⁡πθ(τl)πref(τl))]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TPO}} = -\,\mathbb{E}_{(\tau_w,\tau_l)}\left[\log \sigma\!\left(\beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(\tau_w)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\tau_w)} - \beta \log \frac{\pi_\theta(\tau_l)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\tau_l)}\right)\right]LTPO​=−E(τw​,τl​)​[logσ(βlogπref​(τw​)πθ​(τw​)​−βlogπref​(τl​)πθ​(τl​)​)]
(17.3)

Read it as: raise the preferred trajectory's likelihood relative to the reference more than you raise the dispreferred one's. The reference policy appears inside the objective rather than as a separate penalty, so the KL anchor of Eq. (17.1) is built in — one of the reasons the DPO form travels well. What it gives up is magnitude: a preference says τw\tau_wτw​ beat τl\tau_lτl​ and never says by how much, so a near-miss and a catastrophe are the same training signal. GRAPE reports success-rate gains of 51.79% in-domain and 58.20% on unseen tasks, and attributes them specifically to modelling reward implicitly from both successful and failed trials rather than cloning successes.

4. Label it and condition on it. Score every state with a learned value function, convert the score into a label, and train the policy to produce the behaviour associated with each label — including the bad one. Failure stops being a penalty and becomes a class. This is RECAP, §17.7, and it is the most complete inversion of the problem in the literature: the training objective is an ordinary likelihood, and the reinforcement learning lives entirely in how the labels were computed.

5. Let it shape a critic. In an off-policy or offline method the failure is a transition with a low return, and fitting the Bellman equation propagates that backwards to every state that leads into the region. This is the only one of the five in which a single bad trajectory changes the policy's behaviour at states that trajectory never visited — bootstrapping is precisely a mechanism for spreading a local observation over a neighbourhood. It is also, for the same reason, the one that a mislabelled reward damages most.

The highest-value datum is neither a success nor a failure

An expert correction — an operator taking over at the moment the policy goes wrong — is simultaneously a negative label for what the policy did and a positive label for what it should have done instead, at a state the policy actually reaches on its own. No autonomous rollout produces that combination, and no demonstration does either, because the demonstrator never visits the states the policy fails in. This is DAgger's insight (§1.2) arriving from the RL side, and it is why HIL-SERL, ConRFT and RECAP all build their data collection around interventions rather than around trials. If you have an hour of operator time and a choice, spend it on corrections, not on more demonstrations.

17.5The paper map

What follows is every significant published attempt at putting reinforcement learning on top of a robot policy, with the technique it used, why that technique and not another, and what it produced. Read the table down the Algorithm column first: the pattern that emerges is the one Figure 16.3 predicted.
