Four conclusions are visible in that table and are worth stating separately from it.

  1. The algorithm follows the venue, not the architecture. Every simulation entry is on-policy — PPO or GRPO — and every hardware entry is off-policy or not RL at all. This is Figure 16.3's trade playing out: simulation makes samples cheap and stability precious, hardware does the reverse.
  2. The largest reported gains come from the worst starting points. RIPT-VLA's 4% → 97% and SimpleVLA-RL's 17.3% → 91.7% are both one-demonstration regimes. Where the SFT policy is already strong, the same methods move 86.5% to 98.5% — still valuable, but a different kind of claim. RL post-training is partly a data-efficiency technique, and reporting it only as a performance technique overstates the case.
  3. Nobody has run large-scale on-policy RL on a real fleet. The hardware results are either single-task and hours-long (HIL-SERL, ConRFT), or they avoid the policy gradient entirely (RECAP, RLDG). The reset requirement and the reward problem, not the optimiser, are what stands in the way.
  4. Every entry starts from an imitation policy. Without exception. The mechanism is in Figure 16.4: a policy that never succeeds produces no advantage signal, so there is nothing for any of these methods to work with.

17.6The hardware cluster: RL without a simulator

The bottom half of Figure 17.1 is a coherent body of work with a shared recipe, and it is worth reading as one system rather than as separate papers. The components:

  • An off-policy learner with symmetric sampling. RLPD (§16.8) underneath, so that twenty or thirty demonstrations keep contributing to every batch no matter how large the online buffer grows.
  • A binary success classifier as the reward. HIL-SERL trains one per task on a few hundred labelled images: positive reward on completion, zero otherwise. This is the cheapest reward that is hard to hack, and it is the single component that makes the rest possible.
  • A human holding a 6-DoF input device. The operator takes over for up to NNN steps whenever the policy is about to do something wrong or unsafe, and the intervention is written into both the demonstration buffer and the online buffer. It provides three things at once — safety, an automatic reset, and the highest-quality data in the system.
  • Time budgets measured in hours. SERL: 25–50 minutes per policy. HIL-SERL: 1–2.5 hours per task, reaching 100% success on nearly all of thirteen tasks including timing-belt assembly, motherboard and dashboard assembly, IKEA shelf assembly, and dynamic tasks like whipping a Jenga block out of a stack and flipping an object in a pan.

The comparison that makes the case is HIL-SERL's own: behavioural cloning on the same demonstrations reaches 49.7% average success, the RL policy reaches 100%, and it is also 1.8× faster per cycle — the speed gain arriving for free because the reward rewards completion and nothing rewards hesitancy. ConRFT reproduces the shape of the result on a VLA rather than a from-scratch policy: eight real tasks, 45–90 minutes of online fine-tuning each, 96.3% success and 1.9× shorter episodes.

The limitation is equally clear and is not a detail. This recipe learns one task on one setup, with a human present throughout. It does not produce a generalist, and it does not scale past the number of robots you can staff. RLDG's response is the pragmatic one: accept that RL works best narrowly, run it there, and then distil the resulting specialist into the generalist by ordinary supervised fine-tuning — which, it reports, beats fine-tuning the generalist on human demonstrations by up to 40%, and yields a policy that generalises better than the specialist it was distilled from. The generalisation comes from the VLA's pretraining; the quality comes from the RL. Neither could have supplied both.

17.7RECAP: reinforcement learning without a policy gradient

RECAP — RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies — is the most important recent idea in this area, and it follows from first principles rather than from a trick. §10.7 and Figure 10.3 give it as a tensor contract, with the 670M distributional critic drawn alongside the policy; this section is the same system read as a learning algorithm.

The move is to convert reinforcement learning into conditional supervised learning. Instead of pushing gradients to increase the probability of high-advantage actions, train a model that takes the advantage as an input: learn πθ(a∣s,A^)\pi_\theta(a\mid s, \hat A)πθ​(a∣s,A^) on all the data, good and bad, with each state labelled by the advantage it actually achieved. At execution time, condition on high advantage and sample. The policy produces the actions associated with good outcomes because that is what it was trained to do — and, in the paper's words, "at execution time, the advantage-conditioned VLA performs high-advantage actions, resulting in a policy that is better than the data it was trained on."

The machinery underneath is worth stating precisely, because "advantage conditioning" hides three separate design decisions.

The reward is a cost, not a bonus. Each step earns −1-1−1, success earns 000, and failure earns a large negative constant. The return is therefore approximately the negative number of steps still to go, which makes the value function a learned estimate of time remaining — dense, informative and available at every state, from a supervision signal that is nothing but success or failure at the end. This is the "sparse ground truth densified by a value function" pattern of §16.10, and it is the reason RECAP needs no shaped reward.

The critic is distributional. The value model outputs a categorical distribution over B=201B=201B=201 discretised value bins rather than a scalar, trained by cross-entropy against the empirical return. This is the same argument the action head makes in §3.5: a regression to the mean of a multimodal quantity lands between the modes, and a state whose outcome is bimodal — this grasp usually works, occasionally fails badly — has a mean that describes neither case.

The conditioning is a single word. The advantage is thresholded against a task-dependent value εℓ\varepsilon_\ellεℓ​, set to the 30th percentile of the value model's predictions for that task, and enters the prompt as text: "Advantage: positive" or "Advantage: negative". Not a scalar, not an embedding — a token, in the same channel as the task instruction, which is why it costs nothing architecturally and why the field is droppable in the same way as π0.7\pi_{0.7}π0.7​'s context bundle (§10.8).

Three properties follow, and the last is the interesting one:

  • The objective is a likelihood, so there is no intractable density, no importance ratio and no policy-gradient variance. Eq. (10.6) is the whole training loss.
  • Failures are training signal rather than data to be filtered out — position 4 in Figure 17.3. A low-advantage trajectory teaches the model what low advantage looks like, which is information a filtering approach discards entirely.
  • It composes three data sources naturally, which is RECAP's actual recipe: initial demonstrations, real-time expert corrections when the robot errs (on-policy relabelling — DAgger, §1.2, reappearing), and autonomous experience from the robot's own trials. Each is just data with an advantage label, so they can be pooled without reconciling three different training objectives.

Reported results: more than doubling throughput on the hardest tasks and reducing failure rate by a factor of two or more, with demonstrations including 18 hours of uninterrupted espresso-drink making, folding 50 novel laundry items in an unseen home, and assembling and labelling 59 factory boxes. Note the metric being emphasised — throughput and consecutive reliability over hours, not per-trial success (§14.8).

What conditioning cannot do

Advantage conditioning is an instance of a general device: any signal can be turned into a supervised label by conditioning the model on it and asking for the value you want at test time. It is the same manoeuvre as classifier-free guidance, as goal-conditioned imitation, and as the return-conditioned decision transformer. The honest limitation is shared across all of them. A conditioned model can only be asked for behaviour that exists somewhere in its training distribution — it interpolates towards the good end of what it has seen, and cannot search for something better than anything it has seen. A policy gradient, for all its variance and fragility, genuinely can. What RECAP demonstrates is that at present scale the interpolation is worth more than the search, because the data contains far more competence than the policy currently expresses. That is an empirical claim about today's data, not a theorem.

17.8A practical recipe

  1. Do not start with RL. Get a competent imitation policy first. RL from scratch on a real dexterous robot is not a viable plan, and Figure 16.4 gives the mechanical reason: with no successes there is no advantage signal and therefore no gradient.
  2. Decide what you have before deciding on an algorithm. A simulator with a success predicate points to the top of Figure 17.1; a real arm and an operator point to the bottom. The architecture of your action head decides only which of the two sub-branches you take.
  3. Harvest corrections before autonomous trials. Expert corrections on the policy's own states are the highest-information-per-minute data available — they carry both a negative and a positive label at a state the policy actually reaches.
  4. Prefer a sparse, verifiable reward, and densify it with a value function rather than with shaping. Binary task success is hard to hack. A learned value function over a sparse signal gives you the density without giving the optimiser a specification to game.
  5. Anchor to the reference policy — by KL, by the DPO form's implicit reference, or structurally via advantage conditioning — and evaluate on a held-out set of other tasks. Forgetting is invisible on the training task by construction; if you are not measuring it elsewhere, you are not measuring it.
  6. Report the starting point alongside the result. "97% success after RL" means something quite different from a 4% baseline than from an 86% one. Both appear in Table 17.1.
  7. Watch for reward hacking in the physical channel (§16.10), and watch video, not curves.
Key takeaways
  1. Standard shape: pretrain → SFT → RL post-training. RL buys three things imitation cannot — exceeding the demonstrator, recovery behaviour, and reliability over hours.
  2. Four obstacles: flow and diffusion heads have no cheap likelihood; a chunk is not an MDP step; a narrow reward destroys pretrained competence; and on hardware no reward function exists until someone builds one.
  3. Four answers to the likelihood problem: keep actions discrete; make the denoising chain a stochastic MDP (DPPO, πRL\pi_{\mathrm{RL}}πRL​); use a value-based method that never forms a ratio (ConRFT, Q-chunking); or convert the reward into a supervised label (RECAP, GRAPE, RLDG).
  4. Failed trajectories can be discarded, used as a group baseline, paired into preferences, labelled and conditioned on, or fed to a critic — in increasing order of how far the lesson generalises, and in exactly the same order of how badly a wrong reward hurts.
  5. The single most valuable datum is an expert correction: a negative and a positive label together, at a state the policy actually reaches.
  6. Simulation papers are on-policy, hardware papers are off-policy, and nobody has yet run large-scale on-policy RL on a real fleet. That split is about resets and rewards, not optimisers.
  7. The hardware recipe is settled: RLPD with symmetric sampling, a binary success classifier, a human on a 6-DoF device, 1–2.5 hours per task. HIL-SERL: 49.7% → 100%, 1.8× faster cycles. ConRFT on a VLA: 96.3%, 1.9× shorter episodes.
  8. The largest headline gains come from the weakest starting points — RIPT-VLA's 4% → 97% is a one-demonstration result. RL post-training is as much a data-efficiency technique as a performance one.
  9. RECAP converts RL into conditional supervised learning. A per-step cost of −1-1−1 makes the critic a time-to-completion estimate; the critic is distributional over 201 bins; the advantage enters as the words "Advantage: positive" thresholded at the 30th percentile. Throughput more than doubled, failure rate roughly halved.
  10. Conditioning interpolates towards the best behaviour in the data. It cannot search beyond it. That it currently wins is a fact about the data, not a theorem.

18Uncertainty and failure detection

Core ideas

One distinction organises this entire literature. Epistemic uncertainty is the model's ignorance — it is high out of distribution and reducible with more data; it is the signal for "stop, or ask a human". Aleatoric uncertainty is genuine ambiguity in the data — it is high where several actions are valid and irreducible; it is the signal for "spend more compute here", never for "stop". Confusing them produces a detector that halts the robot every time it reaches a legitimate decision point. The beautiful part, from §3.6, is that both are readable off the generative loss you already compute.

18.1The distinction, and why it is not academic

Table 18.1 — The organising distinction.
EpistemicAleatoric
SourceModel ignoranceGenuine multimodality in the data
Reducible by more data?YesNo
High whenOut of distribution; novel sceneSeveral valid strategies; a fork in the task
Correct responseStop; ask for help; collect data hereAllocate more compute; commit to one mode
Read from the flow loss asBias term ∥vθ−v⋆∥2\|v_\theta - v^\star\|^2∥vθ​−v⋆∥2Variance term σ2(xt,t∣c)\sigma^2(\mathbf{x}_t,t\mid\mathbf{c})σ2(xt​,t∣c)

The failure of conflating them is concrete and worth stating: an ensemble-disagreement detector on a multimodal policy flags every legitimate decision point as uncertain, because the ensemble members correctly disagree about which of several valid modes to take. Diff-DAgger's paper makes exactly this criticism of the prior standard: existing methods like Ensemble-DAgger "struggle with highly expressive policies: they often misinterpret policy disagreements as uncertainty at multi-modal decision points"[Diff-DAgger].

18.2The families

Table 18.2 — Six approaches. The last column is the practical question: what does it cost you at runtime?
FamilySignalTypeRuntime cost
EnsemblesDisagreement among independently trained policiesEpistemic (but confounded by aleatoric)N×N\timesN× inference — usually prohibitive
Generative lossThe training objective evaluated at deploymentBoth, separablyOne extra forward pass
Observation densityLikelihood of the observation embedding under a learned densityEpistemicOne small forward pass
Temporal consistencyDisagreement between overlapping action chunksBothFree
Learned headsNetwork predicts its own errorDepends on the targetNegligible
Conformal predictionCalibrated set size at a guaranteed coverage levelWraps any scoreCalibration set only

A generative action head computes a training loss that is a function of the observation, and nothing stops you evaluating that loss at deployment time on observations the robot is actually seeing. On states resembling the training distribution the model fits well and the loss is low; on states it has never seen, the fit is poor and the loss is high. That makes the training objective double as an epistemic score at no extra cost — no ensemble, no second network, no separate calibration model. The cost is that it is a bias signal: it detects unfamiliarity, and says nothing about whether a familiar state is simply ambiguous.

18.3Reading the bias term: the training loss as a score

Diff-DAgger's observation is that the diffusion training objective, evaluated on a deployment state, is an uncertainty estimate. From Eq. (3.8), the measured loss is bias + variance; the bias term is small on in-distribution states where the model has learned the field, and grows out of distribution. So compute the loss you already know how to compute, threshold it, and hand control to the expert when it exceeds the threshold — a robot-gated DAgger that does not need an ensemble.

Reported: task failure prediction improved by 39.0%, task completion rate by 20.6%, and wall-clock time reduced by a factor of 7.8 — the last because you no longer train or run NNN ensemble members. The framing to remember: the training loss is a free, already-calibrated epistemic signal, and the reason it beats ensembles on expressive policies is that it does not mistake multimodality for ignorance.

18.4Reading the variance term: adaptive sampling

The decomposition in §3.6 has two terms, and the previous section used only one of them. The variance term measures something different from error: it measures how much the conditional velocity disagrees with itself at a given state — that is, how multimodal the action distribution is there. That is not a failure signal, and treating it as one is the mistake §18.1 warns about. It is, however, exactly the quantity that tells you how hard the integration will be. Where the field is nearly deterministic the ODE is almost straight and one step suffices; where it is ambiguous the trajectory curves and needs many. A sampler that reads this term can spend its step budget where it is needed instead of uniformly.

AdaFlow[Hu et al., NeurIPS 2024] reads the other term and uses it for a completely different purpose. It "reveals an intriguing connection between the conditional variance of their training loss and the discretization error of the ODEs", and builds a variance-adaptive ODE solver that adjusts step size at inference.

The logic is clean. Where the conditional variance is near zero, the action distribution is effectively deterministic, the marginal velocity field is locally almost constant, and one large Euler step is accurate. Where variance is high, the field bends sharply as probability mass routes toward different modes, and you need fine steps. So: "it identifies the behavioral complexity at a state before allocating computation. If the state has a deterministic choice of action, it outputs the required action rapidly; otherwise, it spends more inference time."

This belongs in a deployment conversation as much as an uncertainty one. It is an adaptive latency mechanism: most states in a manipulation episode are unambiguous (moving through free space toward a known target) and can be resolved in one or two NFEs, with the budget reserved for the genuinely ambiguous moments. Pairing this observation with §14.5 — "the number of function evaluations is the latency budget" — is a strong answer to "how would you make your policy faster without making it worse?"

18.5Observation-side density: logpZO and FAIL-Detect

Everything above scores the action. The complementary approach scores the observation: is the scene I am looking at one I was trained on? FAIL-Detect evaluated OOD-based, smoothness-based and consistency-based strategies and found "a learned flow-matching density estimation model in the observation embedding space performs best", with the novel logpZO score "the most consistently high performance among the considered candidates".

Why the embedding space rather than pixels: a density model over raw images spends its capacity on lighting and texture, and a change in either will read as OOD even though the scene is functionally familiar. The policy's own observation embedding is already invariant to the things the policy has learned to ignore, which is exactly the right notion of "familiar" for this purpose.

The practical argument for having both an action-side and an observation-side detector is that they fail differently. A novel object can produce a confident (low-loss) but wrong action — the action-side signal misses it, the observation-side signal catches it. Conversely, a familiar scene in which the policy has entered a genuinely confusing configuration gives a normal observation density but a high action loss. Fusing them is cheap and strictly better than either.

The cheapest failure signal of all requires no model, no calibration set and no extra forward pass. A policy that has understood the scene produces consistent predictions from one moment to the next: the chunk it generates now, over the timesteps it shares with the chunk it generated a moment ago, should say roughly the same thing. When those two disagree, the policy is unsure — and you already have both chunks, because chunking made you compute them. The test is a distance between overlapping segments, and it costs nothing you had not already paid for.

18.6Temporal consistency: disagreement between overlapping chunks

STAC[Sentinel, CoRL 2024] is the one to implement first because it costs nothing. If you run the policy faster than the chunk duration — which you do, to get closed-loop behaviour — you hold several overlapping chunk predictions for the same future timesteps. STAC "samples multiple action chunks and measures disagreement among their overlapping predictions as an indicator of policy uncertainty."

stSTAC=D(At:t+m(i)⏟predicted at step i,  At:t+m(i+1)⏟predicted at step i+1)s_t^{\mathrm{STAC}} = D\Big(\underbrace{\mathbf{A}^{(i)}_{t:t+m}}_{\text{predicted at step } i},\ \ \underbrace{\mathbf{A}^{(i+1)}_{t:t+m}}_{\text{predicted at step } i+1}\Big)stSTAC​=D(predicted at step iAt:t+m(i)​​​,  predicted at step i+1At:t+m(i+1)​​​)
(18.1)

You are already computing both terms. The distance DDD (MMD between sampled sets, or a simple norm between means) is microseconds. This makes STAC the highest value-per-unit-effort monitor in the entire manual — and note that the same quantity is the chunk-boundary discontinuity of §14.7, so one computation serves two purposes.

Sentinel combines STAC with a VLM-based video question-answering check, and the pairing is deliberate: STAC catches erratic failures — the policy thrashing between incompatible plans — while a VLM asking "has the robot completed the task correctly?" catches quiet failures where the policy confidently and smoothly does the wrong thing. Those are genuinely different error classes and a single detector will not catch both — the paper reports that unifying them detects 18% more failures than either detector alone.

18.7Calibration and acting on uncertainty

A raw score is not actionable; you need a threshold with a known error rate. Conformal prediction supplies one distribution-free: given a calibration set and a target coverage 1−α1-\alpha1−α, take the appropriate empirical quantile of the calibration scores as the threshold, and you obtain a finite-sample guarantee under exchangeability. KnowNo applies this to robot planning to decide when to ask a human for clarification, with a statistical guarantee on task completion. ReconVLA applies conformal prediction directly to VLA action-token outputs for calibrated uncertainty.

The exchangeability caveat

Conformal guarantees require the calibration and test data to be exchangeable. In a deployed robot this is exactly what is violated — the policy's own actions determine subsequent states (that is the covariate-shift problem of §1.2), and the environment changes over an eight-hour shift. So treat conformal thresholds as well-principled heuristics with a good calibration procedure, not as guarantees that survive deployment. Being able to state this caveat is a mark of understanding the method rather than citing it.

Evaluate a detector as a detector, not by task success: report AUROC and AUPRC — area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve and under the precision–recall curve — for predicting failure, and — this is the number that matters operationally — detection lead time, how many timesteps before the failure the alarm fires. A detector that fires simultaneously with the failure is useless; you need enough lead time to stop safely.

What to do when the alarm fires, in order of decreasing preference: (1) slow down, which buys time and often resolves marginal cases on its own; (2) re-plan or re-query at a higher chunk rate; (3) ask a human — robot-gated DAgger, and the collected correction is high-value training data (§17.4); (4) execute a safe retreat; (5) stop. Note that (1) and (3) generate value, while (5) merely avoids damage.

18.8The recommended stack

Assembled from published components, a defensible failure-detection stack for a deployed VLA looks like this:

  1. STAC as the always-on monitor. Free, catches erratic failures, doubles as the chunk-boundary discontinuity metric.
  2. logpZO on observation embeddings as the OOD detector. One small forward pass; catches the confidently-wrong case STAC misses.
  3. The generative loss (Diff-DAgger) as the action-side epistemic signal, gating requests for human help.
  4. Conformal calibration of the fused score on a held-out set, with the exchangeability caveat stated.
  5. A VLM video-QA check at episode or sub-task boundaries (Sentinel) for quiet semantic failures — too slow for the control loop, appropriate at stage transitions.
  6. Hard physical limits below all of it, in the control thread, non-bypassable (§14.2). Learned detectors are probabilistic; force limits are not.
Key takeaways
  1. Epistemic → stop or ask. Aleatoric → spend compute. Confusing them makes the robot halt at every legitimate fork.
  2. Ensembles conflate the two on expressive policies — they read valid multimodality as ignorance. This is Diff-DAgger's stated critique of Ensemble-DAgger.
  3. The generative loss decomposes into both (Eq. 3.8). Diff-DAgger reads the bias term: +39.0% failure prediction, +20.6% completion, 7.8× less wall-clock than ensembles.
  4. AdaFlow reads the variance term and links it to ODE discretisation error → adaptive step size. This is simultaneously an uncertainty method and a latency method.
  5. logpZO (FAIL-Detect): flow-matching density on observation embeddings, not pixels. Catches confident-but-wrong; complementary to action-side scores.
  6. STAC is free — you already compute overlapping chunks. Implement it first. Sentinel adds VLM video-QA to catch quiet failures STAC cannot see.
  7. Conformal prediction calibrates thresholds distribution-free, but exchangeability is violated under closed-loop deployment. Say so.
  8. Evaluate detectors by AUROC and detection lead time. An alarm that fires at the moment of failure is worthless.
Part VII

Synthesis and Reference

Worked system designs, a bank of questions to test understanding against, and the paper map.

19System-design playbooks

Core ideas

Designing a system is won by structure, not by recall. Use the same skeleton every time — requirements → sensors → representation → architecture → data → training stages → deployment → monitoring → what to measure — and state the trade-off at each branch rather than asserting a choice. What follows are four worked designs, each carried through that skeleton end to end.

19.1The skeleton

  1. Pin the requirements. Control rate, latency budget, embodiment, task family, data budget, safety constraints. Ask for what you are not given rather than assuming it.
  2. Choose sensors from the task, not from habit. For each, say what information it adds that nothing else provides.
  3. Choose representations per modality. Rate, dimensionality, token budget.
  4. Choose the fusion architecture from the token-count and rate ratios (Table 8.1).
  5. Design the data strategy. Collection interface, taxonomy, quantity, annotation.
  6. Lay out the training stages and what each buys.
  7. Design deployment: threads, rates, chunk handling, latency budget.
  8. Design monitoring and what each alarm triggers.
  9. Say what you would measure and what would falsify your design.

19.2Design 1 — "Build a tactile-reactive policy for inserting a key and turning a lock"

Requirements. Sub-millimetre alignment; the key is fully occluded by the fingers at the moment that matters; success requires detecting the key seating before applying torque. Control at 300 Hz, policy budget ~150 ms.

Sensors. Head camera for scene and approach; wrist cameras for the last 10 cm; per-fingertip wrench because the decisive event — the key entering the keyway — is invisible to every camera; fingertip deformation maps to distinguish "key edge against the faceplate" from "key in the slot", which produce similar net wrenches but different contact patches. This is the argument from §7.4 and it is the crux of the design.

Representation. Vision 256 tokens/camera. Wrench: a 16-frame window per fingertip through a temporal encoder, not a single sample (§7.3) — the signature of the key finding the keyway is a discontinuity in the force gradient, which one sample cannot contain. Deformation maps through a frozen autoencoder-pretrained truncated ResNet.

Architecture. Two-rate. A vision-conditioned action expert producing chunks at ~5 Hz, and a tactile expert refining at ~30 Hz, either as T-Rex's cascaded flow split or RDP's asymmetric-tokenizer decoder. Justify the choice: cascade if you are training a VLA from a pretrained base, asymmetric tokenizer if you are training task-specific from scratch on limited data. Reject naive token concatenation explicitly and cite the π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile result.

Data. Teleoperation with force feedback to the operator. This matters more than it sounds: Tactile-VLA's observation is that "conventional teleoperation is insufficient… the human operator typically lacks direct force feedback. A policy collected this way would inherently not depend on tactile information." If the demonstrator could not feel, the demonstrations do not contain force-conditioned behaviour, and no architecture recovers it. Use TactAR-style AR feedback or a bilateral rig.

Training. Start from a large pretrained VLA. Mid-train on broad contact-rich primitives (insert, twist, slide, press) across many objects — not just locks, per §9.5. Post-train on ~100 lock demonstrations.

Deployment. 300 Hz control thread; low-pass filtered targets; RTC at chunk boundaries; hard force ceiling below the policy so a mis-aligned key cannot be forced.

What I would measure. Success rate over ≥50 randomised trials; and specifically an ablation with tactile removed — if it does not drop substantially, the tactile pathway is not being used and the whole design is unjustified (§13.4).

19.3Design 2 — "Add a depth camera to an existing RGB VLA without retraining it"

The constraint is the interesting part: without retraining. That rules out native 3D tokens and points at two of the four strategies in Table 6.1.

Preferred: additive side-injection (PointVLA pattern). Freeze the action expert entirely. Train a small point encoder — DP3-style, 3-layer MLP with max-pool, ~59k parameters — whose output is added into a few selected blocks of the frozen expert. Zero-initialise the injection so the model is bit-identical to the original at step zero and can only improve. Train only the encoder and the injection on a small paired dataset.

Alternative: Ego3D positional encoding (SpatialVLA pattern). Inject depth into the existing visual tokens as positional information rather than adding tokens. Elegant because it adds no context length and therefore causes no drowning, but it requires touching the visual tokeniser, which is a deeper intervention than it sounds.

Preprocessing, which will dominate the result. Camera-frame, not world-frame, if the head moves (iDP3). Crop to the workspace. Drop colour — you already have RGB, so the point cloud's job is purely geometric. FPS to 1024 points. Watch out for depth sensor failure on specular and transparent surfaces, which is a real and common source of holes in the cloud; decide explicitly whether to inpaint or to mask.

What I would measure. Not average success — that may not move. Measure specifically on the failure mode depth is supposed to fix: viewpoint generalisation. Evaluate at camera heights and angles not seen in training. If depth does not improve that, it is not earning its place.

19.4Design 3 — "Our policy works in the lab and fails in the field"

A diagnostic exercise. Work through causes in order of prior probability, and say what evidence would distinguish them:

Table 19.1 — Lab-to-field failure triage.
HypothesisDistinguishing testFix
Visual distribution shift (lighting, background)Run the lab task under field lighting; check observation-space density (logpZO)Augmentation, wrist cameras, dual encoders, more diverse backdrops
Viewpoint shiftRe-mount the camera at the lab pose in the fieldExplicit 3D or extrinsics conditioning (§6.7) — not more same-view data
Control-rate or latency changeLog the actual cycle-time histogram in both settingsMatch dtdtdt; resample chunks; RTC (§14.6)
Sensor drift / different unitCompare tared no-contact baselines in both settingsRe-tare; per-sensor normalisation; discretisation (§13.3)
Longer episodes than evaluatedMeasure per-trial success vs. consecutive-repetition reliabilityReliability was never measured; it is a different metric (§14.8)
Causal confusion surfacingFreeze proprioception and see if lab performance is unaffectedProprio dropout; retrain

The general point to make explicitly: "works in the lab, fails in the field" is not one problem, and the first job is to make it one problem by isolating a single variable. Changing the model before doing that is the most common and most expensive mistake.

19.5Design 4 — "You have a 100-hour data-collection budget. Spend it."

This is the design where the intuitive answer is wrong, and the T-Rex dataset result is what shows why.

The intuitive answer is to collect ~9 hours on each of your 11 target tasks. The evidence says do not. T-Rex ran exactly this controlled comparison — 100 hours organised by compositional primitives versus 100 hours of task-specific data from 11 tasks, matched budget — and the primitive-organised set "achieves stronger generalization and zero-shot transfer".

So: build a taxonomy by crossing objects with motor primitives, prune infeasible pairs manually, and collect roughly uniformly over the surviving pairs. T-Rex's numbers: 207 objects × 22 primitives = 4,554 candidates, pruned to 502 feasible pairs, ~16 demonstrations each. Add scene diversity deliberately — multiple backdrops, 0–5 distractors from a large pool, randomised initial poses. Reserve a small budget (~100 demonstrations per target task) for post-training.

Also budget for the things that are not demonstrations: a data-cleaning pass removing unstable tactile measurements, corrupted streams and teleop artefacts (T-Rex does this explicitly); language annotation, which can be VLM-generated from sampled frames plus recorded object and primitive labels but must be human-verified to filter hallucinations; and enough synchronisation engineering that every stream shares a timestamp.

The one-sentence version: at a fixed budget, coverage of compositional primitives beats depth on target tasks, because post-training on ~100 demonstrations is cheap while the priors that make those 100 demonstrations sufficient are not.

Key takeaways
  1. Use the nine-step skeleton. State trade-offs at branches instead of asserting choices.
  2. Justify each sensor by the information nothing else provides — for the lock, the seating event is invisible to cameras.
  3. If the teleoperator could not feel force, the demonstrations contain no force-conditioned behaviour. No architecture recovers it.
  4. To add a modality without retraining: freeze, inject additively, zero-initialise. The model starts bit-identical and can only improve.
  5. Measure the failure mode the change is supposed to fix, not average success.
  6. "Works in lab, fails in field" is several problems. Isolate one variable before touching the model.
  7. At fixed data budget, compositional primitive coverage beats task-specific depth.

20Question bank

Core ideas

A self-check. Each answer is written as an argument rather than a fact, because the reasoning is the part that transfers; if you can reconstruct the reasoning, the numbers follow. Questions marked ◆ are the ones where a memorised answer and real understanding look different.

20.1Foundations

1. Why does behavioural cloning error scale as O(ϵT2)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T^2)O(ϵT2) and DAgger's as O(ϵT)\mathcal{O}(\epsilon T)O(ϵT)?
One factor of TTT is paying an error per step. The second is that after a mistake you are off-distribution for all remaining steps, where the ϵ\epsilonϵ guarantee says nothing — worst case, wrong at every one. Summing gives T2/2T^2/2T2/2. DAgger trains on the learner's own visited states, so the guarantee applies at deployment and the second factor disappears. The win is distributional, not architectural.
2. ◆ "Just collect more data" — why does that not fix multimodality?
Multimodality is aleatoric: it is a property of the data-generating process. More data estimates the same bimodal conditional distribution more precisely, and the mean of a precisely-estimated bimodal distribution still sits between the modes. More data reduces epistemic error only. The fix is a head that represents distributions.
3. Does action chunking remove the need for a generative head?
No — it removes temporal multimodality (step-to-step flip-flopping) by committing to a coherent sub-trajectory, but not chunk-level multimodality. If two operators execute the whole sub-trajectory differently, an L1L_1L1​/L2L_2L2​ head still regresses toward an invalid average. That residual is exactly when you need flow or diffusion. Conversely, when the residual is small — clean unimodal data — OpenVLA-OFT shows L1L_1L1​ + chunking matches diffusion at 25–50× the speed.
4. Why 6D rotation rather than 5, given the theoretical bound is d≥5d\ge5d≥5?
The bound is an existence result about continuous embeddings of RP3\mathbb{RP}^3RP3; it does not provide a usable inverse map. The 6D construction does: regress two 3-vectors, Gram–Schmidt into two orthonormal columns, cross product for the third — continuous, differentiable, always valid, four lines of code. There is no comparably simple continuous map from a raw 5-tuple.
5. Why quantile normalisation and not min–max? And why globally rather than per-timestep?
Min–max lets a single teleop spike compress the entire useful range toward zero; quantiles clip the outlier tails. Per-timestep rescaling within a chunk injects artificial jitter and destroys the temporal smoothness that chunk coherence — and FAST's DCT compression — depend on.

20.2Generative heads

6. ◆ Derive why flow matching works, in three sentences.
Each training pair defines a straight path from noise to action whose velocity is the constant a−x0\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{x}_0a−x0​, so the regression target is trivial. Many pairs pass through the same xt\mathbf{x}_txt​, so the network — unable to distinguish them — converges to the conditional mean E[a−x0∣xt]\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{x}_0\mid\mathbf{x}_t]E[a−x0​∣xt​]. That conditional mean is the marginal velocity field whose flow transports the Gaussian onto the action distribution, so the ambiguity is the mechanism rather than a defect.
7. ◆ "Flow paths are straight, so one Euler step is exact." Correct this.
The conditional paths are straight. The marginal field that you integrate is not — it must curve, because a single noise sample has to be routed toward one of several modes and a globally constant field cannot implement a branching transport map. The correct claim is that it is nearly straight, so ~10 Euler steps have low error versus 50–100 for DDPM. It is a latency argument, not an exactness argument.
8. π0\pi_0π0​ and T-Rex define flow matching with opposite signs. Reconcile them.
Same line, opposite labelling of the ends. π0\pi_0π0​: x0x_0x0​ = noise, x1x_1x1​ = action, target a−x0\mathbf{a}-x_0a−x0​, integrate 0→10\to10→1. T-Rex: x0x_0x0​ = action, x1x_1x1​ = noise, target ϵ−Ademo\boldsymbol\epsilon - \mathbf{A}^{\text{demo}}ϵ−Ademo, integrate 1→01\to01→0 with Δτ=−1/N\Delta\tau=-1/NΔτ=−1/N. Related by t↔1−τt\leftrightarrow1-\taut↔1−τ, which flips the velocity sign. It matters in T-Rex because τ=0\tau=0τ=0 is the executable action, so the tactile expert owning [0,0.4][0,0.4][0,0.4] owns the final, finest part.
9. Why sample flow timesteps from Beta(1.5,1.0)\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1.0)Beta(1.5,1.0) rather than uniform?
Its density ∝τ0.5\propto\tau^{0.5}∝τ0.5 puts more mass at high τ\tauτ — the noisy end in T-Rex's labelling. Errors made there propagate through every remaining integration step; errors near the clean end have few steps left to do damage. You over-sample where mistakes are most costly.
10. ◆ Why does DCT make action tokenisation work, and when does it fail?
Naive per-timestep binning gives long, highly-correlated, low-entropy token sequences on which an autoregressive model learns the trivial copy-previous shortcut. DCT decorrelates: a smooth trajectory concentrates nearly all energy in the lowest one or two coefficients (99% of the energy in the first two, 8× compression at 6% error), producing a sparse zero-heavy stream that BPE compresses into short dense tokens. It fails on high-frequency jitter, where energy spreads across all coefficients and nothing is sparse — which makes token-sequence length a useful diagnostic for how noisy your action data is.
11. Is FAST a learned tokeniser?
No. It is fixed and deterministic — quantile normalise, DCT, quantise, flatten, BPE — with no trainable parameters and no codebook. The policy's objective over its outputs is plain next-token cross-entropy. Contrast with T-Rex's force VQ-VAE, which is learned.
12. Why does very high classifier-free guidance hurt dexterity?
CFG extrapolates: guided=uncond+w(cond−uncond)\text{guided} = \text{uncond} + w(\text{cond} - \text{uncond})guided=uncond+w(cond−uncond). Large www pushes past the conditional mode into low-probability regions, collapsing the action distribution onto extremes. You built a generative head to preserve multimodality and then destroyed it with the sampler. There is a sweet spot, not a monotone improvement.

20.3Architecture

13. ◆ On denoising step 7 of 10 in π0\pi_0π0​, what is recomputed?
Only the small action expert. The VLM's keys and values were computed once and cached; by the block mask, nothing the VLM produces depends on the action tokens, so it never needs re-running. The expert's attention reads the cached KV plus proprioception and the current noisy action tokens.
14. ◆ Beyond losing the KV cache, what breaks if you let the VLM attend to action tokens?
The grounding becomes unstable. The design intent is that the VLM produces a fixed representation of the scene and instruction that conditions action generation. If it attends to the noisy action tokens, that representation becomes a function of the current noise level and the partially-denoised action — it wobbles across the integration steps, and during RL exploration it moves with the policy. Wasteful and destabilising.
15. What does MoT buy, and what does it cost?
Modality-specific weights for every non-embedding parameter (FFN, attention projections, LayerNorm) with global attention. Routing by modality id, so no learned router, no load-balancing loss, no bi-level instability. Cost is memory: 3 experts = 3× parameters at identical per-token FLOPs. You buy capacity with memory rather than compute.
16. Why two vision encoders?
SigLIP is language-supervised, so its features are semantic and text-aligned — needed for instruction following. DINOv2 is self-supervised without language, so its features are spatial and geometric — correspondence, part structure, localisation. A language-aligned encoder is systematically worse at the second because nothing in its training rewarded it. Complementary, not redundant.

20.4Multimodality

17. ◆ T-Rex's π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ + tactile baseline scores 6% versus π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​'s 17%. Explain three mechanisms by which adding information made things worse.
(i) It perturbs a pretrained representation — 60 new unnormalised high-variance dimensions shift the distribution downstream layers expect, damaging a good representation to add a signal the model cannot yet use. (ii) A single-timestep wrench is nearly useless: contact information is in df/dtd\mathbf{f}/dtdf/dt — onset, slip, release — and one sample carries the sensor's drift at full strength while carrying almost none of the dynamics. (iii) Shortcut risk: force correlates strongly with task phase, so the policy can read phase off force magnitude and stop attending to vision — causal confusion with a new variable.
18. ◆ Quantify modality drowning. Then state where the argument is weak.
Under approximately uniform attention, modality mmm receives mass nm/Ln_m/Lnm​/L. With 256 visual tokens, 12 language, 1 proprio, 1 force: L=270L=270L=270 and force gets 1/270. At three cameras, L=782L=782L=782 and force gets 1/782 — adding cameras drowns force, linearly. Gradient to the force encoder scales with that mass, so it trains hundreds of times slower. The weakness: attention is not uniform after training, and a trained network can absolutely attend to force at contact. The argument is about optimisation conditioning at initialisation — a chicken-and-egg problem where an under-trained force encoder gives attention no reason to attend to it — not about expressive capacity. Say that caveat; it is the mark of understanding it.
19. ◆ Why does an additive pre-softmax logit bias rebalance modalities where rescaling the force embedding does not?
Additive before softmax becomes multiplicative after exponentiation: αij∝ebmexp⁡(q⊤k/d)\alpha_{ij}\propto e^{b_m}\exp(q^\top k/\sqrt d)αij​∝ebm​exp(q⊤k/d​), a content-independent factor on every key of that modality (b=+4b=+4b=+4 gives 45× more force attention mass). Rescaling the embedding is renormalised away by the next LayerNorm. Upweighting a force loss term shapes the readout, not the mixing — you can predict force accurately from an auxiliary head while the action head still ignores those tokens. Caveat to state: this is a sound proposal, not a published robotics result; the validated fixes are FACTR's curriculum, ForceVLA's MoE, RDP's asymmetry and T-Rex's dedicated expert.
20. ◆ You make the bias state-conditioned. What is the trap?
Force matters at contact, not in free space, so a static bias wastes attention on noise most of the time — hence a gate. But if you compute the gate from the full attended representation, its input is dominated by vision and you have relocated drowning into the gate. Condition it on a signal that is not itself drowned: raw ∥ft∥\|\mathbf{f}_t\|∥ft​∥ through a tiny dedicated branch, the flow timestep τ\tauτ, or a lightweight proprioception feature.
21. Why does cross-attention beat concatenation for a small modality?
The small modality gets its own queries. A 10×25610\times25610×256 tactile→vision attention matrix gives each tactile token a full normalised distribution over visual tokens, and that normalisation is independent of how many visual tokens there are. Adding a camera does not dilute it. Under concatenated self-attention the tactile token is one key among LLL and its share falls as LLL grows.
22. ◆ Force is kHz and low-dimensional; vision is 30 Hz and high-dimensional. Should you fuse them at the token level?
No. Early token fusion does two damaging things at once: it drowns force by token count, and it resamples force to the vision rate, which aliases away every contact transient above 15 Hz. The second is irreversible — no downstream architecture can recover discarded information. Use a two-rate design: RDP (slow latent diffusion at 1–2 Hz, fast tactile decoder at 20–30 Hz, <1 ms) or T-Rex (action expert once per chunk, tactile expert 4× per chunk). Best of all, make tactile use structurally unavoidable — RDP puts tactile only in the decoder so the latent chunk cannot encode reactive detail.
23. Why does T-Rex quantise force with a VQ-VAE instead of using a continuous embedding?
Drift robustness, stated explicitly in the paper. A continuous embedding moves whenever the sensor's zero point moves with temperature or hours of use. A discrete code does not move at all until drift is large enough to cross a codebook decision boundary — the quantiser acts as a deadband. Quantisation here is a defence against a physical failure mode, not just compression.
24. Why is the VQ reconstruction loss magnitude-weighted?
Most frames in any manipulation dataset are free space. Under a uniform loss the optimal codebook reconstructs silence perfectly, which is the wrong allocation of 64 codes. Weighting by force magnitude directs capacity to contact frames. The paper frames it as preventing "the codebook from collapsing onto dominant non-contact states".
25. Why does DP3's 59k-parameter MLP beat PointNet++ and Point Transformer?
Three reasons. Task mismatch — those encoders preserve fine local geometry for segmentation, while a policy conditioned on a 64-D vector needs coarse spatial layout. Data regime — DP3 trains on 10–40 demonstrations, where a 10M-parameter encoder overfits and a 59k one cannot. Pretraining mismatch — pretrained point encoders saw ShapeNet scans or driving LiDAR, not cropped 1024-point tabletop clouds. The generalisation is not "big encoders are bad" but "match capacity to what the head consumes and the data you have".
26. Why farthest point sampling rather than uniform?
Uniform over-represents dense regions and can miss thin structures, and — worse — produces a different subsample every frame, so the policy sees the world flicker. FPS greedily picks the point farthest from all chosen so far, giving approximately uniform spatial cover and a far more stable subsample.
27. How does PTv3 get locality without kkk-NN?
It sorts. Quantise to a grid, interleave the bits of x,y,zx,y,zx,y,z into a Morton code, sort by it — two codes agreeing in their high bits lie in the same coarse octree cell, so a contiguous window in the sorted sequence is approximately a spatial neighbourhood. Mean consecutive-point distance drops from 2.957 to 0.759, a 3.9× locality improvement, from a sort. PTv3 uses four orderings shuffled across layers, patch size 1024.
28. Does a VLA encode 3D implicitly? Why does more data not fix viewpoint brittleness?
Yes, implicitly — from monocular cues, multiple views giving implicit disparity, and action–image correlations. But there is no 3D inductive bias: nothing enforces that rotating the camera transforms the representation correspondingly. So it is brittle to viewpoint, camera height, and precise depth. More data from the same viewpoint cannot help because the missing quantity is information, not samples. Fix with explicit geometry or genuine extrinsics variation.
29. Why does modality dropout use a learned null embedding rather than zeros?
Zero is a valid value in a normalised feature space, so the network cannot distinguish "the force is zero" from "there is no force sensor". A dedicated per-modality null token signals absence unambiguously. Also drop whole modalities, not tokens — token dropout teaches interpolation, modality dropout teaches solving the task without that sensor.
30. ◆ Why does FACTR's curriculum beat i.i.d. modality dropout?
Dropout is i.i.d., so on any batch the network can still use vision with probability 1−p1-p1−p, and greedy gradient descent preferentially exploits that easy pathway. A curriculum removes it for a sustained period, long enough for the force pathway to become competent, then anneals back. It is an intervention on the optimisation path, not on the loss. +43% generalisation to unseen objects.

20.5T-Rex specifics

31. ◆ Why split the flow trajectory at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​ rather than running two full policies?
Because a flow trajectory already resolves coarse-to-fine: early steps decide gross motion — which object, which strategy — and late steps decide precise values. Gross motion is a slow vision-and-language question; precise values are a fast contact question. The split aligns the trajectory's own structure with the physical structure of the task and gives each half to the modality that can answer it. Both experts regress the same target on disjoint intervals, so it is one coherent trajectory, not two policies to reconcile.
32. What breaks if τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​ is too large or too small?
Too small: the action expert has done too little, so the tactile expert receives insufficient visuomotor prior to refine. Too large: the tactile expert has too little of the trajectory left to incorporate feedback into. The paper reports an interior optimum, exactly as the coarse-to-fine argument predicts.
33. ◆ Why is the KV cache passed to the tactile expert detached?
So the tactile objective cannot backpropagate into the vision tower and corrupt the pretrained visual representation — the exact failure mode of the naive baseline. It is run under torch.no_grad. The cache is also re-encoded at τsplit\tau_{\text{split}}τsplit​ rather than at noise time, so the tactile expert attends to a coherent partially-denoised context.
34. Why train the action expert over the full (0,1](0,1](0,1] when it only deploys on [0.4,1][0.4,1][0.4,1]?
Graceful degradation and pretraining consistency. The paper's reason: it "ensures it retains standalone competency of action generation and keeps consistency with the pretraining paradigm". If tactile sensing fails, the action expert can still produce a complete action alone. A robustness property bought with a choice of sampling range.
35. What is delay augmentation and why does it exist?
Fast ticks run asynchronously, so there is real staleness between the frozen visual cache and the live tactile stream. T-Rex draws δ∼Uniform{0,4,8,12}\delta\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\{0,4,8,12\}δ∼Uniform{0,4,8,12} during training to shift tactile frame indices relative to visual ones, "strictly matching the deployment-time staleness distribution". The principle generalises: train on the distribution you deploy under, including its timing artefacts.
36. ◆ Pretraining alone gives +27, mid-training alone +16, both give +47. What does the super-additivity mean?
The stages are complementary rather than redundant. Human-video pretraining supplies broad visuomotor priors with no grounding in robot-executable contact dynamics; tactile mid-training supplies grounding with nothing to generalise over. Each is a prerequisite for the other paying off, so together they exceed the sum. The operational implication is that you cannot substitute more of one for the other.

20.6Deployment

37. ◆ Naive diffusion runs 50 steps with the VLM at 80% of per-step compute. Switch to 10-step flow matching and cache the VLM. Compute the speedup.
Naive: 50×(0.8+0.2)=5050\times(0.8+0.2)=5050×(0.8+0.2)=50 units. Cached: VLM once (0.8) plus 10 expert steps (10×0.2=210\times0.2=210×0.2=2) =2.8=2.8=2.8 units. 50/2.8≈17.9×50/2.8\approx\mathbf{17.9\times}50/2.8≈17.9×. The point is that it is the product of two independent wins — fewer steps (5×) and not paying the heavy model per step (3.6×). Step reduction alone gives only ~10×.
38. Why do chunk boundaries produce jerks, and why do both naive fixes fail?
Chunk i+1i+1i+1 is computed from an observation at the start of chunk iii, so by the time it executes it was planned for a state that no longer holds. Waiting for it gives a stutter at every boundary — and pausing mid-contact changes the physics, since static and kinetic friction differ. Not waiting gives a discontinuity and potentially an OOD state.
39. ◆ Explain RTC's two weight regions.
The hard freeze on the first ddd steps is correctness: those actions will execute regardless of what the model wants, so generating anything else there is fiction. The soft decay over the next β\betaβ steps is smoothness: it pulls the new chunk toward the old immediately after handover and releases progressively, giving continuity in value and approximately in derivative while restoring the policy's freedom further out. It is inpainting — training-free, works on any flow/diffusion VLA.
40. ◆ Why does inference-time RTC fail at 1–2 NFEs, and what replaces it?
RTC propagates its constraint through the denoising process; that takes iterations. A model never trained to inpaint cannot propagate a consistency constraint in one or two steps, so the seams reappear. The successor moves the conditioning into training — the model takes the committed actions as an input and is trained to stay consistent in one shot. General lesson: inference-time constraints need compute to propagate; without it, the constraint must be trained in.
41. You trained at 20 Hz and deploy at 50 Hz. What happens?
Every implied velocity is scaled by dttrain/dtdeploy=2.5×dt_{\text{train}}/dt_{\text{deploy}} = 2.5\timesdttrain​/dtdeploy​=2.5× too fast. Symptoms: uniformly fast motion, overshoot on every reach, and a policy that works in a simulator stepping at the training rate but fails on hardware. Assert the rate from dataset metadata; if you must change it, resample the chunk temporally rather than executing it faster.
42. What would you instrument at runtime, and what is nearly free?
STAC (disagreement between overlapping chunks) and chunk-boundary discontinuity are both essentially free — you already compute overlapping chunks, and the boundary norm is one subtraction. They also measure exactly what goes wrong at deployment. Add logpZO on observation embeddings (one small forward pass) for OOD, sensor staleness from timestamps, a cycle-time histogram to catch thermal throttling before it becomes a jerk, and hard force limits as a non-bypassable interlock below the policy.
43. ◆ Your policy has 90% per-trial success. Is it deployable?
Probably not, and the distinction that matters is between success rate and reliability. At 90% per trial, the probability of surviving 100 consecutive repetitions is 0.9100≈0.003%0.9^{100}\approx0.003\%0.9100≈0.003%. Industrial deployment is measured in consecutive reps and uninterrupted hours — folding 50 items, 200 consecutive services, an 18-hour run. Reliability is a different and much harder metric, and you must measure it directly rather than extrapolating from per-trial success.

20.7World models, RL, uncertainty

44. Why do JEPAs collapse and Dreamer does not?
Dreamer's decoder forces the latent to retain enough information to reconstruct the observation, which structurally prevents a constant representation. JEPA drops the decoder to avoid spending capacity on unpredictable pixel detail, and thereby admits the degenerate solution fθ≡cf_\theta\equiv\mathbf{c}fθ​≡c, which achieves zero prediction loss with zero information. Every JEPA training trick exists to exclude it.
45. ◆ Give a distribution that passes VICReg but fails SIGReg.
The best answer is LeJEPA's own "X" distribution: draw u∼N(0,1)u\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)u∼N(0,1) and a random sign sss, and emit (u,su)(u, su)(u,su). All the mass lies on two crossing lines, yet the marginals are standard Gaussian and the covariance is exactly the identity, so VICReg scores it 0.0008 — measurably perfect. SIGReg scores 15.3, and the direction sweep shows why: near zero at 0° and 90° (the axes, which is all a moment-based method inspects) and spiking to ~41 and ~53 at 45° and 135°. A second, milder answer is a product of independent Laplace coordinates rescaled to unit variance: unit variance and zero covariance, so VICReg passes, but every projection is too peaked and too heavy-tailed, so the statistic is uniformly elevated rather than spiky.
46. How does SIGReg certify a ddd-dimensional distribution from 1-D projections?
By the Cramér–Wold theorem: a probability distribution is uniquely determined by the set of all its 1-D projections. So "is this cloud N(0,I)\mathcal{N}(0,I)N(0,I)?" reduces to "is every 1-D projection N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1)N(0,1)?" Testing all directions is infeasible, so SIGReg sketches it with random unit directions resampled each iteration, enforcing the property in expectation. Two details earn credit: it averages over directions rather than taking the max, because a max would route gradient through a single direction per step; and the univariate test is Epps–Pulley, which compares empirical and target characteristic functions in a weighted L2L_2L2​ norm. That choice is about optimisation, not statistical power — moment tests are polynomial in the data and explode, CDF tests (Cramér–von Mises, Anderson–Darling) need sorting, while the empirical CF is a bounded mean of complex exponentials with gradient bounded by 4σ2/N4\sigma^2/N4σ2/N.
46b. ◆ You are training a JEPA and the loss is falling beautifully. How do you know it has not collapsed?
You cannot tell from the loss — a collapsed encoder achieves the best loss. In a measured run the naive symmetric variant reached 3.3e−07, four orders of magnitude below every regularised variant, with embedding std 0.058. And you cannot tell from effective rank alone either: that collapsed run scored 11.79, higher than the healthy stop-gradient run's 11.04, because effective rank is computed from the normalised covariance spectrum and is therefore blind to scale — a cloud shrunk uniformly keeps its spectral shape. Track embedding norm and effective rank together, and ideally a linear probe on a downstream task.
47. Why does DPPO apply PPO to the denoising chain rather than the policy directly?
A flow or diffusion policy has no tractable log⁡πθ(a∣s)\log\pi_\theta(a|s)logπθ​(a∣s) — the action is the endpoint of an ODE integration. Treating each denoising step as its own MDP step makes each transition Gaussian with a tractable per-step log-probability, which gives you a valid PPO ratio where the one-shot sample's likelihood was intractable.
48. ◆ How does RECAP avoid the likelihood problem entirely?
It converts RL into conditional supervised learning. Train πθ(a∣s,A^)\pi_\theta(a\mid s,\hat A)πθ​(a∣s,A^) on all data labelled by the advantage actually achieved; at execution, condition on high advantage. No policy gradient, no likelihood, no variance problem. Failures become training signal rather than data to discard, and demonstrations + expert corrections + autonomous experience compose naturally since each is just data with an advantage label. Result: throughput more than doubled, failure rate at least halved, 18-hour autonomous runs.
49. ◆ Why do ensembles make bad uncertainty estimators for expressive policies?
They conflate epistemic and aleatoric. At a legitimate multimodal decision point, ensemble members correctly disagree about which valid mode to take, and a disagreement-based detector reads that as ignorance — flagging every fork in the task. Diff-DAgger makes exactly this criticism and instead reads the generative loss, whose bias term is epistemic and whose variance term is aleatoric, separably. Result: +39.0% failure prediction, +20.6% completion, 7.8× less wall-clock.
50. ◆ AdaFlow and Diff-DAgger both read the flow loss. What is the difference and why does it matter?
Diff-DAgger reads the bias term — epistemic, high out of distribution — and uses it to decide when to stop and ask a human. AdaFlow reads the variance term — aleatoric, high where several actions are valid — and links it to ODE discretisation error, using it to allocate integration steps: few where the action is nearly deterministic, many where it is genuinely multimodal. Same loss, opposite terms, opposite actions. Stopping the robot on high aleatoric uncertainty would halt it at every legitimate decision point.
51. What is the caveat on conformal prediction in a deployed robot?
Conformal guarantees require exchangeability between calibration and test data. Closed-loop deployment violates it by construction — the policy's own actions determine subsequent states, which is precisely the covariate-shift problem — and the environment drifts over a shift. Treat conformal thresholds as well-principled heuristics with a good calibration procedure, not as guarantees that survive deployment.
52. How do you evaluate a failure detector?
AUROC/AUPRC for predicting failure, and — the operationally decisive one — detection lead time: how many timesteps before the failure the alarm fires. A detector that fires simultaneously with the failure has no value; you need enough lead time to stop safely or hand over.

21.5Appendix D — the se(3)↔SE(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)\leftrightarrow SE(3)se(3)↔SE(3) refresher

Section 2.3 established that poses do not live in a vector space. That leaves an obvious question, often asked sideways: if you cannot add rotations, how does a network — which emits nothing but vectors — command one? The answer is the pair of maps between a curved group and its flat tangent space at the identity, and it is worth having the whole picture in one place because almost every practical decision in an action pipeline is a disguised choice about which of the two spaces you are working in.

Two objects, two jobs. SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) is the set of rigid poses — a 4×44\times44×4 homogeneous matrix, a rotation and a translation, curved, closed under composition but not under addition. se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) is its Lie algebra: the tangent space at the identity, an honest 666-dimensional vector space whose elements are twists ξ=(v,ω)\xi=(v,\omega)ξ=(v,ω). You may add twists, scale them, average them, normalise them, put a Gaussian on them and run a diffusion or flow-matching head over them. You may do none of those things to poses.

Table 21.2 — The division of labour. Everything a learning system wants to do happens on the left; everything the robot actually executes lives on the right.
se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) — the algebraSE(3)SE(3)SE(3) — the group
An element isa twist ξ=(v,ω)∈R6\xi=(v,\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{6}ξ=(v,ω)∈R6a pose T=[Rp01]T=\begin{bmatrix}R&p\\0&1\end{bmatrix}T=[R0​p1​]
Add two of them?Yes — it is a vector spaceNo. T1+T2T_1+T_2T1​+T2​ is not a pose
Compose two of them?Not directly (see BCH, below)Yes — matrix product
Natural home fornetwork outputs, deltas, velocities, noise, lossobservations, targets, IK input, what the arm executes
Get to the other side byexp⁡\expexplog⁡\loglog

The bridge is built from a single antisymmetric matrix. The hat operator turns a 333-vector into the generator of a rotation about it, and its inverse, vee (⋅)∨(\cdot)^{\vee}(⋅)∨, reads the vector back out.

ω^=[0−ω3ω2ω30−ω1−ω2ω10]∈so(3),ξ^=[ω^v00]∈se(3)\hat\omega=\begin{bmatrix}0&-\omega_3&\omega_2\\\omega_3&0&-\omega_1\\-\omega_2&\omega_1&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathfrak{so}(3), \qquad \hat\xi=\begin{bmatrix}\hat\omega&v\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathfrak{se}(3)ω^=​0ω3​−ω2​​−ω3​0ω1​​ω2​−ω1​0​​∈so(3),ξ^​=[ω^0​v0​]∈se(3)
(21.1)

ω^\hat\omegaω^ is exactly the matrix for which ω^ x=ω×x\hat\omega\,x=\omega\times xω^x=ω×x, which is the whole intuition: an element of so(3)\mathfrak{so}(3)so(3) is an angular velocity, and applying it to a point gives that point's instantaneous velocity. Integrating that constant angular velocity for unit time is the matrix exponential, and because ω^3=−θ2ω^\hat\omega^{3}=-\theta^{2}\hat\omegaω^3=−θ2ω^ the infinite series collapses into three terms — Rodrigues' formula.

R=exp⁡(ω^)=I+sin⁡θθ ω^+1−cos⁡θθ2 ω^2,θ=∥ω∥R=\exp(\hat\omega)=I+\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}\,\hat\omega+\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^{2}}\,\hat\omega^{2}, \qquad \theta=\lVert\omega\rVertR=exp(ω^)=I+θsinθ​ω^+θ21−cosθ​ω^2,θ=∥ω∥
(21.2)

Going back is the logarithm. The trace of a rotation matrix knows its angle and the antisymmetric part knows its axis, so both fall out in two lines.

θ=cos⁡−1 ⁣(tr⁡R−12),ω^=θ2sin⁡θ(R−R⊤)\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}R-1}{2}\right), \qquad \hat\omega=\frac{\theta}{2\sin\theta}\big(R-R^{\top}\big)θ=cos−1(2trR−1​),ω^=2sinθθ​(R−R⊤)
(21.3)

Lifting this to full poses costs one extra matrix. A twist's rotational part ω\omegaω curves the path that its translational part vvv sweeps out, so the translation that actually accumulates is not vvv but V(ω) vV(\omega)\,vV(ω)v:

exp⁡(ξ^)=[exp⁡(ω^)V(ω) v01],V(ω)=I+1−cos⁡θθ2 ω^+θ−sin⁡θθ3 ω^2\exp(\hat\xi)=\begin{bmatrix}\exp(\hat\omega)&V(\omega)\,v\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad V(\omega)=I+\frac{1-\cos\theta}{\theta^{2}}\,\hat\omega+\frac{\theta-\sin\theta}{\theta^{3}}\,\hat\omega^{2}exp(ξ^​)=[exp(ω^)0​V(ω)v1​],V(ω)=I+θ21−cosθ​ω^+θ3θ−sinθ​ω^2
(21.4)

Note that V(ω)→IV(\omega)\to IV(ω)→I as θ→0\theta\to0θ→0, so for the small rotations that make up a single control step the two spaces very nearly coincide. That is not a coincidence; it is the reason the whole scheme is practical, and we return to it below.

What the exponential actually does: screws

The geometric content of equation (21.4) is the Mozzi–Chasles theorem: every rigid motion is a screw — a rotation about some axis in space combined with a translation along that same axis. Given a twist with ω≠0\omega\neq0ω=0, the axis is the line through q=(ω×v)/∥ω∥2q=(\omega\times v)/\lVert\omega\rVert^{2}q=(ω×v)/∥ω∥2 in direction ω^/θ\hat{\omega}/\thetaω^/θ, and over unit time the motion advances (ω⋅v)/∥ω∥(\omega\cdot v)/\lVert\omega\rVert(ω⋅v)/∥ω∥ along it. The tool frame therefore travels a helix, not a straight line, even for a perfectly constant twist. Dial that in below.

Why a manipulation stack cares

Four consequences, each of which is a real design decision rather than a piece of formalism.

1. A delta action is a twist. Section 2.2 argued for predicting deltas. The correct way to say that is: the policy emits ξt∈se(3)\xi_t\in\mathfrak{se}(3)ξt​∈se(3) and the controller composes it onto the current pose. Composition, never addition:

Tt+1=Tt exp⁡(ξ^t)(body frame),ξt=log⁡ ⁣(Tt−1Tt+1)∨T_{t+1}=T_t\,\exp(\hat\xi_t)\quad\text{(body frame)}, \qquad \xi_t=\log\!\big(T_t^{-1}T_{t+1}\big)^{\vee}Tt+1​=Tt​exp(ξ^​t​)(body frame),ξt​=log(Tt−1​Tt+1​)∨
(21.5)

The right-hand equation is how you build the label: given a demonstration as a sequence of poses, the supervision target for each step is the log of the relative transform. This is the moment where a 666-vector regression target with no singularity and no double cover appears out of a sequence of matrices, and it is why delta actions are natural for learning rather than merely convenient. The side matters: Ttexp⁡(ξ^)T_t\exp(\hat\xi)Tt​exp(ξ^​) expresses the motion in the tool's frame (move forward along my own gripper axis), exp⁡(ξ^)Tt\exp(\hat\xi)T_texp(ξ^​)Tt​ in the base frame. They are different actions, and the two conventions are related by the adjoint, AdT=[Rp^R0R]\mathrm{Ad}_T=\begin{bmatrix}R&\hat p R\\0&R\end{bmatrix}AdT​=[R0​p^​RR​], which maps a body twist to the equivalent spatial one. Getting this backwards is a classic silent bug: the policy trains fine and the robot moves in the wrong direction whenever the wrist is rotated away from the base frame.

2. You cannot add twists either — not exactly. The algebra is a vector space, but exp⁡\expexp is not a homomorphism. Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff says log⁡(exp⁡A^ exp⁡B^)=A+B+12[A,B]+…\log(\exp\hat A\,\exp\hat B)=A+B+\tfrac12[A,B]+\dotslog(expA^expB^)=A+B+21​[A,B]+…, and the bracket term is not small for realistic motions. Concretely, for A=(0.1,0,0 ∣ 0,0,1.2)A=(0.1,0,0\,|\,0,0,1.2)A=(0.1,0,0∣0,0,1.2) and B=(0,0.1,0 ∣ 0.9,0,0)B=(0,0.1,0\,|\,0.9,0,0)B=(0,0.1,0∣0.9,0,0):

A + B                = [0.1 0.1 0.   0.9 0.   1.2 ]
log(exp(A) exp(B))   = [0.039 0.092 0.009 0.787 0.538 1.114]

The third rotational component moved from 000 to 0.5380.5380.538 — over half a radian of rotation about an axis that appears in neither input. That is rotations failing to commute, and it is why action chunks are executed as a sequence of composed transforms rather than summed.

3. Averaging poses requires the log. Temporal ensembling (§14.4) averages overlapping predictions from successive chunks; a diffusion or flow head averages samples; a kkk-nearest-neighbour baseline averages demonstrations. Averaging rotation matrices entrywise leaves the group, as Figure 21.1 shows numerically. The correct operation is the geodesic:

T(α)=T0exp⁡ ⁣(α log⁡(T0−1T1)),Tˉ=arg⁡min⁡T∑i∥log⁡(T−1Ti)∨∥2T(\alpha)=T_0\exp\!\big(\alpha\,\log(T_0^{-1}T_1)\big), \qquad \bar T=\arg\min_{T}\sum_i\big\lVert\log(T^{-1}T_i)^{\vee}\big\rVert^{2}T(α)=T0​exp(αlog(T0−1​T1​)),Tˉ=argTmin​i∑​​log(T−1Ti​)∨​2
(21.6)

The left expression is the constant-twist interpolation — the unique screw taking T0T_0T0​ to T1T_1T1​, traversed at uniform rate. The right is the Karcher (Fréchet) mean, computed by a few iterations of "log everything into the tangent space at the current guess, average, exponentiate back". The same identity supplies the right metric too: the geodesic distance between two rotations is ∥log⁡(R1⊤R2)∨∥\lVert\log(R_1^{\top}R_2)^{\vee}\rVert∥log(R1⊤​R2​)∨∥, which is the honest rotation loss, in radians, that a ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ loss on matrix entries only approximates.

But note what Figure 21.1 measures. At a 15°15°15° separation the componentwise average followed by a Gram–Schmidt repair lands within 0.26°0.26°0.26° of the true geodesic, and at 45°45°45° within 2.4°2.4°2.4°. This is the honest justification for the shortcut that real ensembling code uses — successive chunk predictions disagree by small angles, so the flat approximation is fine there. It is not fine for blending distant modes: the gap grows to 10°10°10° at 90°90°90° and 39°39°39° at 150°150°150°. One subtlety worth knowing, because it is easy to assume otherwise: those numbers depend on the axis, not only the angle. Gram–Schmidt privileges the first column, so it is not equivariant under rotating the frame, and sweeping the axis as well as the angle pushes the worst case to 0.28°0.28°0.28°, 2.6°2.6°2.6°, 12°12°12° and 48°48°48° at the same four separations. The conclusion is unchanged and the reason to state it is that the error is a property of your coordinate convention, not just of how far apart the poses are.

4. The Jacobian is the same object. The manipulator Jacobian J(q)J(q)J(q) maps joint velocities to a twist, ξ=J(q)q˙\xi=J(q)\dot qξ=J(q)q˙​; differential IK inverts it. That is precisely the retargeting machinery §2.5 describes, and a kinematic singularity is exactly a configuration where JJJ loses rank so some direction of se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) becomes unreachable — the concrete form of the "IK can fail" entry in Table 2.1.

Where it breaks, and how that squares with §2.3

exp⁡:so(3)→SO(3)\exp:\mathfrak{so}(3)\to SO(3)exp:so(3)→SO(3) is surjective but not injective, and that is the same topological fact as before wearing different clothes. Rotating by θ\thetaθ and by θ+2π\theta+2\piθ+2π about the same axis give the same matrix, so log⁡\loglog must choose: it returns the representative with ∥ω∥≤π\lVert\omega\rVert\le\pi∥ω∥≤π. Run the maps in anger and you see it immediately:

round trip inside ||w|| < pi : max |log(exp(xi)) - xi| = 6.45e-10
w                    = [0.    0.    3.77]
log(exp(w))          = [ 0.    0.   -2.513]  same rotation, other name

Inside the ball of radius π\piπ the maps are exact inverses to machine precision. Outside it, the logarithm silently hands back a different vector naming the same rotation — and at exactly θ=π\theta=\piθ=π the axis itself becomes ambiguous, because sin⁡θ=0\sin\theta=0sinθ=0 in equation (21.3) and ω\omegaω and −ω-\omega−ω are both correct. A well-behaved implementation special-cases this branch; see code/e_se3.py.

So does the exponential map rescue axis–angle as a regression target? No, and the distinction is the whole answer. As a global target it fails for precisely the reason Table 2.3 gives: the parameterisation is three-dimensional and RP3\mathbb{RP}^3RP3 does not embed continuously in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3, so the cut locus at θ=π\theta=\piθ=π is unavoidable and a physically tiny motion across it demands a large jump in the target. As a local target — a delta over one control step, a few degrees at 303030 Hz — it is excellent, because the whole trajectory stays in a small neighbourhood of the identity where exp⁡\expexp is a diffeomorphism and V(ω)≈IV(\omega)\approx IV(ω)≈I. That is the reconciliation: absolute orientations get 6D + Gram–Schmidt; relative orientations get se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) twists. Both of the representations §2.3 recommends are still what you regress; what this appendix adds is the map that turns a stream of measured poses into those targets and the commanded targets back into motion.

Key takeaways
  1. SE(3)SE(3)SE(3) composes but does not add; se(3)≅R6\mathfrak{se}(3)\cong\mathbb{R}^{6}se(3)≅R6 adds but does not compose. Learning happens in the algebra, execution in the group, and exp⁡\expexp/log⁡\loglog are the only legal doors between them.
  2. A delta action is a twist. Labels come from ξt=log⁡(Tt−1Tt+1)∨\xi_t=\log(T_t^{-1}T_{t+1})^{\vee}ξt​=log(Tt−1​Tt+1​)∨; execution is Tt+1=Ttexp⁡(ξ^t)T_{t+1}=T_t\exp(\hat\xi_t)Tt+1​=Tt​exp(ξ^​t​). Body-frame versus base-frame composition differ by AdT\mathrm{Ad}_TAdT​ and confusing them is a silent, direction-reversing bug.
  3. Average poses with log⁡\loglog, not entrywise — though for the small disagreements seen in temporal ensembling the entrywise average plus a Gram–Schmidt repair is within a fraction of a degree.
  4. log⁡\loglog is a true inverse only for ∥ω∥<π\lVert\omega\rVert<\pi∥ω∥<π; θ=π\theta=\piθ=π is the cut locus where the axis is ambiguous. This is why se(3)\mathfrak{se}(3)se(3) is the right space for small rotations and 6D + Gram–Schmidt for arbitrary ones.

21.6Appendix E — a re-reading order

  1. Chapter 20 in full. The ◆ questions first.
  2. The Core ideas and Key takeaways boxes of Chapters 5–9. That is the multimodal core.
  3. Table 5.2 and Table 9.2 — the π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​+tactile failure and the T-Rex ablations. If only two tables survive the re-reading, these are the two.
  4. Eq. (3.3)–(3.4) and Eq. (3.8): flow matching, and the bias/variance decomposition that connects Chapters 3 and 15.
  5. Eq. (9.2)–(9.4): the cascade, including which end of τ\tauτ is noise.
  6. §8.2 including the caveat in the trap box. The argument's limits matter more than the calculation.
  7. Chapter 14's checklist and the latency-budget table.
  8. Appendix C. Twenty numbers.
  9. Chapter 19's skeleton — work one design end to end without looking at the worked version.
Five sentences worth carrying
  1. "Chunking fixes temporal multimodality; a generative head fixes chunk-level multimodality; they are different problems."
  2. "Flow matching regresses a constant per-sample velocity, and least squares turns that into the marginal field for free — the ambiguity is the mechanism."
  3. "Adding tactile naively cost π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ eleven points of success; the same information encoded temporally and given its own expert is worth thirty over the best visual baseline."
  4. "A force token gets one-in-270 of the attention with one camera and one-in-782 with three — so improving your camera rig drowns your contact signal. That is an argument about optimisation conditioning at initialisation, not about what the architecture can represent."
  5. "Per-trial success is not reliability: 90% per trial is a 0.003% chance of surviving a hundred consecutive repetitions."
